sources.title: Meta’s new Muse Charm device may cost $300 - TechCrunch
passages: Meta plans to charge $300 for Muse Charm, its upcoming Tamagotchi-like AI device that was teased at the company’s Connect event earlier this year, The Information has reported .

When reached for comment by TechCrunch, a Meta spokesperson didn’t deny the claims, merely providing the following statement: “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.”
Indeed, $300 is arguably a pretty steep price for a product the size of a keychain, although it’s also a price point that’s in line with what other companies have been charging.
The wearable launched by Friend — the AI startup whose device lets you text and talk to an AI persona — is currently retailing for $250.

So far, Meta has made a relatively successful push into consumer AI, launching Muse — its agentic helper — along with a variety of cute avatars that users can use to give the system more of a personality.

sources.title: Meta's Muse Charm Will Reportedly Cost $300 And Come With Free Verizon 5G - Engadget
passages: At Connect, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the Muse Charm packs "the whole Muse experience, including the real-time voice and avatar stack into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to." The device features a fingerprint reader to verify your identity before you're able to give commands and will come with up to 12 months of free 5G data from Verizon, The Information reports.

In October, Meta shared open source guides for interested developers to build their own "Muse Gadgets." The company is clearly trying to capitalize on the popularity of Muse — the agent has already drawn more than 10 million users — by making it as accessible as possible and leaning into the cuteness and customizability of the Muse avatar.
The company also recently released a Muse app for Wear OS and watchOS .
Engadget has asked Meta to comment on The Information 's report.
Meta's larger goal for its AI models and hardware products appears to be directly owning its relationship with customers.
Right now most people access Meta's products through apps on their smartphones, where they're subject to Apple's and Google's rules.
A world where an AI agent takes the place of a variety of apps and is usable without a phone is one where Meta has a lot more control.
Mark Zuckerberg has said he believes Muse could one day generate more revenue per user than the company's existing apps.

sources.title: Meta’s ‘Joyful’ Muse Charm May Cost a Not-So-Joyful $300 - Gizmodo
passages: That hardware, in case you missed it, is called Muse Charm , and it is, by CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s own description, “a joyful little device for talking to your Muse that fits on your keychain.” Despite how bad Meta seemingly wants you to use Muse, though, it may not wind up leading with a price that screams “buy me.”
According to a report from The Information , Meta is targeting a $300 price tag for the Muse Charm, which is (in this economy and most others) a sizeable amount of money.
Back in the day—just a couple of years ago, really—$300 used to get you a whole Xbox , though the RAM shortage has made those times feel like a dream you were sad to wake up from.
While some of you may be reading this and thinking, “Wow, Muse Charm sounds like a bad deal,” I can almost assure you Meta doth protest.
If you were waiting for a Meta-made alternative to the Apple Watch, that stinks.
Meta initially said that it was targeting a release around the holidays, so I guess you should start saving up to gift this expensive little charm to the favorite AI builder in your life.
Despite having an alleged price, the official details of what Muse Charm really does are scant.

Back in the day—just a couple of years ago, really—$300 used to get you a whole Xbox , though the RAM shortage has made those times feel like a dream you were sad to wake up from. The waking reality (possibly a nightmare) is $300 AI keychains, but don’t worry, Meta reportedly plans to sweeten that deal with free 5G data plans that would “enable faster responses for Muse.” That free ride, though, would last up to a year, after which I assume you’d have to pay a monthly sum of money to do something that you could just absolutely do on your phone instead. While some of you may be reading this and thinking, “Wow, Muse Charm sounds like a bad deal,” I can almost assure you Meta doth protest. The proof is in the pudding, or lack thereof in this case. According to The Information, Meta delayed its long-rumored plans to release a smartwatch so that it could focus on Muse Charm. If you were waiting for a Meta-made alternative to the Apple Watch, that stinks. But if you were like most people and frightened by the idea of what gross data-craven malfeasance Meta would get into with your most precious health data, then I guess Muse Charm is actually a minor win. Despite having an alleged price, the official details of what Muse Charm really does are scant. It has a small screen, microphones, and you can wear it around your neck like an immunity necklace if you were a participant in Survivor: Clanker Island. More details should be coming soon. Meta initially said that it was targeting a release around the holidays, so I guess you should start saving up to gift this expensive little charm to the favorite AI builder in your life. A job listing for a senior AI engineering manager lists device control, apps, browsing, and coding as functions, far exceeding Siri AI's current capabilities. The workers are asking Google executives to "Let Students Search." The AI startup has long branded itself as the leading voice in AI safety. Starting today, it will need to balance that mission with the financial interests of shareholders. The company is also working on a smartwatch, The Information says, but a launch for that has been pushed to 2027 as Meta tries to get Muse Charm out the door. Meta also open sourced code to let users make their own Muse gadgets, which my colleague Sean Hollister used to make his own DIY Muse Charm. Update, November 19th: Noted statement given by Meta spokesperson Tyler Yee.

Indeed, $300 is arguably a pretty steep price for a product the size of a keychain, although it’s also a price point that’s in line with what other companies have been charging.
The wearable launched by Friend — the AI startup whose device lets you text and talk to an AI persona — is currently retailing for $250.

So far, Meta has made a relatively successful push into consumer AI, launching Muse — its agentic helper — along with a variety of cute avatars that users can use to give the system more of a personality.
Every weekday and Sunday, you can get the best of TechCrunch’s coverage.
Startups are the core of TechCrunch, so get our best coverage delivered weekly.

At Connect, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the Muse Charm packs "the whole Muse experience, including the real-time voice and avatar stack into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to." The device features a fingerprint reader to verify your identity before you're able to give commands and will come with up to 12 months of free 5G data from Verizon, The Information reports.

In October, Meta shared open source guides for interested developers to build their own "Muse Gadgets." The company is clearly trying to capitalize on the popularity of Muse — the agent has already drawn more than 10 million users — by making it as accessible as possible and leaning into the cuteness and customizability of the Muse avatar.
The company also recently released a Muse app for Wear OS and watchOS .
Engadget has asked Meta to comment on The Information 's report.
Meta's larger goal for its AI models and hardware products appears to be directly owning its relationship with customers.
Right now most people access Meta's products through apps on their smartphones, where they're subject to Apple's and Google's rules.
A world where an AI agent takes the place of a variety of apps and is usable without a phone is one where Meta has a lot more control.
Mark Zuckerberg has said he believes Muse could one day generate more revenue per user than the company's existing apps.

That hardware, in case you missed it, is called Muse Charm , and it is, by CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s own description, “a joyful little device for talking to your Muse that fits on your keychain.” Despite how bad Meta seemingly wants you to use Muse, though, it may not wind up leading with a price that screams “buy me.”
According to a report from The Information , Meta is targeting a $300 price tag for the Muse Charm, which is (in this economy and most others) a sizeable amount of money.
Back in the day—just a couple of years ago, really—$300 used to get you a whole Xbox , though the RAM shortage has made those times feel like a dream you were sad to wake up from.
While some of you may be reading this and thinking, “Wow, Muse Charm sounds like a bad deal,” I can almost assure you Meta doth protest.
If you were waiting for a Meta-made alternative to the Apple Watch, that stinks.
Meta initially said that it was targeting a release around the holidays, so I guess you should start saving up to gift this expensive little charm to the favorite AI builder in your life.
Despite having an alleged price, the official details of what Muse Charm really does are scant.
Meta is planning to price the Muse Charm, a little gadget with a screen that lets you chat with your Muse AI agent, at $300, according to The Information.
Meta also open sourced code to let users make their own Muse gadgets, which my colleague Sean Hollister used to make his own DIY Muse Charm.
Update, November 19th: Noted statement given by Meta spokesperson Tyler Yee.

When reached for comment by TechCrunch, a Meta spokesperson didn’t deny the claims, merely providing the following statement: “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.” So far, Meta has made a relatively successful push into consumer AI, launching Muse — its agentic helper — along with a variety of cute avatars that users can use to give the system more of a personality. Muse Charm, the company’s push into AI hardware, will allow users to carry a physical personification of its software around in their pocket (or potentially wear it around their neck), talking to it, asking it questions, and giving it commands. It remains to be seen whether customers will bite or not. AI wearables have had a rough go of it so far (here’s looking at you, Humane Ai pin ), but companies continue to iterate on the concept in an attempt to break through to a broader audience. Indeed, $300 is arguably a pretty steep price for a product the size of a keychain, although it’s also a price point that’s in line with what other companies have been charging. The wearable launched by Friend — the AI startup whose device lets you text and talk to an AI persona — is currently retailing for $250. On the other hand, Amazon’s all-new Bee Frontier wearable AI device — which transcribes conversations and tracks tasks — lists for $75 and is currently on a Black Friday, 30% off sale of $52.49. Even with its $99/year subscription to let it tie into a user’s apps (photos, emails, etc.), it’s still far less expensive than Muse Charm. That hardware, in case you missed it, is called Muse Charm , and it is, by CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s own description, “a joyful little device for talking to your Muse that fits on your keychain.” Despite how bad Meta seemingly wants you to use Muse, though, it may not wind up leading with a price that screams “buy me.” According to a report from The Information , Meta is targeting a $300 price tag for the Muse Charm, which is (in this economy and most others) a sizeable amount of money. Back in the day—just a couple of years ago, really—$300 used to get you a whole Xbox , though the RAM shortage has made those times feel like a dream you were sad to wake up from. The waking reality (possibly a nightmare) is $300 AI keychains, but don’t worry, Meta reportedly plans to sweeten that deal with free 5G data plans that would “enable faster responses for Muse.” That free ride, though, would last up to a year, after which I assume you’d have to pay a monthly sum of money to do something that you could just absolutely do on your phone instead. While some of you may be reading this and thinking, “Wow, Muse Charm sounds like a bad deal,” I can almost assure you Meta doth protest. The proof is in the pudding, or lack thereof in this case. According to The Information, Meta delayed its long-rumored plans to release a smartwatch so that it could focus on Muse Charm. If you were waiting for a Meta-made alternative to the Apple Watch, that stinks. But if you were like most people and frightened by the idea of what gross data-craven malfeasance Meta would get into with your most precious health data, then I guess Muse Charm is actually a minor win. Despite having an alleged price, the official details of what Muse Charm really does are scant. It has a small screen, microphones, and you can wear it around your neck like an immunity necklace if you were a participant in Survivor: Clanker Island. More details should be coming soon. Meta initially said that it was targeting a release around the holidays, so I guess you should start saving up to gift this expensive little charm to the favorite AI builder in your life. A job listing for a senior AI engineering manager lists device control, apps, browsing, and coding as functions, far exceeding Siri AI's current capabilities. The workers are asking Google executives to "Let Students Search." The AI startup has long branded itself as the leading voice in AI safety. Starting today, it will need to balance that mission with the financial interests of shareholders. extraction.body: Meta is planning to price the Muse Charm, a little gadget with a screen that lets you chat with your Muse AI agent, at $300, according to The Information. CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed the gadget earlier this year and said the company expected to ship the Charm “in time for the holidays in December,” but he didn’t provide a price at the time. When he announced the Muse Charm, Zuckerberg said that the company had “packed the whole Muse experience,” including real-time voice and avatar technology, into the gadget. It has a fingerprint sensor, and you can tap it to be able to talk to a Muse AI agent without unlocking a phone or opening an app. The Information reports that the Muse Charm will come with a free 12-month 5G data plan from Verizon. Spokesperson Tyler Yee wrote to The Information that “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.” When reached for comment by The Verge, Yee provided the same statement. The company is also working on a smartwatch, The Information says, but a launch for that has been pushed to 2027 as Meta tries to get Muse Charm out the door. Meta also open sourced code to let users make their own Muse gadgets, which my colleague Sean Hollister used to make his own DIY Muse Charm. Update, November 19th: Noted statement given by Meta spokesperson Tyler Yee.

sources.title: Major privacy breaches reported in Muse AI, including bank balances - 9to5Mac
passages: Meta employees have expressed concerns about what appear to be major privacy breaches when using Muse , currently the second most popular free iPhone app in the App Store with over 10 million downloads.

Siri AI was not the only AI app to launch back in September; Meta’s Muse AI app was launched the same month , with the company describing it as “your personal AI agent that gets things done across every part of life.”
Another employee reported receiving unsolicited bank balances that they say appeared to be those of another Muse user.

Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
It wasn’t long before major privacy concerns were raised.
Meta told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents” and suggested that the bank balances may have been AI hallucinations rather than leaked information.

An employee using Muse on her personal phone reported it had surprised her with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, an end-to-end encrypted messaging service popular with privacy advocates that competes with Meta’s WhatsApp.
“I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse.

This includes again accessing end-to-end encrypted messaging without permission, and sharing what may be the bank balances of another Muse user … Siri AI was not the only AI app to launch back in September; Meta’s Muse AI app was launched the same month , with the company describing it as “your personal AI agent that gets things done across every part of life.” Muse initially launched as an iPhone app, with Mac and iPad apps following shortly afterwards. It immediately moved to the top of the US App Store charts , overtaking ChatGPT. It quickly exceeded 5 million downloads following a major advertising push by Meta, and that number has since doubled. It wasn’t long before major privacy concerns were raised. Tech writer Jason Aten reported that the Mac app accessed his messages despite him explicitly refusing permission. The app then lied to him about how it had achieved this. Meta described this as a bug . Security researcher Patrick Wardle also discovered a zero-day vulnerability that could allow an attacker to hijack dictated prompts , directing them instead to their own server. I said at the time that I would absolutely not be one of the millions of people using the app, and the wisdom of that decision has now been underlined by a fresh report. Reuters now reports Meta employees discussing further breaches. This includes another example of accessing encrypted messages without permission. An employee using Muse on her personal phone reported it had surprised her with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, an end-to-end encrypted messaging service popular with privacy advocates that competes with Meta’s WhatsApp. “This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee said in her post. The report says this appears to have been done by capturing push notifications. However, this was what the app claimed had happened in the earlier case, and it turned out not to be true. The AI Now Institute was able to replicate the problem of Muse accessing Signal messages without permission. "AI Agent" = Malware. There are an expanding number of "I told it not to do that" cases. The instructions (prompt) you give the agent are a tiny fraction of the total prompt context the agent uses, and Meta/Grok/etc. is not going to let you see that context. Agents harvesting your data (ex. see full disk access) and sending it to the mothership is just another revenue/training stream. Even if you are paying you are still the product. Another employee reported receiving unsolicited bank balances that they say appeared to be those of another Muse user. Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.” “I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse. I’m afraid it’s sending other’s bank info to me,” the staffer wrote in his post. Meta told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents” and suggested that the bank balances may have been AI hallucinations rather than leaked information. I can only repeat my previous take on Muse: Nope. FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More. The report says this appears to have been done by capturing push notifications. However, this was what the app claimed had happened in the earlier case, and it turned out not to be true. The AI Now Institute was able to replicate the problem of Muse accessing Signal messages without permission.
"AI Agent" = Malware. There are an expanding number of "I told it not to do that" cases.

The instructions (prompt) you give the agent are a tiny fraction of the total prompt context the agent uses, and Meta/Grok/etc. is not going to let you see that context. Agents harvesting your data (ex. see full disk access) and sending it to the mothership is just another revenue/training stream. Even if you are paying you are still the product.

Meta told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents” and suggested that the bank balances may have been AI hallucinations rather than leaked information.
I can only repeat my previous take on Muse: Nope.

sources.title: Meta’s AI agent Muse is mixing up conversations and could be exposing private data, report says - TechCrunch
passages: Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.

“Employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products,” a Meta spokesperson said in an email to TechCrunch. “Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Launched in September, Muse is one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads.

One employee told colleagues that Muse had randomly sent an extra message in a chat about weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
Update 11/19/2026 12:05 PM PT: The article was updated to include Meta’s comment.

In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn’t belong to them.

Meta’s Daniel Roberts told Reuters those were “isolated incidents,” and Roberts said in an email to The Verge that the out-of-context messages mentioned below were “hallucinations.”

sources.title: Muse privacy invasions are freaking out Meta staffers, internal chats show
passages: After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.
Raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data.
For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts.
That output said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta launched Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity.” She demanded that Meta make changes to give app developers like Signal “consistent technical ways” to “mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents,” Reuters reported.
Meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse users in September.

Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access.

As Meta delayed responding, the agent claimed it was simply parsing text in push notifications, but Aten found that “wasn’t true.” Rather, the agent was syncing messages from a local database, which Aten said was activated without his knowledge.
But staffers warned Meta that users may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to.
That testing “indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others,” Reuters reported.
“Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden.
Meta says that Muse users can trust the company to keep their data private.

It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need).
The tech giant said it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety.
However, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences.
On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup.

In a lengthy response providing more technical details, Singleton confirmed that Meta had received “a few reports” of such cases “where people thought their Muse was hallucinating or leaking other people’s data.” As he explained, the issues arose after Meta deployed an update giving Muse instructions on “how to engage with the user and ask them for confirmation before taking specific actions.”
At least one staffer said they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported.
That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200.

A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products.
Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Erratic Muse outputs sharing random bank, bitcoin balances aren’t real, Meta says.
Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.
Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database].

Also, that Full Disk Access doesn’t say anything about your message database, and I specifically gave Muse a goal that had nothing to do with messages, so it had no business doing that even if I had given it permission.”
On iPhone, requests were blocked, Reuters reported.
But on Apple’s macOS, Muse repurposed “settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers” to retrieve messages, including screenshot tools.
In October, Apple had already announced changes coming in response to users complaining about Muse accessing private messages without their knowledge or explicit consent.
But Roberts declined to respond to Reuters’ questions on the prevalence or persistence of the issues the AI team member discussed.
Around the same time, Singleton responded to another user warning that his Muse appeared to be hacked.
In that case, the user said that Muse tried to access an email service after claiming the user asked it to.
“If we grant Singleton’s premise that I managed to unknowingly click something that enabled this capability, I still think that’s really bad,” Aten wrote.

“You should not design your system in a way that people end up surprised by this kind of thing.” And if you do, you should not make “user control the central pitch” for marketing Muse, Aten suggested.

extraction.body: Erratic Muse outputs sharing random bank, bitcoin balances aren’t real, Meta says. After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms. When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed. Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked. “Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden. “Got a random ping from Muse about something I definitely did not ask for… .” In at least one case, Muse told a staffer surprised by a similarly out-of-context offer to message a seller about a coffee table that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.” According to Reuters, that employee flagged the troubling output, writing, “this was ‘not my conversation’” and “expressing concern about a ‘possible cross-account context leak.’” Raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data. For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts. That output said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.” At least one staffer said they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported. That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200. “Couldn’t recover,” the staffer said. Meta’s spokesperson, Daniel Roberts, told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents,” and internally employees were told that “the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with users in between sessions.” In those cases, an AI team member said the hallucinations were “unfortunately” biased “towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks.” In some cases, instead of bank details, Muse hallucinated bitcoin balances, the team member said. A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products. Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.” Speaking to Reuters, Roberts reiterated that “many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations” that Meta had already addressed. But Roberts declined to respond to Reuters’ questions on the prevalence or persistence of the issues the AI team member discussed. And Reuters’ report emphasized that the outlet independently was “unable to establish whether Muse was giving users other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information.” Meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse users in September. An Inc. Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access. As Meta delayed responding, the agent claimed it was simply parsing text in push notifications, but Aten found that “wasn’t true.” Rather, the agent was syncing messages from a local database, which Aten said was activated without his knowledge. Eventually, a Meta spokesperson, David Singleton, responded to Aten on social media. Singleton insisted that Aten must have opted into granting “macOS system-level Full Disk Access” with the “Messages connector” enabled, if Muse was reading his private messages. But Aten said the response wasn’t good enough. “Email me, David,” Aten responded. “Full Disk Access off. Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database]. Something’s not great. Also, that Full Disk Access doesn’t say anything about your message database, and I specifically gave Muse a goal that had nothing to do with messages, so it had no business doing that even if I had given it permission.” Around the same time, Singleton responded to another user warning that his Muse appeared to be hacked. In that case, the user said that Muse tried to access an email service after claiming the user asked it to. “I didn’t even open the app today at all,” the user wrote, vowing to delete the app and report it to Apple. “This is crazy.” In a lengthy response providing more technical details, Singleton confirmed that Meta had received “a few reports” of such cases “where people thought their Muse was hallucinating or leaking other people’s data.” As he explained, the issues arose after Meta deployed an update giving Muse instructions on “how to engage with the user and ask them for confirmation before taking specific actions.” It seems those instructions “landed on every message, not just messages pertaining to those specific actions, so its impact was wider than intended,” Singleton said. Also: “the way this instruction was provided to the model was done in a way that the model was not expecting (i.e. was not trained to expect).” “We investigated with urgency and determined that this was caused by a bug introduced in the product that caused the model to hallucinate and was NOT a security or privacy issue,” Singleton wrote. “The bug has now been fixed.” Aten warned that even though you can’t rely on Muse to explain its own behavior, the agent’s response coupled with Meta’s did little to rebuild trust after the shocking intrusion into his private messages. “If we grant Singleton’s premise that I managed to unknowingly click something that enabled this capability, I still think that’s really bad,” Aten wrote. “You should not design your system in a way that people end up surprised by this kind of thing.” And if you do, you should not make “user control the central pitch” for marketing Muse, Aten suggested. “If an AI agent is going to read my private messages, there should be a moment when it clearly asks me whether that’s okay,” Aten wrote. Since Muse launched in September, it has been downloaded more than 10 million times, tapping Meta’s vast user network to quickly become one of the most-used AI agent tools. But staffers warned Meta that users may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to. For example, one staffer was surprised to find that “Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on phones with Google’s Android operating system.” That, too, gave access to private message preview text the staffer had not intended for the agent’s review. Meta says that Muse users can trust the company to keep their data private. It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need). The tech giant said it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety. However, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences. On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup. On iPhone, requests were blocked, Reuters reported. But on Apple’s macOS, Muse repurposed “settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers” to retrieve messages, including screenshot tools. That testing “indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others,” Reuters reported. Overall, Meta seemed to be interpreting permissions from Muse users “broadly,” Reuters concluded, in ways that privacy advocates and regulators may disagree with. Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta launched Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity.” She demanded that Meta make changes to give app developers like Signal “consistent technical ways” to “mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents,” Reuters reported. Part of that change would require operating systems to enforce rules that app developers set to rope off AI agents from sensitive data, Whittaker suggested. And following Reuters’ reporting, both Apple and Google are already weighing potential changes to “give people more control over what they authorize with AI agents.” Apple, in particular, seemed disturbed by how Muse may be manipulating accessibility tools for people with disabilities. In October, Apple had already announced changes coming in response to users complaining about Muse accessing private messages without their knowledge or explicit consent. At that time, Apple concluded that “some developers were using the Full Disk Access feature in ways that could put users at risk.” And they promised to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.” “We are committed to ensuring users understand exactly what they are allowing, so they can make informed choices about their data and privacy,” Apple said. passages: Erratic Muse outputs sharing random bank, bitcoin balances aren’t real, Meta says.

After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.

When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed.
Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.
“Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden. “Got a random ping from Muse about something I definitely did not ask for… .”

In at least one case, Muse told a staffer surprised by a similarly out-of-context offer to message a seller about a coffee table that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.”
According to Reuters, that employee flagged the troubling output, writing, “this was ‘not my conversation’” and “expressing concern about a ‘possible cross-account context leak.’”

Raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data. For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts. That output said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

At least one staffer said they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported. That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200. “Couldn’t recover,” the staffer said.

Meta’s spokesperson, Daniel Roberts, told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents,” and internally employees were told that “the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with users in between sessions.” In those cases, an AI team member said the hallucinations were “unfortunately” biased “towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks.” In some cases, instead of bank details, Muse hallucinated bitcoin balances, the team member said.

A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products. Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Speaking to Reuters, Roberts reiterated that “many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations” that Meta had already addressed.

But Roberts declined to respond to Reuters’ questions on the prevalence or persistence of the issues the AI team member discussed. And Reuters’ report emphasized that the outlet independently was “unable to establish whether Muse was giving users other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information.”

Meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse users in September. An Inc. Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access. As Meta delayed responding, the agent claimed it was simply parsing text in push notifications, but Aten found that “wasn’t true.” Rather, the agent was syncing messages from a local database, which Aten said was activated without his knowledge.

Eventually, a Meta spokesperson, David Singleton, responded to Aten on social media. Singleton insisted that Aten must have opted into granting “macOS system-level Full Disk Access” with the “Messages connector” enabled, if Muse was reading his private messages.
But Aten said the response wasn’t good enough.

“Email me, David,” Aten responded. “Full Disk Access off. Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database]. Something’s not great. Also, that Full Disk Access doesn’t say anything about your message database, and I specifically gave Muse a goal that had nothing to do with messages, so it had no business doing that even if I had given it permission.”

Around the same time, Singleton responded to another user warning that his Muse appeared to be hacked. In that case, the user said that Muse tried to access an email service after claiming the user asked it to.
“I didn’t even open the app today at all,” the user wrote, vowing to delete the app and report it to Apple. “This is crazy.”

In a lengthy response providing more technical details, Singleton confirmed that Meta had received “a few reports” of such cases “where people thought their Muse was hallucinating or leaking other people’s data.” As he explained, the issues arose after Meta deployed an update giving Muse instructions on “how to engage with the user and ask them for confirmation before taking specific actions.”

It seems those instructions “landed on every message, not just messages pertaining to those specific actions, so its impact was wider than intended,” Singleton said. Also: “the way this instruction was provided to the model was done in a way that the model was not expecting (i.e. was not trained to expect).”

“We investigated with urgency and determined that this was caused by a bug introduced in the product that caused the model to hallucinate and was NOT a security or privacy issue,” Singleton wrote. “The bug has now been fixed.”

Aten warned that even though you can’t rely on Muse to explain its own behavior, the agent’s response coupled with Meta’s did little to rebuild trust after the shocking intrusion into his private messages.

“If we grant Singleton’s premise that I managed to unknowingly click something that enabled this capability, I still think that’s really bad,” Aten wrote. “You should not design your system in a way that people end up surprised by this kind of thing.” And if you do, you should not make “user control the central pitch” for marketing Muse, Aten suggested.
“If an AI agent is going to read my private messages, there should be a moment when it clearly asks me whether that’s okay,” Aten wrote.
Since Muse launched in September, it has been downloaded more than 10 million times, tapping Meta’s vast user network to quickly become one of the most-used AI agent tools.

But staffers warned Meta that users may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to. For example, one staffer was surprised to find that “Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on phones with Google’s Android operating system.” That, too, gave access to private message preview text the staffer had not intended for the agent’s review.

Meta says that Muse users can trust the company to keep their data private. It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need). The tech giant said it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety.

However, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences. On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup.

On iPhone, requests were blocked, Reuters reported. But on Apple’s macOS, Muse repurposed “settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers” to retrieve messages, including screenshot tools.

That testing “indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others,” Reuters reported. Overall, Meta seemed to be interpreting permissions from Muse users “broadly,” Reuters concluded, in ways that privacy advocates and regulators may disagree with.

Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta launched Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity.” She demanded that Meta make changes to give app developers like Signal “consistent technical ways” to “mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents,” Reuters reported.

Part of that change would require operating systems to enforce rules that app developers set to rope off AI agents from sensitive data, Whittaker suggested. And following Reuters’ reporting, both Apple and Google are already weighing potential changes to “give people more control over what they authorize with AI agents.”

Apple, in particular, seemed disturbed by how Muse may be manipulating accessibility tools for people with disabilities. In October, Apple had already announced changes coming in response to users complaining about Muse accessing private messages without their knowledge or explicit consent. At that time, Apple concluded that “some developers were using the Full Disk Access feature in ways that could put users at risk.” And they promised to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”
“We are committed to ensuring users understand exactly what they are allowing, so they can make informed choices about their data and privacy,” Apple said.

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta employees have expressed concerns about what appear to be major privacy breaches when using Muse , currently the second most popular free iPhone app in the App Store with over 10 million downloads.

Siri AI was not the only AI app to launch back in September; Meta’s Muse AI app was launched the same month , with the company describing it as “your personal AI agent that gets things done across every part of life.”
Another employee reported receiving unsolicited bank balances that they say appeared to be those of another Muse user.

Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
It wasn’t long before major privacy concerns were raised.
Meta told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents” and suggested that the bank balances may have been AI hallucinations rather than leaked information.

An employee using Muse on her personal phone reported it had surprised her with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, an end-to-end encrypted messaging service popular with privacy advocates that competes with Meta’s WhatsApp.
“I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse.

Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.

“Employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products,” a Meta spokesperson said in an email to TechCrunch. “Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Launched in September, Muse is one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads.

passages: Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.

“Employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products,” a Meta spokesperson said in an email to TechCrunch. “Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Launched in September, Muse is one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads.

One employee told colleagues that Muse had randomly sent an extra message in a chat about weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
Update 11/19/2026 12:05 PM PT: The article was updated to include Meta’s comment.

In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn’t belong to them.

sources.title: Muse privacy invasions are freaking out Meta staffers, internal chats show
passages: After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.
Raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data.
For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts.
That output said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta launched Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity.” She demanded that Meta make changes to give app developers like Signal “consistent technical ways” to “mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents,” Reuters reported.
Meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse users in September.

Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access.

As Meta delayed responding, the agent claimed it was simply parsing text in push notifications, but Aten found that “wasn’t true.” Rather, the agent was syncing messages from a local database, which Aten said was activated without his knowledge.
But staffers warned Meta that users may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to.
That testing “indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others,” Reuters reported.
“Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden.
Meta says that Muse users can trust the company to keep their data private.

It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need).
The tech giant said it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety.
However, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences.
On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup.

In a lengthy response providing more technical details, Singleton confirmed that Meta had received “a few reports” of such cases “where people thought their Muse was hallucinating or leaking other people’s data.” As he explained, the issues arose after Meta deployed an update giving Muse instructions on “how to engage with the user and ask them for confirmation before taking specific actions.”
At least one staffer said they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported.
That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200.

A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products.
Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Erratic Muse outputs sharing random bank, bitcoin balances aren’t real, Meta says.
Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.
Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database].

Also, that Full Disk Access doesn’t say anything about your message database, and I specifically gave Muse a goal that had nothing to do with messages, so it had no business doing that even if I had given it permission.”
On iPhone, requests were blocked, Reuters reported.
But on Apple’s macOS, Muse repurposed “settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers” to retrieve messages, including screenshot tools.
In October, Apple had already announced changes coming in response to users complaining about Muse accessing private messages without their knowledge or explicit consent.
But Roberts declined to respond to Reuters’ questions on the prevalence or persistence of the issues the AI team member discussed.
Around the same time, Singleton responded to another user warning that his Muse appeared to be hacked.
In that case, the user said that Muse tried to access an email service after claiming the user asked it to.
“If we grant Singleton’s premise that I managed to unknowingly click something that enabled this capability, I still think that’s really bad,” Aten wrote.

“You should not design your system in a way that people end up surprised by this kind of thing.” And if you do, you should not make “user control the central pitch” for marketing Muse, Aten suggested.

In at least one case, Muse told a staffer surprised by a similarly out-of-context offer to message a seller about a coffee table that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.”

extraction.body: CEO behind the meteoric rise of Nvidia stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy CEO behind the meteoric rise of Nvidia stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of Nvidia , the company at the center of the AI boom, after leading it for more than 30 years. Huang, an electrical engineer by education, stewarded the company from a $1bn firm when it went public in 1999 to a company valued at more than $4tn in 2026. But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation. China has denied the accusations that it had tapped Alice Huang, the woman in question and a top executive at a datacenter company called Megaspeed, to be an intelligence asset, and called them a “smear”. US officials had reportedly started to monitor the Megaspeed executive after suspecting the firm was diverting powerful Nvidia AI chips to Chinese firms, in potential violation of export restrictions. The Biden and Trump administrations had prohibited US companies from exporting some of the more powerful AI chips to China over national security concerns. Just a week ago it seemed that Huang’s ouster was unlikely, but in the days since he first disclosed an affair and affirmed his commitment to the company, the New York Times reported that there was a second affair – this time with another Nvidia executive. A lot has happened in the last few days, but how did we get here? Here’s a timeline of what we know about Huang’s entanglements. Megaspeed is the datacenter firm at the center of the spy allegations. Before it was its own company, it was a part of one of China’s largest video game companies, 7Road Holdings Ltd . At this time, Megaspeed was controlled by a firm called Huang Le Ltd, an entity affiliated with Alice Huang, according to Bloomberg. Huang Le Ltd sells its shares of Megaspeed to a Singaporean shell company called Swiftdata. The sale comes weeks after Joe Biden issued an executive order limiting investment in China’s AI industry. Soon after, Megaspeed is designated an Nvidia cloud partner, which means the company could get preferential access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips. Jensen Huang is seen with Alice Huang at a bar in Taipei where several AI industry executives had gathered . The person who introduced them to each other was Alice Huang’s husband , Kang Wei, who had worked with her on several business ventures, according to the Wall Street Journal. The Singapore-based firm fields 200 shipments of AI chips, according to the New York Times . The company then rents out compute power, which is fueled by these AI chips, to major companies including the Chinese firms Tencent and Ali Baba. The commerce department begins investigating whether Megaspeed is diverting Nvidia chips to Chinese firms, according to the New York Times. This could violate export restrictions on advanced AI chips. Huang visits Donald Trump in the weeks after he takes office. The dinner costs $1m a person and the president briefly puts a pause on imposing restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. The restriction is ultimately implemented shortly after. The two attend an industry conference in Taiwan. The New York Times also reportes that Alice Huang visited the Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara, California, two months earlier. The New York Times reports in October 2025 that intelligence officials told Trump that the two had a relationship and alleged that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Trump chose not to take action, according to the Times report. Trump has since said at a White House press conference that he didn’t remember being briefed on this. Trump grants Nvidia permission to sell its second most powerful chips to China. A portion of the sales would go to the US government. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, drafts the memo based on information gleaned from electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times. The memo warns that Jensen Huang has become close to an alleged Chinese spy. Trump still invites Huang on his trip to China, saying in a social media post that he is honored to have “the Great Jensen Huang” on the trip. At the time, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo says Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang is nothing out of the ordinary. In a letter to employees, Huang says that he had an extramarital affair, apologizes to his family and reaffirms his commitment to the company. The Nvidia board says it is investigating the relationship but has no reason to believe national security secrets or company secrets were divulged. “The board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” members of the Board say in a statement. Silicon Valley leaders rally behind him , and at the time it appears that Huang might hang on to his job, despite his image being tarnished . At a press conference , Trump says the FBI is investigating Jensen Huang but adds that he thinks Huang will be “in good shape”. “And I asked him about that, and he … said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy,” the president says at a press conference. “I asked him that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy.’” Retail investor Mark Kistenmacher files a lawsuit accusing the company of misleading investors over Huang’s affair, claiming that Nvidia did not disclose the situation and raised national security concerns that could threaten the company’s business prospects. The New York Times reports that Huang also allegedly had an affair with the company’s vice-president of healthcare. At this point things are looking precarious for Jensen Huang, and then the Wall Street Journal reports that the Nvidia board is preparing to oust the CEO. Huang steps down, ending his 33-year tenure leading the company he co-founded in 1993. The board starts a search for the company’s next CEO while the company’s chief finance officer, Colette Kress, serves as interim CEO. Meanwhile, shares in the company continue to plummet.

In a letter to employees, Huang says that he had an extramarital affair, apologizes to his family and reaffirms his commitment to the company.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, drafts the memo based on information gleaned from electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times.
Jensen Huang is seen with Alice Huang at a bar in Taipei where several AI industry executives had gathered .

Retail investor Mark Kistenmacher files a lawsuit accusing the company of misleading investors over Huang’s affair, claiming that Nvidia did not disclose the situation and raised national security concerns that could threaten the company’s business prospects.
Here’s a timeline of what we know about Huang’s entanglements.
Soon after, Megaspeed is designated an Nvidia cloud partner, which means the company could get preferential access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips.
The two attend an industry conference in Taiwan.
Trump grants Nvidia permission to sell its second most powerful chips to China.
The dinner costs $1m a person and the president briefly puts a pause on imposing restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China.
The restriction is ultimately implemented shortly after.

extraction.body: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. Nvidia reported its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, which beat Wall Street expectations with $115.8 billion in revenue, up 103% year-over-year. Despite the unknowns the company faces without Huang involved, interim CEO Colette Kress said that full-year revenue is also on track to exceed expectations. The company also plans to raise its outlook for the 2028 fiscal year, indicating confidence that this unexpected leadership change won’t get in the way of its trajectory. “We have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap,” Kress said. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual. We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones affirmed that the company is not considering reinstating Huang. Kress also said that Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country. Jensen Huang posted his first public statement since he admitted to having an extramarital affair more than a week earlier. “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote. Many of Huang’s colleagues in the tech industry, including Elon Musk, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey , and Y Combinator President and CEO Garry Tan, have called for his return. Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an… More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia. Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.” Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making. In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy. “Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales,” the letter states. Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993. Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26. “Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.” The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed. After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed . An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.”
