Nvidia’s board launched an independent probe after a classified U.S. memo alleged Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to target Jensen Huang Nvidia makes the processors that power large-scale artificial intelligence systems. U.S. export controls restrict the most advanced of those chips from reaching China, a country competing directly with the United States in AI development. Those rules reflect bipartisan concern that advanced AI processors could accelerate China’s military and surveillance capabilities, which is what transforms the following sequence of events from a corporate personnel matter into a national-security concern. Jensen Huang leads Nvidia; Alice Huang ran operations at a firm built on Nvidia’s technology. Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led it since. Alice Huang , also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen and former senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data-center company that rents computing capacity built on Nvidia processors. She is not related to Jensen Huang. Media accounts placed the pair together in Taiwan multiple times before any investigation became public. During 2024 and into 2025 , media reports said Jensen Huang and Alice Huang were photographed or observed socializing in Taiwan, where Jensen Huang was born. Those encounters later became relevant to intelligence reporting about the alleged operation, according to the cited reporting. No public statement about the relationship was identified in that reporting from either Nvidia or U.S. officials at the time. U.S. and Singapore authorities opened parallel inquiries into whether Nvidia chips reached China through a third-party operator. In October 2025 , U.S. and Singapore authorities reportedly examined whether Megaspeed had helped Chinese firms, including Alibaba, obtain Nvidia processors in potential violation of U.S. export restrictions. Export controls are rules that restrict the sale of certain advanced technology to designated countries, entities, or uses, sometimes requiring government licensing. Officials also questioned the disposition of Nvidia equipment observed at a Malaysian facility, according to the supplied reporting, as AI is making enforcement of such controls increasingly complex. The president learned of the intelligence months before it became public. The New York Times reported that in late 2025, President Trump was informed about intelligence concerning Alice Huang’s alleged activities and her relationship with Jensen Huang. No publicly announced action was identified in the cited reporting at that time. The briefing was not disclosed until reporting on the broader story emerged in late October 2026. U.S. officials reportedly concluded Alice Huang was working for Chinese intelligence, though that assessment has not been independently verified. In spring 2026 , U.S. officials reportedly circulated a classified memo alleging that Alice Huang was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security , the country’s primary civilian intelligence agency. The memo allegedly stated she had been recruited to gather information about Jensen Huang . It also alleged she was tasked with influencing Nvidia’s commercial position on advanced chip sales to China. This is an intelligence assessment reported by news organizations citing unnamed officials; it is not an established legal or investigative finding. Such government restrictions on technology access echo broader debates over how authorities worldwide handle sensitive data, as seen when Europe restricts major cloud providers from handling sensitive public-sector information. A New York Times report in October 2026 brought the relationship and the investigation into public view. On October 29, 2026 , the New York Times disclosed that U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year and that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Nvidia responded by characterizing Jensen Huang’s interactions with her as ordinary customer-related contact. A rapid sequence of corporate and political responses followed that disclosure. Three House committee chairmen asked Jensen Huang to appear before a closed-door session. The chairmen of the House Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and the House Intelligence Committee formally requested a closed-door briefing from Jensen Huang, with the request reported around November 5, 2026. The letter cited concerns about Chinese access to sensitive U.S. technology and possible infiltration of American technology companies. No public response from Huang or Nvidia was identified in the cited reporting at that time. The CEO issued a public apology on November 8 without naming Alice Huang. On November 8, 2026 , Jensen Huang publicly acknowledged that he had been unfaithful, apologizing to his wife, children, Nvidia employees, and the company. He linked his statement to national-security concerns described in media coverage but did not identify Alice Huang by name. He also withdrew from planned appearances at the ElevenLabs Summit and the Anthropic CEO Forum. The board acted the following day, saying it had no immediate evidence of compromised secrets. On November 9, 2026 , Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation into whether Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The board said it had no reason at that stage to believe Nvidia secrets or U.S. national security had been compromised. President Trump said Jensen Huang should remain CEO. Trump later added that Huang had told him he did not know Alice Huang was allegedly a spy. Beijing’s Foreign Ministry called the espionage claim “groundless speculation.” On November 10, 2026 , China’s Foreign Ministry characterized the allegation that Alice Huang was working for Chinese intelligence as a smear and rejected it as unsubstantiated. Corporate records, as reported by media, separately identified her as a Megaspeed director from March to November 2023. The supplied reporting does not identify her current status or whereabouts. The investigation is ongoing, and several core questions have no public answers yet. Public reporting has not established what information Alice Huang allegedly obtained, whether any Nvidia proprietary information was transferred, or whether export-control violations involving Megaspeed occurred. Nvidia’s independent board investigation has not released findings. Congressional committees have requested access to Jensen Huang ; no hearing date has been announced, and until investigators publish conclusions or authorities bring formal charges, the espionage allegations remain unproven. Media accounts placed the pair together in Taiwan multiple times before any investigation became public.

During 2024 and into 2025 , media reports said Jensen Huang and Alice Huang were photographed or observed socializing in Taiwan, where Jensen Huang was born. Those encounters later became relevant to intelligence reporting about the alleged operation, according to the cited reporting. No public statement about the relationship was identified in that reporting from either Nvidia or U.S. officials at the time.
U.S. and Singapore authorities opened parallel inquiries into whether Nvidia chips reached China through a third-party operator.

In October 2025 , U.S. and Singapore authorities reportedly examined whether Megaspeed had helped Chinese firms, including Alibaba, obtain Nvidia processors in potential violation of U.S. export restrictions. Export controls are rules that restrict the sale of certain advanced technology to designated countries, entities, or uses, sometimes requiring government licensing. Officials also questioned the disposition of Nvidia equipment observed at a Malaysian facility, according to the supplied reporting, as AI is making enforcement of such controls increasingly complex.
The president learned of the intelligence months before it became public.

The New York Times reported that in late 2025, President Trump was informed about intelligence concerning Alice Huang’s alleged activities and her relationship with Jensen Huang. No publicly announced action was identified in the cited reporting at that time. The briefing was not disclosed until reporting on the broader story emerged in late October 2026.
U.S. officials reportedly concluded Alice Huang was working for Chinese intelligence, though that assessment has not been independently verified.

In spring 2026 , U.S. officials reportedly circulated a classified memo alleging that Alice Huang was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security , the country’s primary civilian intelligence agency. The memo allegedly stated she had been recruited to gather information about Jensen Huang . It also alleged she was tasked with influencing Nvidia’s commercial position on advanced chip sales to China. This is an intelligence assessment reported by news organizations citing unnamed officials; it is not an established legal or investigative finding. Such government restrictions on technology access echo broader debates over how authorities worldwide handle sensitive data, as seen when Europe restricts major cloud providers from handling sensitive public-sector information.
A New York Times report in October 2026 brought the relationship and the investigation into public view.

On October 29, 2026 , the New York Times disclosed that U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year and that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Nvidia responded by characterizing Jensen Huang’s interactions with her as ordinary customer-related contact. A rapid sequence of corporate and political responses followed that disclosure.
Three House committee chairmen asked Jensen Huang to appear before a closed-door session.

The chairmen of the House Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and the House Intelligence Committee formally requested a closed-door briefing from Jensen Huang, with the request reported around November 5, 2026. The letter cited concerns about Chinese access to sensitive U.S. technology and possible infiltration of American technology companies. No public response from Huang or Nvidia was identified in the cited reporting at that time.
The CEO issued a public apology on November 8 without naming Alice Huang.

On November 8, 2026 , Jensen Huang publicly acknowledged that he had been unfaithful, apologizing to his wife, children, Nvidia employees, and the company. He linked his statement to national-security concerns described in media coverage but did not identify Alice Huang by name. He also withdrew from planned appearances at the ElevenLabs Summit and the Anthropic CEO Forum.
The board acted the following day, saying it had no immediate evidence of compromised secrets.

On November 9, 2026 , Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation into whether Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The board said it had no reason at that stage to believe Nvidia secrets or U.S. national security had been compromised. President Trump said Jensen Huang should remain CEO. Trump later added that Huang had told him he did not know Alice Huang was allegedly a spy.
Beijing’s Foreign Ministry called the espionage claim “groundless speculation.”

On November 10, 2026 , China’s Foreign Ministry characterized the allegation that Alice Huang was working for Chinese intelligence as a smear and rejected it as unsubstantiated. Corporate records, as reported by media, separately identified her as a Megaspeed director from March to November 2023. The supplied reporting does not identify her current status or whereabouts.
The investigation is ongoing, and several core questions have no public answers yet.

Public reporting has not established what information Alice Huang allegedly obtained, whether any Nvidia proprietary information was transferred, or whether export-control violations involving Megaspeed occurred. Nvidia’s independent board investigation has not released findings. Congressional committees have requested access to Jensen Huang ; no hearing date has been announced, and until investigators publish conclusions or authorities bring formal charges, the espionage allegations remain unproven.

What began as reports of his close relationship with Alice Huang, suspected of spying for China, has developed into a wider national security and corporate governance issue. The controversy has drawn attention from US lawmakers, prompted an independent investigation by Nvidia's board and reportedly raised questions about Huang's future at the company. Here is how the events unfolded, from the initial investigations into a Singapore-based business to the latest developments surrounding the Nvidia chief. October 2025: Chip smuggling investigation The controversy has its roots in investigations into Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company and Nvidia customer. In October 2025, authorities in the US and Singapore began investigating the company over suspicions that it was helping Chinese businesses obtain Nvidia chips despite American export restrictions. According to reports, Megaspeed had been renting computing capacity to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other companies. Concerns grew after a US Commerce Department official visiting one of its data centres in Malaysia in 2024 reportedly discovered Nvidia equipment still packed in boxes, raising questions about whether the hardware was being shipped elsewhere rather than deployed for cloud computing. Huang had also been seen socialising with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang in Taiwan as early as 2024. Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is not related to the Nvidia CEO. 2025: Trump reportedly briefed on Huang's relationship US President Donald Trump was reportedly briefed towards the end of 2025 about intelligence findings concerning Alice Huang and her relationship with the Nvidia chief. Huang has been an ally of Trump and has repeatedly argued that the US government should allow Nvidia to expand its business in China. May 2026: Secret memo raises concerns about suspected Chinese spy The matter took another turn in spring 2026 when a confidential memo circulated among Trump administration officials. The document reportedly identified Alice Huang as a suspected Chinese intelligence operative working for China's Ministry of State Security. According to reports, Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the preparation of the memo. It warned policymakers about her alleged relationship with Huang and the potential implications for American national security. October 29, 2026: Huang's relationship with Alice Huang becomes public The controversy became public when the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, who was already under investigation by American authorities. He also said Nvidia would expect the US government to inform the company if it believed someone posed a threat to American industry. They said Congress needed to establish whether US national security had been compromised through potential Chinese infiltration. The Information reported that the company had facilitated purchases worth $7.5 billion, including chips restricted under US export controls. Separately, Bloomberg reported that Nvidia's head lawyer, Tim Teter, had intervened during a 2025 US government investigation into suspected chip smuggling involving Megaspeed.

coreStoryFacts.text: Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of Nvidia , the company at the center of the AI boom, after leading it for more than 30 years.
At this point things are looking precarious for Jensen Huang, and then the Wall Street Journal reports that the Nvidia board is preparing to oust the CEO.
In a letter to employees, Huang says that he had an extramarital affair, apologizes to his family and reaffirms his commitment to the company.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, drafts the memo based on information gleaned from electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times.
Jensen Huang is seen with Alice Huang at a bar in Taipei where several AI industry executives had gathered .

Retail investor Mark Kistenmacher files a lawsuit accusing the company of misleading investors over Huang’s affair, claiming that Nvidia did not disclose the situation and raised national security concerns that could threaten the company’s business prospects.
Here’s a timeline of what we know about Huang’s entanglements.
Soon after, Megaspeed is designated an Nvidia cloud partner, which means the company could get preferential access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips.
The two attend an industry conference in Taiwan.
Trump grants Nvidia permission to sell its second most powerful chips to China.
The dinner costs $1m a person and the president briefly puts a pause on imposing restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China.
The restriction is ultimately implemented shortly after.
U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.
This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times.
Jensen Huang posted his first public statement since he admitted to having an extramarital affair more than a week earlier.
Nvidia reported its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, which beat Wall Street expectations with $115.8 billion in revenue, up 103% year-over-year.
Despite the unknowns the company faces without Huang involved, interim CEO Colette Kress said that full-year revenue is also on track to exceed expectations.
The company also plans to raise its outlook for the 2028 fiscal year, indicating confidence that this unexpected leadership change won’t get in the way of its trajectory.

Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him.
Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report.
Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.
Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said .
As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.

Huang, an electrical engineer by education, stewarded the company from a $1bn firm when it went public in 1999 to a company valued at more than $4tn in 2026. But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation. China has denied the accusations that it had tapped Alice Huang, the woman in question and a top executive at a datacenter company called Megaspeed, to be an intelligence asset, and called them a “smear”. US officials had reportedly started to monitor the Megaspeed executive after suspecting the firm was diverting powerful Nvidia AI chips to Chinese firms, in potential violation of export restrictions. The Biden and Trump administrations had prohibited US companies from exporting some of the more powerful AI chips to China over national security concerns. Just a week ago it seemed that Huang’s ouster was unlikely, but in the days since he first disclosed an affair and affirmed his commitment to the company, the New York Times reported that there was a second affair – this time with another Nvidia executive. A lot has happened in the last few days, but how did we get here? Here’s a timeline of what we know about Huang’s entanglements. Megaspeed is the datacenter firm at the center of the spy allegations. Before it was its own company, it was a part of one of China’s largest video game companies, 7Road Holdings Ltd . At this time, Megaspeed was controlled by a firm called Huang Le Ltd, an entity affiliated with Alice Huang, according to Bloomberg. Huang Le Ltd sells its shares of Megaspeed to a Singaporean shell company called Swiftdata. The sale comes weeks after Joe Biden issued an executive order limiting investment in China’s AI industry. Soon after, Megaspeed is designated an Nvidia cloud partner, which means the company could get preferential access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips. Jensen Huang is seen with Alice Huang at a bar in Taipei where several AI industry executives had gathered . The person who introduced them to each other was Alice Huang’s husband , Kang Wei, who had worked with her on several business ventures, according to the Wall Street Journal. The Singapore-based firm fields 200 shipments of AI chips, according to the New York Times . The company then rents out compute power, which is fueled by these AI chips, to major companies including the Chinese firms Tencent and Ali Baba. The commerce department begins investigating whether Megaspeed is diverting Nvidia chips to Chinese firms, according to the New York Times. This could violate export restrictions on advanced AI chips. Huang visits Donald Trump in the weeks after he takes office. The dinner costs $1m a person and the president briefly puts a pause on imposing restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. The restriction is ultimately implemented shortly after. The two attend an industry conference in Taiwan. The New York Times also reportes that Alice Huang visited the Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara, California, two months earlier. The New York Times reports in October 2025 that intelligence officials told Trump that the two had a relationship and alleged that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Trump chose not to take action, according to the Times report. Trump has since said at a White House press conference that he didn’t remember being briefed on this. Trump grants Nvidia permission to sell its second most powerful chips to China. A portion of the sales would go to the US government. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, drafts the memo based on information gleaned from electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times. The memo warns that Jensen Huang has become close to an alleged Chinese spy. Trump still invites Huang on his trip to China, saying in a social media post that he is honored to have “the Great Jensen Huang” on the trip. At the time, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo says Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang is nothing out of the ordinary. In a letter to employees, Huang says that he had an extramarital affair, apologizes to his family and reaffirms his commitment to the company. The Nvidia board says it is investigating the relationship but has no reason to believe national security secrets or company secrets were divulged. “The board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” members of the Board say in a statement. Silicon Valley leaders rally behind him , and at the time it appears that Huang might hang on to his job, despite his image being tarnished . The New York Times reports that Huang also allegedly had an affair with the company’s vice-president of healthcare. At this point things are looking precarious for Jensen Huang, and then the Wall Street Journal reports that the Nvidia board is preparing to oust the CEO. Huang steps down, ending his 33-year tenure leading the company he co-founded in 1993. The board starts a search for the company’s next CEO while the company’s chief finance officer, Colette Kress, serves as interim CEO. Meanwhile, shares in the company continue to plummet.

extraction.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is at the centre of a controversy that has moved well beyond his personal life. What began as reports of his close relationship with Alice Huang, suspected of spying for China, has developed into a wider national security and corporate governance issue. The controversy has drawn attention from US lawmakers, prompted an independent investigation by Nvidia's board and reportedly raised questions about Huang's future at the company. Here is how the events unfolded, from the initial investigations into a Singapore-based business to the latest developments surrounding the Nvidia chief. October 2025: Chip smuggling investigation The controversy has its roots in investigations into Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company and Nvidia customer. In October 2025, authorities in the US and Singapore began investigating the company over suspicions that it was helping Chinese businesses obtain Nvidia chips despite American export restrictions. According to reports, Megaspeed had been renting computing capacity to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other companies. Concerns grew after a US Commerce Department official visiting one of its data centres in Malaysia in 2024 reportedly discovered Nvidia equipment still packed in boxes, raising questions about whether the hardware was being shipped elsewhere rather than deployed for cloud computing. Huang had also been seen socialising with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang in Taiwan as early as 2024. Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is not related to the Nvidia CEO. 2025: Trump reportedly briefed on Huang's relationship US President Donald Trump was reportedly briefed towards the end of 2025 about intelligence findings concerning Alice Huang and her relationship with the Nvidia chief. However, the president did not take action following the briefing, according to the New York Times. Huang has been an ally of Trump and has repeatedly argued that the US government should allow Nvidia to expand its business in China. May 2026: Secret memo raises concerns about suspected Chinese spy The matter took another turn in spring 2026 when a confidential memo circulated among Trump administration officials. The document reportedly identified Alice Huang as a suspected Chinese intelligence operative working for China's Ministry of State Security. According to reports, Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the preparation of the memo. It warned policymakers about her alleged relationship with Huang and the potential implications for American national security. October 29, 2026: Huang's relationship with Alice Huang becomes public The controversy became public when the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, who was already under investigation by American authorities. Nvidia pushed back against suggestions that their interactions were unusual. Company spokesperson John Rizzo said meetings with customers were part of Huang's responsibilities as chief executive, adding that he interacted with thousands of customer executives every year. He also said Nvidia would expect the US government to inform the company if it believed someone posed a threat to American industry. November 5, 2026: Republican lawmakers seek answers from Huang Three Republican committee chairmen asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing with members of their committees. The lawmakers included John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. Their letter highlighted concerns about China's access to sensitive American technology and information. They said Congress needed to establish whether US national security had been compromised through potential Chinese infiltration. Although he did not identify Alice Huang by name, he acknowledged the national security concerns raised in media reports. Huang also confirmed that Nvidia's board had initiated an independent investigation, pledging to cooperate fully and reiterating his commitment to protecting the company and American national security. The admission had an immediate impact on investor sentiment, with Nvidia shares falling more than 5 per cent the following day. US President Donald Trump also weighed in on the controversy on November 8. Despite acknowledging that he did not know all the details, Trump described Huang as a 'fine person' and said he believed the Nvidia chief should remain in charge of the company. November 9-10, 2026: More about Alice Huang's business network Further reporting shed light on the business connections between Alice Huang, her family and Nvidia's chip supply chain. According to reports, Alice Huang and her family had established a network of businesses across China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia processors. One of these was Shanghai Century Litong, a Chinese company founded in 2023 that reportedly became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips. The Information reported that the company had facilitated purchases worth $7.5 billion, including chips restricted under US export controls. Separately, Bloomberg reported that Nvidia's head lawyer, Tim Teter, had intervened during a 2025 US government investigation into suspected chip smuggling involving Megaspeed.

relevantPassages.text: California Attorney General Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia on Thursday as part of a probe of whether the company's advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China i n contravention of U.S. export restrictions, his office said.
The probe comes a week after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang , a suspected Chinese spy.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," the attorney general said.

"My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law," Bonta said.
Nvidia shares are down 22% in the nine trading days since Huang admitted to an extramarital affair.
The stock is on pace for its seventh straight weekly loss, shedding 38% of its value over that stretch.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bonta's subpoena.

sources.title: California attorney general issues subpoena to Nvidia over chip sales to China - AOL.com
passages: California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) issued subpoenas to Nvidia regarding reports that the company sold advanced AI computer chips to China, his office announced Thursday.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said in a press release.

“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”
Bonta's office said the information obtained through the subpoenas will help it to determine if Nvidia, which is based in Santa Clara, Calif., violated state law through its alleged actions.
“Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China,” the spokesperson added.

Following the Huang scandal, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents Thursday showing the U.S. authorized the sale of nearly 900,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips to Defense Department-designated Chinese military companies.
The Securities and Exchanges Commission (SEC) is reportedly leading a similar probe into Nvidia, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this week — citing people familiar with the matter.
The investigations into the tech giant come after its co-founder and former CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned after being accused of having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

coreStoryFacts.text: California has served an investigative subpoena on the AI chip designer Nvidia in the wake of a scandal that ended in the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang.

The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public.
Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday.
Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November.

Earlier this week, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang after the longtime Nvidia boss and co-founder issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return, as some tech leaders including Elon Musk campaigned on his behalf.

The Commerce statement said it and the Justice Department “have an extremely strong track record of bringing semiconductor smugglers to justice” and “will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred.”

The explanations have reassured few, and criticism has not been limited to Democrats. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also blamed the Commerce Department for failing to blacklist Megaspeed over possible export violations.

Harvey C. Jones, Nvidia’s chairman, has said the company’s board unanimously accepted Jensen Huang’s resignation and does not intend to reinstate him — despite calls for exactly that from President Trump and other administration allies.

“While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company’s employees, customers, partners, and shareholders,” Jones said. Colette Kress, Nvidia’s executive vice president and chief financial officer, is now serving as interim CEO.

In a post on X on Tuesday, Jensen Huang said he “did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA,” had “made serious mistakes” in his personal life and “created problems for” the company’s board.

But he also said he had received many messages from supporters encouraging him to return as CEO, which he would consider if the board wanted him to help the company as it “navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics.”

California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta on Thursday subpoenaed the AI chip manufacturer Nvidia — asking whether its advanced chips or other confidential information went to China and whether it had misled investors and the public on the issue.
Nvidia, which is based in Santa Clara, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The subpoena follows Nvidia co-founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang's resignation after it was revealed he was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and after Bonta's office sued OpenAI — another AI company — over similar claims that it had misled the public about its advanced AI capabilities.
Bonta's office said information gleaned from the subpoenas "will help the California Department of Justice evaluate whether Nvidia's actions violated California law."

Bonta said both Nvidia's and Jensen's conduct raises "bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," and his office intends to determine whether it did so.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said.

The shake-up at Nvidia has rattled markets . It has also raised questions about the company's handling of its AI chips, whether it facilitated those chips being smuggled to China, and whether the U.S. Commerce Department was complicit or incompetent in failing to prevent such diversions despite its stated interest in preventing the powerful chips — crucial for supporting AI models — from getting into Chinese hands.

Democrats on the House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committees in particular are investigating whether the administration's response to Nvidia's chip business was improperly influenced by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick — whose family has holdings in the company.

"Did Trump's Commerce Secretary compromise our national security so that his family firm could profit from hundreds of millions of dollars invested in Nvidia?" Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee asked on social media Thursday.

The Democrats' questions hold extra weight since their party won control of both chambers of Congress in this month's midterm elections, which will give them greater investigative and subpoena powers come January.

In a Commerce statement shared by Lutnick on Monday, the department acknowledged an ongoing, years-long investigation into the Singaporean company Megaspeed and allegations it may have skirted export rules governing Nvidia's powerful AI chips. It credited that investigation to its own "excellent work" under Lutnick.

The department noted that the investigation involved an interview of former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman with whom Nvidia's Huang acknowledged having an affair and who U.S. intelligence officials suspect may be a Chinese spy.

The Commerce statement said it and the Justice Department "have an extremely strong track record of bringing semiconductor smugglers to justice" and "will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred."
Megaspeed has said that Alice Huang left the company in 2025 and that it is conducting its own internal investigation .

The explanations have reassured few, and criticism has not been limited to Democrats. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also blamed the Commerce Department for failing to blacklist Megaspeed over possible export violations.

Harvey C. Jones, Nvidia's chairman, has said the company's board unanimously accepted Jensen Huang's resignation and does not intend to reinstate him — despite calls for exactly that from President Trump and other administration allies.

"While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company's employees, customers, partners, and shareholders," Jones said. Colette Kress, Nvidia's executive vice president and chief financial officer, is now serving as interim CEO.

On Tuesday, the company announced third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year prior. The company's reporting has raised additional questions, as it stopped reporting Singapore revenue separately just as scrutiny of Megaspeed was arising.

In a post on X on Tuesday, Jensen Huang said he "did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA," had "made serious mistakes" in his personal life and "created problems for" the company's board.

But he also said he had received many messages from supporters encouraging him to return as CEO, which he would consider if the board wanted him to help the company as it "navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics."
This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

sources.title: California subpoenas Nvidia over possible China chip transfers and investor disclosures - Superpower Daily
passages: Nvidia faces a California investigation into both possible transfers of advanced chips or confidential information to China and what it told investors about those risks.
Attorney General Rob Bonta issued the company an investigative subpoena on November 19, 2026, seeking information to assess whether its conduct violated state law.
The investigation is not a finding that any transfer occurred or that Nvidia misled investors; its outcome could clarify how California applies securities law to export-control risks.
Bonta is examining the company’s communications as well as the underlying conduct.
His statement frames the investor question around California corporate securities law, rather than treating possible chip diversion as the only issue.
Bonta described the conduct of Nvidia and Huang as raising “bright red flags,” including about possible misleading statements to investors.
The subpoena is part of an ongoing investigation.
His office said the information sought would help the California Department of Justice evaluate whether Nvidia’s actions violated California law , the Los Angeles Times reported.
His stated investigative questions also cover confidential information —not just the physical movement of chips—and whether actions by Nvidia or Jensen Huang resulted in China obtaining either.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC’s request for comment on the subpoena.

sources.title: Job posting seemingly confirms Apple is working on its own AI agent for coding and other tasks - Engadget
passages: Apple appears to be developing its own in-house AI agent.
While we picked up on this development via Mark Gurman at Bloomberg , the news actually comes direct from the company this time.
Apple has an open job listing for a senior engineering manager of agentic AI that was posted earlier this week.

The description states: "As a senior leader in this org, you will own the technical direction and delivery of our agent platform and the AI capabilities built on it." It includes both general computer use and more technical coding tasks as falling within the future AI agent's purview, with the goal of being "capable, reliable and safe."
Apple, on the other hand, has been a bit more cautious when it comes to agents.
It recently warned developers that working with agentic AI "could put users at risk" by unwittingly allowing Full Disk Access.
Privacy is a frequent buzzword in Apple's recent software launches, so it will be interesting to see how the company walks the line whenever it unveils its own service.
But other businesses not directly working in artificial intelligence are also embracing the agentic path.

coreStoryFacts.text: Apple appears to be developing its own in-house AI agent.
While we picked up on this development via Mark Gurman at Bloomberg , the news actually comes direct from the company this time.
Apple has an open job listing for a senior engineering manager of agentic AI that was posted earlier this week.

The description states: "As a senior leader in this org, you will own the technical direction and delivery of our agent platform and the AI capabilities built on it." It includes both general computer use and more technical coding tasks as falling within the future AI agent's purview, with the goal of being "capable, reliable and safe."
Apple, on the other hand, has been a bit more cautious when it comes to agents.
It recently warned developers that working with agentic AI "could put users at risk" by unwittingly allowing Full Disk Access.
Privacy is a frequent buzzword in Apple's recent software launches, so it will be interesting to see how the company walks the line whenever it unveils its own service.
But other businesses not directly working in artificial intelligence are also embracing the agentic path.

“We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.” With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update, Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.
That’s according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant.
An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhone maker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks.

Apple is staffing an early-stage effort to build an agent that can plan and carry out multi-step work across apps, browsers, command lines, code and APIs, including coordinating specialized sub-agents.
Bloomberg reported that Apple has considered launching it as soon as the end of 2027, but that timing is tentative, not a product commitment.
The immediate development is a search for an engineering leader; the listings describe intended capabilities and privacy goals, not a released system or verified safeguards.
The role’s title, “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” places the work around an assistant that takes actions.
Apple’s description says the team is building the foundation for that system.
The scope extends beyond taking one action at a time.
Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for more information.
Apple is hiring for an AI assistant designed to do computer work on a user’s behalf , not just answer questions.
Bloomberg identified job listings describing software that would browse websites, control apps and write code.
The November 19 disclosure offers a detailed view of the company’s ambitions, but not a finished product.
The listing says the agent would do its work “privately” and with the polish users expect from Apple.
But the same account describes progress as remaining in the early stages.
That makes the date a reported possibility, not an announced delivery commitment.

Apple posted a job to lead an agentic AI assistant that browses, works across apps, writes code and runs sub-agents. What the listing says and what it does not.

Apple is hiring an engineer to lead an AI agent that can browse the web, work across apps, write code and call services. The Verge reported on November 19 that the listing was spotted by Bloomberg, and that it describes "an agentic AI assistant" built with Apple's Siri, UI Frameworks and Apple Foundation Models teams.

A job listing is a hiring signal. It shows what Apple wants to build, not what it will ship or when. Still, the wording is specific enough to tell us how Apple frames the next stage of Siri. This post covers what the listing says, how it fits what Apple has already shipped, how the competition looks, and what builders can do today.

The Verge quotes the listing directly. The core passage reads: "People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service." It continues: "We're building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way."
The listing does not give a product name, a platform, a model size or a launch window.

The Verge notes that Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which can answer questions about what is on your screen and perform actions across apps. It also says a Bloomberg report suggested Siri could gain abilities such as rotating and cropping images in Photos or organizing Safari tabs. With iOS 27.3, Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into "all apps," as part of a Developer Preview.
The listing is the first public sign that the hiring side is moving in the same direction as the reported roadmap. It does not confirm that roadmap.

The Verge frames the listing as Apple joining a crowded field. It names Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dots, Anthropic's Duet and Google's Tasks, and says Muse, ChatGPT and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps. It adds that Google just started letting Gemini do the same.

Apple's difference is distribution. Siri lives in every iPhone, iPad and Mac, and Apple controls the operating system, so an agent could reach app interfaces more directly than a third-party assistant can. The constraint is also Apple's: privacy and on-device processing limit what it will send to servers, and the Ternus interview stresses shipping only what is ready.

Hiring a lead for an agent that works across apps, browsers, terminals and APIs means taking on problems that no assistant has fully solved. Reading between the lines of the listing, four design questions stand out.

Reading interfaces reliably. An agent that operates apps needs a stable picture of what is on screen and what each control does. Apple controls UI Frameworks, so it can expose structure to the agent directly instead of guessing from pixels. That is the likely reason the team is named. Third-party agents on the Mac have to work from screenshots and accessibility data.

Permissions and confirmation. Writing code, calling services and sending messages are actions with side effects. An agent needs rules about which steps it may take alone and which need a tap. Apple's public stance, as in the Ternus interview, is caution, so expect confirmation prompts to be a feature, not a bug.

Privacy and where the model runs. Apple Foundation Models is the third team in the listing. Apple has long argued for on-device processing. A multi-step agent that browses and codes is heavier than a single request, so the split between device and server will matter, and it will shape both cost and usage limits. The iOS 27.3 beta already shows daily limits on Siri AI, which hints at how Apple may meter heavier work.

It improves results on long tasks but multiplies cost and failure points. Apple will have to decide how visible the sub-agents are to users and developers.

California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta on Thursday subpoenaed the AI chip manufacturer Nvidia — asking whether its advanced chips or other confidential information went to China and whether it had misled investors and the public on the issue.
Nvidia, which is based in Santa Clara, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The subpoena follows Nvidia co-founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang's resignation after it was revealed he was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and after Bonta's office sued OpenAI — another AI company — over similar claims that it had misled the public about its advanced AI capabilities.
Bonta's office said information gleaned from the subpoenas "will help the California Department of Justice evaluate whether Nvidia's actions violated California law."

Bonta said both Nvidia's and Jensen's conduct raises "bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," and his office intends to determine whether it did so.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said.

The shake-up at Nvidia has rattled markets . It has also raised questions about the company's handling of its AI chips, whether it facilitated those chips being smuggled to China, and whether the U.S. Commerce Department was complicit or incompetent in failing to prevent such diversions despite its stated interest in preventing the powerful chips — crucial for supporting AI models — from getting into Chinese hands.

Democrats on the House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committees in particular are investigating whether the administration's response to Nvidia's chip business was improperly influenced by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick — whose family has holdings in the company.

"Did Trump's Commerce Secretary compromise our national security so that his family firm could profit from hundreds of millions of dollars invested in Nvidia?" Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee asked on social media Thursday.

The Democrats' questions hold extra weight since their party won control of both chambers of Congress in this month's midterm elections, which will give them greater investigative and subpoena powers come January.

In a Commerce statement shared by Lutnick on Monday, the department acknowledged an ongoing, years-long investigation into the Singaporean company Megaspeed and allegations it may have skirted export rules governing Nvidia's powerful AI chips. It credited that investigation to its own "excellent work" under Lutnick.

The department noted that the investigation involved an interview of former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman with whom Nvidia's Huang acknowledged having an affair and who U.S. intelligence officials suspect may be a Chinese spy.

The Commerce statement said it and the Justice Department "have an extremely strong track record of bringing semiconductor smugglers to justice" and "will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred."
Megaspeed has said that Alice Huang left the company in 2025 and that it is conducting its own internal investigation .

The explanations have reassured few, and criticism has not been limited to Democrats. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also blamed the Commerce Department for failing to blacklist Megaspeed over possible export violations.

Harvey C. Jones, Nvidia's chairman, has said the company's board unanimously accepted Jensen Huang's resignation and does not intend to reinstate him — despite calls for exactly that from President Trump and other administration allies.

"While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company's employees, customers, partners, and shareholders," Jones said. Colette Kress, Nvidia's executive vice president and chief financial officer, is now serving as interim CEO.

On Tuesday, the company announced third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year prior. The company's reporting has raised additional questions, as it stopped reporting Singapore revenue separately just as scrutiny of Megaspeed was arising.

In a post on X on Tuesday, Jensen Huang said he "did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA," had "made serious mistakes" in his personal life and "created problems for" the company's board.

But he also said he had received many messages from supporters encouraging him to return as CEO, which he would consider if the board wanted him to help the company as it "navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics."
This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

Rob Bonta on Thursday subpoenaed the AI chip manufacturer Nvidia — asking whether its advanced chips or other confidential information went to China and whether it had misled investors and the public on the issue. Nvidia, which is based in Santa Clara, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The subpoena follows Nvidia co-founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang's resignation after it was revealed he was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and after Bonta's office sued OpenAI — another AI company — over similar claims that it had misled the public about its advanced AI capabilities. Bonta's office said information gleaned from the subpoenas "will help the California Department of Justice evaluate whether Nvidia's actions violated California law." Bonta said both Nvidia's and Jensen's conduct raises "bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," and his office intends to determine whether it did so. "Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said. The shake-up at Nvidia has rattled markets . It has also raised questions about the company's handling of its AI chips, whether it facilitated those chips being smuggled to China, and whether the U.S. Commerce Department was complicit or incompetent in failing to prevent such diversions despite its stated interest in preventing the powerful chips — crucial for supporting AI models — from getting into Chinese hands. Democrats on the House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committees in particular are investigating whether the administration's response to Nvidia's chip business was improperly influenced by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick — whose family has holdings in the company. The approvals for 879,000 chip shipments by the Commerce Department included 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu, ‌and 4,000 for BYD, all on the Pentagon's list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies, the committee noted. The unusual release of chip export licensing data comes as the administration of President ​Donald Trump faces heightened scrutiny following news about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has fueled renewed calls in Washington for a tougher stance on China. Companies had sought permission to ship over 3.4 million chips to China during the period, the documents showed. It was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipments of chips, which included Nvidia's H200 and AMD's equivalent MI325X. News surrounding Huang has turned ‌a spotlight on instances of Nvidia AI chips ⁠being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialing up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech threats. The Commerce Department said its approach to H200 licensing "is based on a rule published in the Federal Register in ⁠January 2026, which imposes significant additional national security-related requirements on license applicants in order to qualify for case-by-case consideration rather than a presumption of denial." Chris McGuire, a former US official and expert on the US-China technology battle, said, "The fact that over 30% of the AI chips sent to China were shipped to companies that ​the Department ​of War has designated as Chinese military companies is astonishing, and calls into ​question whether Commerce conducted any serious national security review before ‌approving these licenses." Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were "subject to strict conditions and limited volumes." It added that "despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China." AMD said it "complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations." Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu, BYD, the Commerce Department and the Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment. WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - The Trump administration approved shipments of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026, the House Foreign Affairs Committee ‌said on Thursday.

The approvals for 879,000 chip shipments by the Commerce Department included 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu, ‌and 4,000 for BYD, all on the Pentagon's list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies, the committee noted.

The unusual release of chip export licensing data comes as the administration of President ​Donald Trump faces heightened scrutiny following news about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has fueled renewed calls in Washington for a tougher stance on China.

Companies had sought permission to ship over 3.4 million chips to China during the period, the documents showed. It was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipments of chips, which included Nvidia's H200 and AMD's equivalent MI325X.

News surrounding Huang has turned ‌a spotlight on instances of Nvidia AI chips ⁠being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialing up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech threats.

The Commerce Department said its approach to H200 licensing "is based on a rule published in the Federal Register in ⁠January 2026, which imposes significant additional national security-related requirements on license applicants in order to qualify for case-by-case consideration rather than a presumption of denial."

Chris McGuire, a former US official and expert on the US-China technology battle, said, "The fact that over 30% of the AI chips sent to China were shipped to companies that ​the Department ​of War has designated as Chinese military companies is astonishing, and calls into ​question whether Commerce conducted any serious national security review before ‌approving these licenses."
Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were "subject to strict conditions and limited volumes." It added that "despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China."
AMD said it "complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations."
Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu, BYD, the Commerce Department and the Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Former President Joe Biden had restricted Chinese access to the prized chips over fears that they would supercharge China's military and erode the US lead ‌in artificial intelligence.

But Trump in December gave the green light for Nvidia to ship ​its H200 chip to China, rolling back Biden-era restrictions and drawing fierce criticism from ​China hawks across the US political spectrum.
Despite the approvals, questions swirled ​as to whether the AI chips were actually reaching Chinese shores.
In May, Reuters reported the US had cleared about ‌10 companies to buy the H200, but that no deliveries ​had taken place.

In testimony before the committee ​in July, Commerce Department official Jeffrey Kessler said shipments had begun but there had been 'very few.' Several major Chinese internet companies had each obtained about 10,000 H200 chips, Reuters has since reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

"This is the most detailed public disclosure in ​the history of the Export Control Reform Act," ‌committee Chair Brian Mast, a Republican from Florida, said upon releasing the data, referring to 2018 legislation that expanded Commerce's authority ​to restrict the export of sensitive technologies for national security reasons.

Companies had sought permission to ship over 3.4 million chips to China during the period, the documents showed. ‌It ​was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipments ⁠of chips, which included Nvidia’s H200 and ⁠AMD’s equivalent MI325X.
Former President Joe Biden had restricted Chinese access to the prized chips over fears that they would supercharge China’s ⁠military and erode the US lead in artificial intelligence.

The unusual release of chip export licensing data comes as the administration of President Donald Trump faces heightened scrutiny following news about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has fueled renewed calls in Washington for a tougher stance on China.

In testimony ​before the ‌committee in July, Commerce Department official Jeffrey Kessler said shipments had begun but there ​had been ‘very few.’ ⁠Several major Chinese internet companies had each obtained about 10,000 H200 chips, Reuters has since reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

The approvals for 879,000 chip shipments by the Commerce ​Department included 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD, all on the ‌Pentagon’s list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies, the committee noted. The unusual release of chip export licensing data comes as the administration of President Donald Trump faces heightened scrutiny following news about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has fueled renewed calls in Washington for a tougher stance on China. Companies had sought permission to ship over 3.4 million chips to China during the period, the documents showed. ‌It ​was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipments ⁠of chips, which included Nvidia’s H200 and ⁠AMD’s equivalent MI325X. News surrounding Huang has turned a spotlight on instances of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialing up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech threats. The Commerce Department said its approach to H200 licensing “is based on a rule published in the Federal Register in January 2026, which imposes ​significant additional national security-related requirements on license applicants in order to qualify for case-by-case consideration rather than a presumption of denial.” Chris McGuire, a former US official and expert on the US-China technology battle, said, “The fact that over 30% of the ⁠AI chips sent to China were shipped to companies that the Department ⁠of War has designated as Chinese military companies is astonishing, and calls into question whether ​Commerce conducted any serious national security review before approving these licenses.” Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were “subject to strict ​conditions and limited volumes.” It added that “despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to ‌China.” AMD said it “complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations.” Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu, BYD, the Commerce Department and the Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment. But Trump in December gave the green light for Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to China, rolling back Biden-era restrictions and drawing fierce criticism from China hawks across the US political spectrum. Despite the ⁠approvals, questions swirled as to whether the ‌AI chips were actually reaching Chinese shores. WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) – The Trump administration approved shipments of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said on Thursday.

The approvals for 879,000 chip shipments by the Commerce ​Department included 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD, all on the ‌Pentagon’s list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies, the committee noted.

The unusual release of chip export licensing data comes as the administration of President Donald Trump faces heightened scrutiny following news about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has fueled renewed calls in Washington for a tougher stance on China.

Companies had sought permission to ship over 3.4 million chips to China during the period, the documents showed. ‌It ​was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipments ⁠of chips, which included Nvidia’s H200 and ⁠AMD’s equivalent MI325X.

News surrounding Huang has turned a spotlight on instances of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialing up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech threats.

The Commerce Department said its approach to H200 licensing “is based on a rule published in the Federal Register in January 2026, which imposes ​significant additional national security-related requirements on license applicants in order to qualify for case-by-case consideration rather than a presumption of denial.”

Chris McGuire, a former US official and expert on the US-China technology battle, said, “The fact that over 30% of the ⁠AI chips sent to China were shipped to companies that the Department ⁠of War has designated as Chinese military companies is astonishing, and calls into question whether ​Commerce conducted any serious national security review before approving these licenses.”

Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were “subject to strict ​conditions and limited volumes.” It added that “despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to ‌China.”
AMD said it “complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations.”
Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu, BYD, the Commerce Department and the Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Former President Joe Biden had restricted Chinese access to the prized chips over fears that they would supercharge China’s ⁠military and erode the US lead in artificial intelligence.

But Trump in December gave the green light for Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to China, rolling back Biden-era restrictions and drawing fierce criticism from China hawks across the US political spectrum.
Despite the ⁠approvals, questions swirled as to whether the ‌AI chips were actually reaching Chinese shores.
In May, Reuters reported the US had cleared ⁠about 10 companies to buy the H200, but that no deliveries had taken place.

In testimony ​before the ‌committee in July, Commerce Department official Jeffrey Kessler said shipments had begun but there ​had been ‘very few.’ ⁠Several major Chinese internet companies had each obtained about 10,000 H200 chips, Reuters has since reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

“This is the most detailed public disclosure in the history of the Export Control Reform Act,” committee Chair Brian Mast, a Republican from Florida, said upon releasing the data, referring to 2018 legislation that expanded Commerce’s authority to restrict the export of sensitive technologies for national security reasons.
(Reporting by Alexandra Alper, Ryan Patrick Jones, Katharine Jackson; Additional Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Scott Malone, ​Chris Sanders and Bill Berkrot)

sources.title: Google will launch Android app verification requirement globally in January 2027
passages: Google announced Android developer verification last year , and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the company is forging ahead .
It began blocking the installation of unregistered apps in some countries this fall, and the system is expanding globally soon.
Google says it will start rolling out the requirement in all regions in January 2027, and it urges devs who still haven’t registered their apps to do so soon.
In September, Google launched verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand.
It says that verification will reach all devices within “several months.”
So far, Google is getting what it wanted from this initiative, with “millions” of non-Play apps already registered.
The company says this accounts for more than 99 percent of global Android app installs.

The verifier system service has already been rolled out to Google-certified devices running Android 8 Oreo or higher, which accounts for just about every Android device in the world outside of China and Russia.
Google has also partnered with the biggest third-party app stores to enforce verification: Galaxy Store, Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Transsion, and Vivo.
The system-level verifier is responsible for blocking installs, but these stores will only list verified apps once Google flips the switch.
As Google moves toward full verification enforcement, it has created guides for developers and app distributors to outline all the salient points.
These guides suggest Google expects verification to be fully online by March 1, 2027.
The apps you download from the Play Store all come from verified developers, and Google’s new requirement expands that requirement to apps from third-party sources.
Once developer verification is live in your region, you won’t be able to sideload apps unless the developer has registered with Google, which is framed as a security measure .
Verification requires providing government identification and paying a $25 fee, which will allegedly make it harder for nefarious actors to distribute malware and scammy apps.
Google also relented and created an opt-out system for users who don’t want their installations limited.
The so-called “ advanced flow ” will let you install whatever you want regardless of verification status, but it’s not a simple toggle.
The option will be buried, and there will be plenty of scary warnings about the risks.
You’ll also have to wait 24 hours to fully activate the feature.
This setting is already live, so you can tell your phone to ignore verification right now.
Google has gotten a lot of feedback since announcing this change, and it has listened to some of it.
Google initially planned to limit this to 25 total installs, but that has since been increased to 50 installs.
There’s also now an API that developers can use to streamline registering new application packages.
Sideloading an app may also require a Google server connection.
Only popular app IDs will be cached on devices for verification purposes.
For others, your phone will have to check with Google before installing.
These will be edge cases, certainly, but still very annoying ones.
Google says almost all developers have already gotten on board with verification.

sources.title: Google to Enforce Android App Verification Worldwide Starting January 2027 - BigGo Finance
passages: Google will begin enforcing its Android developer verification requirement across all regions in January 2027, extending to third-party app sources a rule that until now applied mainly to software distributed through the Play Store.
The company said the system will reach all eligible devices within a few months of the rollout, with its own developer documentation pointing to full coverage by March 1, 2027.
Separately, Google is tightening rules for large-screen devices.

Beginning in April 2027, apps must meet the company's "Tier 3 - Adaptive ready" standard, meaning they fill the display without letterboxing or compatibility modes and preserve state such as scroll position, text input and media playback through rotation, folding and resizing.
Listings will also need three foldable screenshots, which developers can submit now.
Once added, BigGo Finance appears first in Google Search Top Stories, so you get the broadest, most up-to-the-minute, and most comprehensive global financial news first.
A system-level verifier has been pushed to Google-certified devices running Android 8 Oreo or later, which covers nearly every Android handset in circulation outside China and Russia.
Once verification goes live in a market, that service blocks installation of any app whose developer has not registered with Google.
Google tested the program first in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand beginning in September, and is now preparing the wider launch.
It says millions of non-Play apps have already been registered, representing more than 99 percent of global Android installs.
Google has adjusted the program in response to criticism.
Hobbyists can register a free account to distribute apps to a limited audience, with the cap raised from an initial 25 installs to 50.
A new API is available to speed the registration of application packages.
The company also built an opt-out path for users who want no installation limits, though it is deliberately hard to find, comes wrapped in warnings about risk, and takes 24 hours to activate.
Even with those concessions, the requirement shifts significant control toward Google.
Developers in sanctioned countries cannot complete identity verification and would be cut off from distribution.
Some sideloads may also depend on a live connection to Google's servers, since only widely used app IDs are cached on handsets for offline checks.
The verification mandate hands Google a gatekeeping role over software installed outside its store, a position that draws antitrust scrutiny in several jurisdictions.
For independent developers, the $25 fee and ID requirement add friction, while the free hobbyist tier and the package-registration API soften the burden for small projects.
Users who rely on sideloaded software face the sharpest change: without registration, apps simply will not install unless they navigate the buried advanced flow.
The parallel foldable rules raise the bar for app quality on premium hardware, but they also add compliance work for smaller studios already stretched across form factors.
Third-party storefronts are being folded into the system as well.
Google has agreements with Samsung's Galaxy Store, along with Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Transsion and Vivo, under which those platforms will list only verified apps once enforcement takes effect.
Note: Foldable deadlines are a separate Google Play policy track from developer verification.

passages: Google will begin enforcing Android developer verification worldwide in January 2027, Matthew Forsythe, director of product management for Android app safety, wrote on the Android Developers Blog on Nov.
Certified Android devices will only install apps from developers who have verified their identity and registered their apps, a requirement that until now applied in four countries [1] [2] .
Google announced developer verification in August 2025 and switched it on for participating stores in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand on Sept.
Verification opened to all developers in March, and Google said millions of apps registered since then account for more than 99% of Android app installs worldwide [1] .
Registering an app takes less than ten minutes, according to the company [1] .
Google listed changes made after developer feedback.

Limited distribution accounts, launched in August for students and hobbyists who want to share apps without paying the registration fee or verifying a government ID, can now share with 50 authorized devices instead of 20 [1] .
An advanced flow lets experienced users install unregistered apps if they accept the risk, while Google keeps what it calls guardrails against social engineering scams for other users [1] .
The global rollout starts with seven app distributors: Google Play, Samsung's Galaxy Store, Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Transsion and Vivo.
That includes apps sideloaded from websites or third-party stores, which is why critics call the rules a limit on Android's openness [3] .
Google also published a guide for developers who distribute through open-source registries such as F-Droid, and a separate guide for app distributors [1] .
