extraction.body: On November 19, 2026, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (“HHS”) Office for Civil Rights (“OCR”) published the “ HIPAA Privacy Rule: Changes to Support Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement and Reduce Regulatory Burdens ” (the “Final Rule”). Finalizing many, though not all, of the proposals in OCR’s January 21, 2021, Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (the “2021 NPRM”), the Final Rule modifies the HIPAA Privacy Rule, making significant changes to the individual right of access, expanding the permissions for care coordination and case management, streamlining Notice of Privacy Practices (“NPP”) requirements, and revising certain provisions affecting business associates, among other modifications. OCR explains that the Final Rule targets Privacy Rule standards that “may impede the nationwide transition to value-based health care by limiting or discouraging individual access or care coordination and case management or posing other unnecessary burdens,” with the goal of promoting “the essential sharing of individuals’ protected health information (PHI) for care coordination and individual engagement while continuing to protect its privacy and security.” OCR frames the Final Rule as part of the Trump Administration’s “Make America Healthy Again” agenda and its broader effort to build a “digital health ecosystem” in which patients can view, manage, use and share their health information through apps and other tools, situating it alongside related federal initiatives, including the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ Digital Health Tech Ecosystem initiative, ONC health IT certification work, and HHS’s crackdown on information blocking. Consistent with OCR’s historical approach, the amendments to the Privacy Rule are generally technology neutral. The Final Rule makes several key changes to the Privacy Rule’s right of access: OCR identifies facilitating care coordination and case management as a central aim of the Final Rule, and the Final Rule makes two targeted changes in this area. First, it amends the definition of “health care operations” at 45 C.F.R. § 164.501 to confirm that the definition encompasses both population-based and individual-focused care coordination and case management, a clarification especially significant for health plans. OCR explains that some covered entities had read the existing definition to reach only population-based activities, which would have excluded individual-level care coordination and case management; the Final Rule confirms that health plans and covered health care providers may use and disclose PHI for care coordination and case management, whether individual-level or population-based. Second, the Final Rule adds 45 C.F.R. § 164.506(c)(6), which expressly permits covered entities to disclose PHI to social services agencies, community-based organizations, home and community-based services (“HCBS”) providers, or similar third parties that provide health or human services to specific individuals, for purposes of individual-level care coordination and case management of the individual. The Final Rule makes two notable changes in this area. First, it amends 45 C.F.R. § 164.502(a)(4)(ii) to codify OCR’s longstanding interpretation that a business associate must disclose PHI as required by its business associate agreement, including, where specified in the business associate agreement, to the individual or the individual’s designee to fulfill the covered entity’s obligations with respect to the right of access and right to direct. OCR advises that covered entities and their business associates should address in their business associate agreements which party will be responsible for responding to such requests. Even where a covered entity delegates that responsibility to a business associate, the covered entity remains ultimately responsible for ensuring the individual receives the requested PHI, and contractual arrangements cannot be used to circumvent that obligation. Second, the Final Rule excludes Telecommunications Relay Services (“TRS”) providers from the definition of “business associate.” TRS enables people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or deaf-blind, or who have a speech disability to communicate by telephone. A longstanding OCR FAQ already provides that a covered entity using TRS to communicate with such individuals does not need a business associate agreement with the TRS provider, but it does not address covered entity workforce members who themselves rely on TRS to share PHI with colleagues or outside persons as needed to perform their duties. The Final Rule closes that gap by excluding TRS providers from the definition of “business associate” at 45 C.F.R. § 160.103 and expressly permitting a regulated entity to disclose PHI to a TRS Communications Assistant as necessary to conduct covered functions. Health care providers with a direct treatment relationship no longer need to obtain an individual’s written acknowledgment that they received the NPP, or document a good faith effort to obtain one, and OCR has eliminated the associated 6-year NPP document retention requirement. The Final Rule also revises NPP content requirements to better explain individuals’ rights and how to exercise them, including by informing individuals of their right to discuss the NPP with a contact person or office designated by the covered entity. It also, among other revisions to NPP requirements, removes the provision that excepted inmates of correctional institutions from the right to receive a copy of the NPP. Covered entities will therefore need to update their NPPs. The Final Rule extends the existing permission to use or disclose PHI of members of the Armed Forces to command authorities for mission readiness to all Uniformed Services, adding the U.S. Public Health Service (“USPHS”) Commissioned Corps and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (“NOAA”) Commissioned Corps to the six branches of the Armed Forces. It also makes a number of technical, non-substantive corrections to the Privacy Rule. Effective and Compliance Dates; Transition Period Effective and compliance dates. The Final Rule takes effect on January 19, 2027, with compliance required by July 19, 2027. Transition period for business associate agreements. The Final Rule modifies the transition provisions at 45 C.F.R. § 164.532(e) to allow regulated entities to continue to operate under certain existing business associate agreements (including subcontractor business associate agreements) for up to one year after the effective date of the Final Rule. If, prior to November 19, 2026, a regulated entity had an existing, compliant business associate agreement in place, and the agreement is not renewed or modified from January 19, 2027, until July 19, 2027, OCR deems such business associate agreement compliant with the modifications to the Privacy Rule until the earlier of (1) the date the business associate agreement is renewed or modified on or after July 19, 2027, or (2) January 18, 2028. This transition period covers only the updating of the business associate agreements themselves; it does not affect any other HIPAA compliance obligations. For example, as of the Final Rule’s compliance date, a business associate that responds to individual requests for access on behalf of a covered entity must respond to such requests as soon as practicable, but no later than 15 calendar days after receiving the request irrespective of whether its business associate agreement with the covered entity has been modified to reflect such requirement. With approximately 240 days between publication and the general compliance date, covered entities and business associates should begin their compliance review now. Priority areas for covered entities include (1) auditing access request workflows against the new 15 calendar day response period, (2) posting the required fee schedule, (3) revising NPPs to satisfy the updated content requirements and to extend the right to receive NPPs to inmates, and (4) updating or creating new policies and procedures and workforce training materials to address the regulatory changes. All covered entities with business associate agreements (and business associates with subcontractor business associate agreements) should review and revise such agreements to ensure compliance with the modified right of access provisions.
passages: On November 19, 2026, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (“HHS”) Office for Civil Rights (“OCR”) published the “ HIPAA Privacy Rule: Changes to Support Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement and Reduce Regulatory Burdens ” (the “Final Rule”). Finalizing many, though not all, of the proposals in OCR’s January 21, 2021, Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (the “2021 NPRM”), the Final Rule modifies the HIPAA Privacy Rule, making significant changes to the individual right of access, expanding the permissions for care coordination and case management, streamlining Notice of Privacy Practices (“NPP”) requirements, and revising certain provisions affecting business associates, among other modifications.

OCR explains that the Final Rule targets Privacy Rule standards that “may impede the nationwide transition to value-based health care by limiting or discouraging individual access or care coordination and case management or posing other unnecessary burdens,” with the goal of promoting “the essential sharing of individuals’ protected health information (PHI) for care coordination and individual engagement while continuing to protect its privacy and security.”

OCR frames the Final Rule as part of the Trump Administration’s “Make America Healthy Again” agenda and its broader effort to build a “digital health ecosystem” in which patients can view, manage, use and share their health information through apps and other tools, situating it alongside related federal initiatives, including the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ Digital Health Tech Ecosystem initiative, ONC health IT certification work, and HHS’s crackdown on information blocking. Consistent with OCR’s historical approach, the amendments to the Privacy Rule are generally technology neutral.
The Final Rule makes several key changes to the Privacy Rule’s right of access:

OCR identifies facilitating care coordination and case management as a central aim of the Final Rule, and the Final Rule makes two targeted changes in this area. First, it amends the definition of “health care operations” at 45 C.F.R. § 164.501 to confirm that the definition encompasses both population-based and individual-focused care coordination and case management, a clarification especially significant for health plans. OCR explains that some covered entities had read the existing definition to reach only population-based activities, which would have excluded individual-level care coordination and case management; the Final Rule confirms that health plans and covered health care providers may use and disclose PHI for care coordination and case management, whether individual-level or population-based. Second, the Final Rule adds 45 C.F.R. § 164.506(c)(6), which expressly permits covered entities to disclose PHI to social services agencies, community-based organizations, home and community-based services (“HCBS”) providers, or similar third parties that provide health or human services to specific individuals, for purposes of individual-level care coordination and case management of the individual.

The Final Rule makes two notable changes in this area. First, it amends 45 C.F.R. § 164.502(a)(4)(ii) to codify OCR’s longstanding interpretation that a business associate must disclose PHI as required by its business associate agreement, including, where specified in the business associate agreement, to the individual or the individual’s designee to fulfill the covered entity’s obligations with respect to the right of access and right to direct. OCR advises that covered entities and their business associates should address in their business associate agreements which party will be responsible for responding to such requests. Even where a covered entity delegates that responsibility to a business associate, the covered entity remains ultimately responsible for ensuring the individual receives the requested PHI, and contractual arrangements cannot be used to circumvent that obligation.

Second, the Final Rule excludes Telecommunications Relay Services (“TRS”) providers from the definition of “business associate.” TRS enables people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or deaf-blind, or who have a speech disability to communicate by telephone. A longstanding OCR FAQ already provides that a covered entity using TRS to communicate with such individuals does not need a business associate agreement with the TRS provider, but it does not address covered entity workforce members who themselves rely on TRS to share PHI with colleagues or outside persons as needed to perform their duties. The Final Rule closes that gap by excluding TRS providers from the definition of “business associate” at 45 C.F.R. § 160.103 and expressly permitting a regulated entity to disclose PHI to a TRS Communications Assistant as necessary to conduct covered functions.

Health care providers with a direct treatment relationship no longer need to obtain an individual’s written acknowledgment that they received the NPP, or document a good faith effort to obtain one, and OCR has eliminated the associated 6-year NPP document retention requirement. The Final Rule also revises NPP content requirements to better explain individuals’ rights and how to exercise them, including by informing individuals of their right to discuss the NPP with a contact person or office designated by the covered entity. It also, among other revisions to NPP requirements, removes the provision that excepted inmates of correctional institutions from the right to receive a copy of the NPP. Covered entities will therefore need to update their NPPs.

The Final Rule extends the existing permission to use or disclose PHI of members of the Armed Forces to command authorities for mission readiness to all Uniformed Services, adding the U.S. Public Health Service (“USPHS”) Commissioned Corps and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (“NOAA”) Commissioned Corps to the six branches of the Armed Forces. It also makes a number of technical, non-substantive corrections to the Privacy Rule.
Effective and Compliance Dates; Transition Period
Effective and compliance dates. The Final Rule takes effect on January 19, 2027, with compliance required by July 19, 2027.

Transition period for business associate agreements. The Final Rule modifies the transition provisions at 45 C.F.R. § 164.532(e) to allow regulated entities to continue to operate under certain existing business associate agreements (including subcontractor business associate agreements) for up to one year after the effective date of the Final Rule. If, prior to November 19, 2026, a regulated entity had an existing, compliant business associate agreement in place, and the agreement is not renewed or modified from January 19, 2027, until July 19, 2027, OCR deems such business associate agreement compliant with the modifications to the Privacy Rule until the earlier of (1) the date the business associate agreement is renewed or modified on or after July 19, 2027, or (2) January 18, 2028. This transition period covers only the updating of the business associate agreements themselves; it does not affect any other HIPAA compliance obligations. For example, as of the Final Rule’s compliance date, a business associate that responds to individual requests for access on behalf of a covered entity must respond to such requests as soon as practicable, but no later than 15 calendar days after receiving the request irrespective of whether its business associate agreement with the covered entity has been modified to reflect such requirement.

With approximately 240 days between publication and the general compliance date, covered entities and business associates should begin their compliance review now. Priority areas for covered entities include (1) auditing access request workflows against the new 15 calendar day response period, (2) posting the required fee schedule, (3) revising NPPs to satisfy the updated content requirements and to extend the right to receive NPPs to inmates, and (4) updating or creating new policies and procedures and workforce training materials to address the regulatory changes. All covered entities with business associate agreements (and business associates with subcontractor business associate agreements) should review and revise such agreements to ensure compliance with the modified right of access provisions.

extraction.body: Federal regulators have finalized substantial changes to the HIPAA Privacy Rule aimed at giving patients faster and easier access to their health records - including through third-party applications - while reducing obstacles to information sharing for patient care coordination. See Also: How to implement a physical security strategy with privacy in mind The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' Office for Civil Rights released the 363-page final rule - HIPAA Privacy Rule: Changes to Support Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement and Reduce Regulatory Burdens - late Monday. It is slated for publication Thursday in the Federal Register. "Americans should never have to fight for access to their own health records," HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in a statement. "This rule modernizes HIPAA to serve patients and help providers spend more time delivering care and less time navigating bureaucracy." The rule becomes effective 60 days after publication, or on Jan. 19, 2027. HIPAA-regulated organizations must comply with applicable provisions 180 days after the effective date, or July 19, 2027, with additional time allowed for certain modifications to written business associate agreements.* HHS OCR issued the proposed HIPAA Privacy Rule modifications in January 2021, during the final days of President Donald Trump's first term. But the proposal remained on the back burner during the Biden administration (see: HHS Reveals Proposed Changes to HIPAA Privacy Rule ). The final rule retains several key patient-access and care-coordination provisions proposed in 2021 but abandons or scales back others that raised privacy concerns or would have increased administrative burdens on healthcare organizations. For example, HHS OCR dropped a proposal that would have relaxed HIPAA's minimum necessary standard for certain disclosures of sensitive health information. Among the most significant changes, the final rule cuts time in half for healthcare organizations to respond to patients' requests for access to their protected health information - from 30 calendar days to 15 days - with a one-time extension of up to 30 additional days under specific circumstances. The regulation also clarifies patients' rights to obtain their electronic health information through personal health applications, including consumer apps that are not subject to HIPAA. Healthcare organizations generally can't refuse to transmit records to patients' chosen personal health apps solely because they believe the applications lack adequate privacy or security protections, such as encryption at rest. The rule also prohibits covered organizations from imposing unreasonable identity verification measures that create barriers to patient access. Another condition involves verifying that demographic information associated with the token matches the patient's information in the covered entity's designated record set. HHS said these procedures can satisfy HIPAA's identity verification obligations. Healthcare organizations also may warn patients about privacy and security risks associated with particular apps. Before the rule's release, several healthcare industry groups signed a letter to HHS last week expressing concerns that potentially loosening identity verification requirements involving third-party apps could expose healthcare providers to security threats and regulatory scrutiny (see: Health Groups Warn HHS on Potential HIPAA Privacy Changes ). The signatories of the letter , including the College of Healthcare Information Management Executives - an association of healthcare CISOs and CIOs - did not immediately respond to ISMG's request for comment on the final rule. But HHS retained the minimum necessary standard for applicable healthcare operations disclosures, rather than adopting a proposed exception for certain care-coordination activities. The final rule also eliminates the requirement for covered healthcare providers to make a good-faith effort to obtain patients' written acknowledgment of receiving a Notice of Privacy Practices, a process HHS deemed unnecessarily burdensome. "I appreciate the deletion of the requirement for healthcare providers to obtain acknowledgments of receipt of the notice of privacy practices. The regulatory requirement was founded on good intentions but led to administrative burden and confusion with minimal corresponding benefit," said privacy attorney Adam Greene of the law firm Davis Wright Tremaine. Privacy attorney Kirk Nahra of the law firm WilmerHale said the final rule involves complicated issues stemming partly from tensions between competing public policy goals. "Given the passage of time I would have liked to see an additional stage to obtain new comments on these issues that have changed significantly since the proposal was first issued" five years ago, he said. Regarding the access to PHI provisions, "it is clear that they are interested in promoting patient access to records - although there is some risk that these principles, especially some of the identity confirmation issues, can create security concerns," he said. As for information sharing for coordinated care, "HHS chose this 'coordination' over individual privacy. That's not necessarily a bad decision but it is a complicated one - the rule essentially allows this disclosure over the objection or lack of permission from the consumer," he said. The provisions easing information sharing among healthcare organizations, health plans, social services agencies and other care-coordination partners could raise privacy concerns, particularly when patient information is disclosed to organizations outside HIPAA's regulatory umbrella. Such disclosures could also increase risks involving unauthorized access, secondary uses of data and cyberattacks. "Companies should remain cautious about these disclosures even if they are permitted," Nahra said. "The proposal would have led to a substantial unfunded mandate that would tax covered entities' already limited resources," he said. Overall, Greene said the final rule includes some helpful changes to the Privacy Rule, "but nothing earth-shattering." "I don't expect that compliance with the final rule will be difficult, but the changes to the notices of privacy practices and to policies and procedures around the right of access will take significant time and resources to implement," he said. Privacy attorney Iliana Peters of the law firm Polsinelli said her biggest concerns involve the administrative burdens HIPAA-covered organizations will face in implementing several of the changes. Those include updating policies and procedures governing uses and disclosures and also complying with patient access requirements, particularly to accommodate the new 15-day access deadline, "which is a very short amount of time," she said. Also, although organizations will no longer need to obtain patients' written acknowledgment of receiving a Notice of Privacy Practices, they still must update, redistribute and post their notices to comply with the rule changes. Regulated entities also must update their websites with required information about fees for accessing health records and revise applicable business associate agreements. extraction.body: On 16 November 2026, the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Office for Civil Rights (OCR) finalized significant amendments to the HIPAA Privacy Rule. Key changes focus on strengthening individuals’ rights to access their protected health information (PHI), including electronic PHI through personal health apps; improving information sharing for care coordination and case management; and reducing regulatory and administrative burdens on covered entities. The final rule also reflects a broader shift in how HHS is adapting HIPAA to a healthcare environment in which individuals increasingly expect their health information to move electronically, including through applications and services that may sit outside the traditional HIPAA ecosystem. This shift has important practical implications for health systems, health plans, and digital health companies. The final rule amends the HIPAA Privacy Rule in three principal areas: Comparing the final rule with OCR’s January 2021 proposed rule offers insight into OCR’s priorities and how it is likely to approach compliance and enforcement: The rule is particularly significant for organizations in the digital health space. By expressly addressing an individual’s ability to obtain electronic PHI through a personal health application when the covered entity can provide the information in the requested form and format, HHS is underscoring the reality that health information no longer moves only from one HIPAA-regulated provider to another. Patients increasingly interact with health information through portals, applications, Application Programming Interfaces, remote-monitoring platforms, connected devices, and other consumer-facing technologies, and not every company receiving health information is a HIPAA business associate. That distinction is important because HIPAA applicability does not turn solely on whether an organization handles health information. As such, the useful compliance question is not simply, “Is this health information?” Instead, it is: Who is receiving the information, on whose behalf do they act, why is it being transmitted, and what happens to it after the transfer? That analysis has become increasingly important as the boundaries between traditional healthcare technology and consumer health technology have blurred. The new rule is straightforward from a requirements standpoint. The more complex question covered organizations will need to wrestle with is what it will take to comply operationally and how the rule implicitly reshapes the analysis around digital health. For example, reducing the access period from 30 days to 15 days sounds like a straightforward compliance change. However, a medical record request often crosses several systems and business functions—it may begin with health information management, involve identity verification, require retrieval from an EHR or another clinical system, and depend on a third-party records vendor before the information reaches the patient. Because existing processes were designed around a 30-day requirement, simply updating the policy may not result in operational compliance. In addition to updating their policies, organizations may also need to reexamine their access process and their data governance and ecosystem. Most organizations will update their access policies before the July 2027 compliance date. Fewer will test whether the people, systems, and vendors behind those policies can actually deliver records in 15 days, or decide in advance how they will respond when a patient asks to send a full record to an unfamiliar app. Those gaps are where the rule is most likely to generate patient complaints and, in time, OCR scrutiny, and closing them depends on each organization’s own data flows, vendor relationships, and contracts. Organizations that address these questions now will be far better positioned than those that discover the gaps with a request already on the clock. extraction.body: Trump Media & Technology Group (DJT) is trying to repay the debt it took on to buy Bitcoin without dumping the cryptocurrency itself. Creditors are now about two weeks away from gaining the right to demand cash repayment, at which point they could require the company to hand over as much as $883.5 million (about NT$29 billion). The company, which owns the social platform Truth Social, issued $1 billion in zero-coupon convertible notes in May 2025, secured by Bitcoin, and used all of the proceeds to purchase Bitcoin. The notes nominally mature in 2028, but holders hold a one-time put right allowing them to demand full cash repayment at face value on Nov. 30, 2026. The company said Tuesday it had used cash on hand to repurchase $100 million (about NT$3.3 billion) of the notes at a discount to face value, leaving about $883.5 million outstanding. "We plan to use our existing cash and credit facilities to optimize our capital structure and will not issue new shares," interim CEO Kevin McGurn said in the announcement. McGurn elaborated on the company's thinking during a Nov. 9 earnings call: "We want to retain as much Bitcoin as possible, continue executing our yield strategy and wait for the asset's price to recover." He also stressed that the company is trying to avoid issuing additional shares, which would dilute existing shareholders including Donald Trump. According to the latest combined prospectus, Trump's revocable trust holds 114.75 million shares; at roughly $4 per share (about NT$130), that stake is worth about $460 million (about NT$15 billion). The trust's holding represents about 41% of Trump Media. The quarterly report itself, however, laid out the risks. The company acknowledged that if other financing efforts fall short of expectations, it may have to "sell Bitcoin or other digital assets" to fund the note repurchase. Trump Media did not respond to a request for comment. Judging by the balance sheet, raising the cash will not be easy. As of Sept. 30, the company held about $393 million (about NT$13 billion) in cash and short-term investments, plus $31 million (about NT$1 billion) in restricted cash. Since that date, the company only moved this week to use cash to repurchase notes, still needs to advance its merger project with TAE Technologies, and on Oct. 7 borrowed an additional $100 million under its existing convertible note structure. The carrying value of its Bitcoin holdings is also shrinking. The quarterly report showed the company held about 15,649 Bitcoin as of Sept. 30; at a price of about $63,750 (about NT$2.1 million) on Thursday afternoon, that position was worth about $998 million (about NT$33 billion). Assuming the holding quantity is unchanged, that marks a clear decline from a market value of about $1.31 billion (about NT$43 billion) at the end of September. For noteholders, conversion holds little appeal. The conversion price is about $34.72 per share (about NT$1,100), while the stock traded near $4 on Thursday, close to a record low — a gap of more than eight times. That also means that once the Nov. 30 put right is exercised, the company will almost certainly have to respond in cash. A wallet tagged by blockchain analytics firm Arkham as the notes' collateral wallet transferred out 4,259 Bitcoin on Nov. 5 to an address linked to Crypto.com. The transfer itself does not mean the Bitcoin has been sold; it only confirms that the collateral has moved. Note: The market value estimate assumes the Bitcoin holding quantity is unchanged since Sept. 30; the repayment demand represents the maximum amount noteholders could claim by exercising the one-time put right. The key thing to watch is whether Trump Media can scrape together enough cash in less than two weeks while holding on to its Bitcoin position. The company's current approach is "discounted repurchases plus a mix of cash and credit" — trimming the outstanding principal on one hand while avoiding a fire sale of Bitcoin at low prices on the other. But a clear gap remains between cash on hand and the potential repayment amount, and with the merger and new borrowing consuming resources at the same time, its room to maneuver on funding is relatively tight. For the market, this is not just one company's financial problem. Trump Media is one of the few listed companies that treats Bitcoin as a core asset and has even borrowed against it. If it is forced to sell its holdings, it would become a negative case study in corporate-level Bitcoin treasury management and could prompt other companies that have put crypto assets on their balance sheets to reassess liquidity risk. As for bond and equity investors, the huge gap between the conversion price and the market price has left the value of these notes almost entirely dependent on whether the company can honor its repayment obligations. extraction.body: Trump Media faces a November 30 deadline on $883.5M in convertible notes after a $100M buyback, raising questions about DJT stock and its Bitcoin treasury. Trump Media & Technology Group ( NASDAQ: DJT ) faces a November 30 deadline that could force the company to repay up to $883.5 million in convertible debt, putting its Bitcoin treasury strategy under pressure as management attempts to preserve cryptocurrency holdings without diluting shareholders. According to a November 17 SEC filing , the Truth Social parent repurchased $100 million in convertible senior secured notes at a discount, reducing outstanding principal to approximately $883.5 million. The transaction was funded using existing cash. Trump Media originally issued $1 billion in zero-coupon convertible notes in May 2025 to support its cryptocurrency investment strategy. The notes carry a conversion price of approximately $34.72 per DJT share, far above the stock's recent trading level near $4. That makes conversion into equity economically unattractive for noteholders under current market conditions. Instead, investors have the option to demand cash repayment at the November 30 repurchase date. Interim CEO Kevin McGurn said the company intends to use available cash and credit to address the obligations without issuing additional shares. During its November 9 earnings call, McGurn also emphasized management's desire to preserve Bitcoin holdings, allowing the company to continue its yield strategy while retaining exposure to a possible cryptocurrency price recovery. However, the company's financial resources are not entirely liquid. At September 30, Trump Media held approximately $182.3 million in cash and cash equivalents and $211.1 million in short-term investments. Together, those balances totaled roughly $393.4 million, substantially below the remaining debt principal. The figures precede the latest $100 million note repurchase and therefore do not represent the company's current available cash. Trump Media's latest quarterly results showed approximately 15,649 BTC held across its treasury and pledged-asset arrangements at September's end. Of that amount, approximately 4,261 BTC served as collateral for convertible notes, while another 11,385 BTC supported the company's Bitcoin options strategy. This distinction matters because pledged Bitcoin cannot necessarily be sold or transferred without satisfying contractual requirements. In its September quarterly filing , Trump Media acknowledged that unsuccessful refinancing efforts could require selling Bitcoin or other digital assets, seeking additional borrowing, or raising equity on unfavorable terms. The warning does not establish that a Bitcoin sale is planned. The company's recent $410 million quarterly profit also offers limited reassurance about immediate liquidity. Much of that result came from investment-related accounting gains rather than operating cash generation. Bitcoin's November selloff introduces another complication. Falling cryptocurrency prices reduce the market value of treasury assets even when the number of tokens remains unchanged. Trump Media's financing challenge arrives after DJT stock plunged nearly 70% during 2026, leaving shareholders increasingly exposed to the company's capital allocation decisions. The company has also pursued a multibillion-dollar Bitcoin treasury strategy alongside a proposed merger with nuclear-fusion developer TAE Technologies, increasing the importance of maintaining financial flexibility. Management has several potential options, including further discounted note repurchases, obtaining additional credit or using existing liquid assets. However, each carries different consequences for borrowing costs, cash reserves and shareholder exposure. Importantly, the November 30 date does not automatically require repayment of every outstanding note. The eventual cash obligation depends on how many holders exercise their repurchase rights and whether Trump Media reduces the balance beforehand. coreStoryFacts.text: The company's $2 billion bitcoin purchase comes as Trump Media looks to roll out a range of investment products, including a plan to sell exchange-traded funds, or ETFs.The bitcoin purchase will "help ensure our Company's financial freedom, help protect us against discrimination by financial institutions and will create synergies with the utility token we're planning to introduce across the Truth Social ecosphere," Nunes said in a statement.The company also said it has set aside $300 million for an "options acquisition strategy for bitcoin-related securities." Trump Media said it plans to continue acquiring bitcoin.Shares of Trump Media rose $1.04, or 5.6%, to $19.71 in Monday morning trading.

The company reported an operating loss for the quarter of $39.5 million, down from $98.3 million a year ago.What is a crypto treasury strategy?A crypto treasury strategy involves buying and holding cryptocurrencies, similar to how companies may invest in more traditional assets like bonds to provide them with financial flexibility.

It owns 607,000 bitcoins — worth more than $72 billion at today's bitcoin price — making it the largest public bitcoin treasury company, according to Bitcointreasuries.net.Saylor's company uses a variety of strategies, such as selling shares or issuing debt, to keep expanding its bitcoin holdings.
Trump, the largest investor in Trump Media, has increasingly focused on cryptocurrencies both through his private businesses and his administration.
Trump signed the GENIUS Act, the first major law governing digital currency."For the past five years, the only thing better than Bitcoin is More Bitcoin," Saylor wrote in a July 17 social media post.
McGurn elaborated on the company's thinking during a Nov.

9 earnings call: "We want to retain as much Bitcoin as possible, continue executing our yield strategy and wait for the asset's price to recover." He also stressed that the company is trying to avoid issuing additional shares, which would dilute existing shareholders including Donald Trump.
According to the latest combined prospectus, Trump's revocable trust holds 114.75 million shares; at roughly $4 per share (about NT$130), that stake is worth about $460 million (about NT$15 billion).
The trust's holding represents about 41% of Trump Media.
The quarterly report itself, however, laid out the risks.
The company acknowledged that if other financing efforts fall short of expectations, it may have to "sell Bitcoin or other digital assets" to fund the note repurchase.
Trump Media did not respond to a request for comment.
The key thing to watch is whether Trump Media can scrape together enough cash in less than two weeks while holding on to its Bitcoin position.

But a clear gap remains between cash on hand and the potential repayment amount, and with the merger and new borrowing consuming resources at the same time, its room to maneuver on funding is relatively tight.
For the market, this is not just one company's financial problem.
Trump Media is one of the few listed companies that treats Bitcoin as a core asset and has even borrowed against it.

If it is forced to sell its holdings, it would become a negative case study in corporate-level Bitcoin treasury management and could prompt other companies that have put crypto assets on their balance sheets to reassess liquidity risk.

As for bond and equity investors, the huge gap between the conversion price and the market price has left the value of these notes almost entirely dependent on whether the company can honor its repayment obligations.
The company, which owns the social platform Truth Social, issued $1 billion in zero-coupon convertible notes in May 2025, secured by Bitcoin, and used all of the proceeds to purchase Bitcoin.
The notes nominally mature in 2028, but holders hold a one-time put right allowing them to demand full cash repayment at face value on Nov.
"We plan to use our existing cash and credit facilities to optimize our capital structure and will not issue new shares," interim CEO Kevin McGurn said in the announcement.
For noteholders, conversion holds little appeal.
The carrying value of its Bitcoin holdings is also shrinking.

extraction.body: Trump Media & Technology Group (DJT) is trying to repay the debt it took on to buy Bitcoin without dumping the cryptocurrency itself. Creditors are now about two weeks away from gaining the right to demand cash repayment, at which point they could require the company to hand over as much as $883.5 million (about NT$29 billion). The company, which owns the social platform Truth Social, issued $1 billion in zero-coupon convertible notes in May 2025, secured by Bitcoin, and used all of the proceeds to purchase Bitcoin. The notes nominally mature in 2028, but holders hold a one-time put right allowing them to demand full cash repayment at face value on Nov. 30, 2026. The company said Tuesday it had used cash on hand to repurchase $100 million (about NT$3.3 billion) of the notes at a discount to face value, leaving about $883.5 million outstanding. "We plan to use our existing cash and credit facilities to optimize our capital structure and will not issue new shares," interim CEO Kevin McGurn said in the announcement. McGurn elaborated on the company's thinking during a Nov. 9 earnings call: "We want to retain as much Bitcoin as possible, continue executing our yield strategy and wait for the asset's price to recover." He also stressed that the company is trying to avoid issuing additional shares, which would dilute existing shareholders including Donald Trump. According to the latest combined prospectus, Trump's revocable trust holds 114.75 million shares; at roughly $4 per share (about NT$130), that stake is worth about $460 million (about NT$15 billion). The trust's holding represents about 41% of Trump Media. The quarterly report itself, however, laid out the risks. The company acknowledged that if other financing efforts fall short of expectations, it may have to "sell Bitcoin or other digital assets" to fund the note repurchase. Trump Media did not respond to a request for comment. Judging by the balance sheet, raising the cash will not be easy. As of Sept. 30, the company held about $393 million (about NT$13 billion) in cash and short-term investments, plus $31 million (about NT$1 billion) in restricted cash. Since that date, the company only moved this week to use cash to repurchase notes, still needs to advance its merger project with TAE Technologies, and on Oct. 7 borrowed an additional $100 million under its existing convertible note structure. The carrying value of its Bitcoin holdings is also shrinking. The quarterly report showed the company held about 15,649 Bitcoin as of Sept. 30; at a price of about $63,750 (about NT$2.1 million) on Thursday afternoon, that position was worth about $998 million (about NT$33 billion). Assuming the holding quantity is unchanged, that marks a clear decline from a market value of about $1.31 billion (about NT$43 billion) at the end of September. The Truth Social owner repurchased $100 million of its convertible notes this week. That leaves about $883.5 million outstanding ahead of a November 30, 2026 date when noteholders can demand their money back. The company says its plan is to pay with cash and new credit, not by selling crypto or issuing fresh shares. Its own filings, however, keep a back door open: if other financing falls short, it may have to sell digital assets. The debt in question traces back to May 2025. That is when TMTG issued roughly $1 billion in zero-coupon convertible senior secured notes, with the proceeds aimed at building a Bitcoin treasury. A quick translation of that mouthful. Zero-coupon means the notes pay no regular interest. Convertible means holders could swap them for stock. Senior secured means these lenders stand near the front of the line, with collateral behind them. The catch is a put feature. On November 30, 2026, holders can ask TMTG to repay the notes at par, meaning full face value. As of November 17, 2026, TMTG had bought back $100 million of the notes at a discount. Paying less than face value to retire debt early is the corporate equivalent of settling a bill before it goes to collections. Interim CEO Kevin McGurn said the approach fits the company's goal of tidying up its capital structure without further equity dilution. Issuing new shares would spread ownership thinner and could weigh on shareholder value, a concern for a stock already under pressure. As of September 30, 2026, TMTG reported total assets of about $2.47 billion. Digital assets, including Bitcoin and Cronos, made up roughly 55% of that figure. The company held around 15,649 BTC at that date. Of those, 4,261 BTC were pledged as collateral for the notes, while other portions were placed in yield generation programs. So the Bitcoin pile is not one tidy vault. Some of it is locked up securing the very debt TMTG is trying to retire, and some is out working to earn yield. Meanwhile, the core business is not carrying much weight. TMTG's media operations are losing money, and the company has leaned on unrealized gains from volatile digital assets for financial support. The stock has not been much help either. TMTG shares traded near record lows of about $4.20 in mid-November 2026, having fallen more than 60% year-to-date. For TMTG shareholders, the company's stated priorities are clear. It wants to avoid dilution, and it wants to keep its crypto. The question is whether cash on hand and new credit facilities can cover whatever noteholders demand on November 30. The $100 million discounted buyback is a modest positive on that front. Each dollar retired early is a dollar that cannot be put back to the company at par later. Third, any disclosure showing changes to its Bitcoin balance, its pledged collateral, or the coins deployed in yield programs. The Cronos position is worth tracking too. Digital assets beyond Bitcoin are part of that 55% share of total assets, and any sales there would offer a clue about which holdings the company considers expendable. The US House Foreign Affairs Committee on Thursday (19 November) made a rare disclosure of chip export licensing data, revealing that President Donald J. Trump’s administration approved exports to Chinese companies of nearly 900,000 advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips made by Nvidia and AMD over the six months from December last year to May this year.

According to documents released by the committee, companies applied to export more than 3.4 million chips to China during that period. The US Commerce Department ultimately approved exports of 879,000 chips, including Nvidia’s H200 and AMD’s comparable MI325X.

Notably, the export approvals covered 75,000 chips for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD. All four companies are on the Pentagon’s list of Chinese military-linked companies. However, the documents did not specify how many of the chips approved for export were ultimately delivered to China.

Releasing the data, House Foreign Affairs Committee chairman Brian Mast, a Republican congressman from Florida, described it as the most detailed public disclosure since the US Export Control Reform Act was enacted in 2018.

The rare US disclosure of sensitive export data comes as the Trump administration faces mounting political scrutiny. Earlier media reports alleged that former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. Renewed attention to the smuggling of Nvidia chips into China without punishment has also fuelled calls in Washington for tougher technology restrictions on China.

Chris McGuire, a former US official and expert on the US-China technology conflict, said it was shocking that more than 30% of AI chips exported to China went to companies designated by the US as Chinese military-industrial firms. He said this raised questions about whether the Commerce Department had conducted rigorous national security reviews before granting approval.

During his presidency, former US president Joe Biden imposed strict restrictions on chip exports to China over concerns that AI chips could bolster China’s military capabilities and erode America’s technological edge. However, Trump overturned the Biden-era ban in December last year, giving Nvidia the green light to sell H200 chips to China and drawing fierce criticism from China hawks across the US political divide.

Responding to the newly disclosed data, Nvidia stressed in a statement that the approvals were subject to strict conditions and quantity limits, and that it had since stopped shipping H200 chips to China. AMD said it strictly adhered to US export control regulations to ensure compliance across its global operations.
The US Commerce Department, the Chinese embassy in the US and the four Chinese companies did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.

extraction.body: Washington DC: The Donald Trump administration had cleared the export of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips manufactured by Nvidia and AMD to Chinese firms between December 2025 and May 2026, according to the US House Foreign Affairs Committee. The Commerce Department authorised the export of 879,000 chips, with Alibaba cleared to receive 75,000, Tencent 150,000, Baidu 43,000 and BYD 4,000, the committee said. Companies had sought permission to export 3.4 million such chips to China during the same period, according to committee records, Al Jazeera reported. The committee released the data on AI chip export licences for the period between December 2025 and May 2026 following reports about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's alleged affair with a woman named Alice Huang, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. The Pentagon has identified all four Chinese firms named in the committee's report as companies allegedly backed by China's military, the media outlet reported. The committee said its chairman, Brian Mast, had invoked powers granted to him under the Export Control Reform Act to make public details of licence applications submitted by Nvidia and AMD for exporting AI chips to China. However, it remains unclear how many of the licences translated into actual shipments to China. The approved chips included Nvidia's H200 and AMD's equivalent MI325X. Meanwhile, Nvidia said in a statement that the export clearances came with strict conditions and volume limits. The company also said it had halted H200 shipments to China despite securing some licences. Citing concerns that advanced AI chips could strengthen China's military capabilities and undermine America's technological edge, the Joe Biden administration had imposed restrictions on their export to Chinese firms. However, after returning to power, the Trump administration reversed that policy in December, authorising Nvidia to export its H200 chips to China. Last week, Reuters reported that US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick could be at risk of losing his job as senior White House officials considered removing him amid the growing spy scandal involving former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang. Lutnick is reportedly facing questions from lawmakers over the administration's decision not to include dozens of Chinese firms on a key US trade blacklist, as well as concerns about its oversight of Nvidia's chip exports to China. However, Trump has come to Lutnick's defence. The White House said it continues to back the Commerce Secretary, despite concerns within the administration that he was slow to act on reports of advanced chips being smuggled into China.

The US House Foreign Affairs Committee on Thursday (19 November) made a rare disclosure of chip export licensing data, revealing that President Donald J. Trump’s administration approved exports to Chinese companies of nearly 900,000 advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips made by Nvidia and AMD over the six months from December last year to May this year. According to documents released by the committee, companies applied to export more than 3.4 million chips to China during that period. The US Commerce Department ultimately approved exports of 879,000 chips, including Nvidia’s H200 and AMD’s comparable MI325X. Notably, the export approvals covered 75,000 chips for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD. All four companies are on the Pentagon’s list of Chinese military-linked companies. However, the documents did not specify how many of the chips approved for export were ultimately delivered to China. Releasing the data, House Foreign Affairs Committee chairman Brian Mast, a Republican congressman from Florida, described it as the most detailed public disclosure since the US Export Control Reform Act was enacted in 2018. The rare US disclosure of sensitive export data comes as the Trump administration faces mounting political scrutiny. Earlier media reports alleged that former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. Renewed attention to the smuggling of Nvidia chips into China without punishment has also fuelled calls in Washington for tougher technology restrictions on China. Chris McGuire, a former US official and expert on the US-China technology conflict, said it was shocking that more than 30% of AI chips exported to China went to companies designated by the US as Chinese military-industrial firms. He said this raised questions about whether the Commerce Department had conducted rigorous national security reviews before granting approval. During his presidency, former US president Joe Biden imposed strict restrictions on chip exports to China over concerns that AI chips could bolster China’s military capabilities and erode America’s technological edge. However, Trump overturned the Biden-era ban in December last year, giving Nvidia the green light to sell H200 chips to China and drawing fierce criticism from China hawks across the US political divide. Responding to the newly disclosed data, Nvidia stressed in a statement that the approvals were subject to strict conditions and quantity limits, and that it had since stopped shipping H200 chips to China. AMD said it strictly adhered to US export control regulations to ensure compliance across its global operations. The US Commerce Department, the Chinese embassy in the US and the four Chinese companies did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment. The US House Foreign Affairs Committee on Thursday (19 November) made a rare disclosure of chip export licensing data, revealing that President Donald J. Trump’s administration approved exports to Chinese companies of nearly 900,000 advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips made by Nvidia and AMD over the six months from December last year to May this year.

According to documents released by the committee, companies applied to export more than 3.4 million chips to China during that period. The US Commerce Department ultimately approved exports of 879,000 chips, including Nvidia’s H200 and AMD’s comparable MI325X.

Notably, the export approvals covered 75,000 chips for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD. All four companies are on the Pentagon’s list of Chinese military-linked companies. However, the documents did not specify how many of the chips approved for export were ultimately delivered to China.

Releasing the data, House Foreign Affairs Committee chairman Brian Mast, a Republican congressman from Florida, described it as the most detailed public disclosure since the US Export Control Reform Act was enacted in 2018.

The rare US disclosure of sensitive export data comes as the Trump administration faces mounting political scrutiny. Earlier media reports alleged that former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. Renewed attention to the smuggling of Nvidia chips into China without punishment has also fuelled calls in Washington for tougher technology restrictions on China.

Chris McGuire, a former US official and expert on the US-China technology conflict, said it was shocking that more than 30% of AI chips exported to China went to companies designated by the US as Chinese military-industrial firms. He said this raised questions about whether the Commerce Department had conducted rigorous national security reviews before granting approval.

During his presidency, former US president Joe Biden imposed strict restrictions on chip exports to China over concerns that AI chips could bolster China’s military capabilities and erode America’s technological edge. However, Trump overturned the Biden-era ban in December last year, giving Nvidia the green light to sell H200 chips to China and drawing fierce criticism from China hawks across the US political divide.

Responding to the newly disclosed data, Nvidia stressed in a statement that the approvals were subject to strict conditions and quantity limits, and that it had since stopped shipping H200 chips to China. AMD said it strictly adhered to US export control regulations to ensure compliance across its global operations.
The US Commerce Department, the Chinese embassy in the US and the four Chinese companies did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.

Kathy Hochul broke ground November 19, 2026, at the University at Buffalo on a supercomputing center that will house Empire AI Gamma, the consortium’s third phase. The project is intended to give researchers across New York’s universities access to more computing power. The Empire AI Research Computing Center will occupy 46,000 square feet on Service Center Road on UB’s North Campus. Hochul’s office says the permanent facility is expected to be completed by early 2028. UB gives a later target for becoming operational: late summer 2028 . The governor’s office describes Empire AI as a public-private initiative worth more than $500 million . That figure covers the initiative, not just this building. Its organizing principle is shared access: bringing public and private research institutions together around computing resources that, the state says, no single university could afford independently. Empire AI’s earlier systems have been operating at UB’s Downtown Campus. Empire AI Board Chair Tom Secunda said the initiative now has more than 1,500 registered users and hundreds of research projects underway. Alpha launched in 2024 with a philanthropic contribution from the Simons Foundation. Beta, a $40 million supercomputer at UB, became fully operational in August 2026. According to UB, the NVIDIA-powered Beta system delivers 11 times Alpha’s AI training capacity, 40 times its inference performance and eight times its data storage. For the permanent center, SUNY Chancellor John B. King Jr. described the goal as working with larger datasets, larger models and more complex simulations, with the hope of making discoveries faster. UB plans to capture heat generated by the computing center and use it to warm buildings across the North Campus. The university presents that reuse as part of its effort to decarbonize the campus. UB says a dry cooler will remove heat using outside air, reducing reliance on water-intensive cooling methods. Buffalo’s cooler climate is expected to help conserve energy and water, with a high-efficiency water-cooling system needed only during the region’s hottest months. Research continues while the permanent home is built. UB says its existing Empire AI projects include early-childhood education, drug discovery, wildfire prediction and quantum materials—work already using the shared infrastructure before Gamma arrives. Governor Kathy Hochul was among those present for the ceremony.

“It's also worth emphasizing that at SUNY we are already on track to achieve a 40-percent reduction in carbon emissions by 2030, and this work at Empire AI actually builds on that effort because we will leverage electricity from renewable and clean sources, and we will use processes like heat capture to make sure that the heat that is produced by the supercomputer is actually recycled to heat other buildings at UB,” King said.

That good, the governor said, includes work by Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute to accurately diagnose lung cancer, work at Columbia University to create better weather tracking models, and at UB, speech therapy for children living with disabilities.

extraction.body: Milestone Complements on New York’s Nation-Leading RAISE Act on Frontier AI Accountability and Launch of Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University to Advance Independent Research Into AI Safety and Security Governor Kathy Hochul today officially broke ground on the permanent home of Empire AI at the University at Buffalo, marking a major milestone in New York’s historic effort to lead artificial intelligence research for the public good. The groundbreaking launches the next phase of development for Empire AI Gamma, the full-scale supercomputing facility that will dramatically expand the computing power available to researchers at New York's leading public and private universities and establishing Empire AI as the most powerful academic AI research computer in the country. First announced by Governor Hochul in her 2024 State of the State address, Empire AI has grown into a more than $500 million public-private initiative that is already supporting groundbreaking research in medicine, climate science, advanced manufacturing and other fields, while establishing New York as a national model for responsible AI innovation. Today's groundbreaking comes just days after Governor Hochul launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University, a first-of-its-kind research initiative bringing together more than 80 scientists to independently study the safety, security and performance of advanced AI systems using Empire AI's computing infrastructure. Together, these investments are advancing the Governor's vision of a statewide AI research ecosystem that gives academic researchers the tools, infrastructure and expertise needed to accelerate scientific discovery and ensure artificial intelligence serves the public good. “Two years ago, we made a commitment to put New York at the forefront of the AI revolution — while ensuring safe and responsible AI development is a top priority — and today we are delivering on that promise,” Governor Hochul said. “Empire AI is already giving our brightest researchers the most powerful academic AI computing resources in the country, and now we're building the permanent home that will take this initiative to an entirely new level. From advancing medical breakthroughs to tackling climate change, we're proving that New York can lead the nation in artificial intelligence while building responsibly, creating opportunities and making sure this technology benefits all New Yorkers.” Building the Future of AI Research in New York Two years ago, we made a commitment to put New York at the forefront of the AI revolution — while ensuring safe and responsible AI development is a top priority — and today we are delivering on that promise.” Empire AI Board Chair Tom Secunda said, “Just two years ago, Empire AI was an ambitious idea, and today it is a national model for putting world-class computing power in the hands of academic researchers, with more than 1,500 registered users and hundreds of research projects already underway. Thanks to Governor Hochul's vision and leadership, New York has brought together government, universities and philanthropy to build a scientific resource that no single institution could create on its own. This groundbreaking takes that commitment to the next level, strengthening New York's leadership and helping shape the future of scientific discovery across the nation.” Rochester Institute of Technology President Bill Sanders said, “RIT has always believed that technology is most powerful when it is applied with purpose. This groundbreaking moves that vision forward on a statewide scale. Through Empire AI, RIT researchers and students will work alongside some of New York’s other leading institutions, combining extraordinary computing power with human creativity and ingenuity to advance responsible AI, accelerate discovery and create meaningful impact for our communities, our economy and our world.” Co-founder and Chair of the Simons Foundation Marilyn Simons said, “Many of the greatest scientific breakthroughs begin with a question no one has been able to answer. Empire AI gives more scientists the tools to tackle those questions. We are grateful to Governor Hochul for bringing together New York's leading research institutions and philanthropic partners to make this extraordinary shared resource possible. Today's groundbreaking is an investment in the next generation of scientists and in discoveries that will benefit us all.” State University of New York Chancellor John B. King Jr. said, “Empire AI is driving New York State’s leadership in leveraging AI to achieve research excellence that advances the public good. From accelerating the search for cures and treatments for disease to enhancing speech language therapy for children, and from advancing biotechnology research to tackling climate change, SUNY researchers are addressing some of society’s most pressing challenges thanks to Empire AI. SUNY is proud to host Empire AI at the State University of New York at Buffalo, and we are grateful to Governor Hochul for her vision and steadfast leadership.” The SUNY Board of Trustees said, “Visionary leadership from Governor Hochul makes it possible for SUNY and our higher education partners to pioneer research for the public good through Empire AI. The permanent Empire AI facility will accelerate groundbreaking research and innovations that improve communities throughout New York State and beyond.” Empire State Development President, CEO & Commissioner Hope Knight said, “Under Governor Hochul’s leadership, New York is proving that when we invest in broad, responsible access to cutting-edge technology, our entire economy wins. Today’s groundbreaking at the University at Buffalo marks a major step forward for Empire AI — creating jobs now while empowering New York’s students, researchers, and businesses to drive innovation, attract new investment, and deliver lasting economic benefits to communities across the state.” U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand said, “New York State is setting the national standard for responsible AI. Empire AI at the University at Buffalo represents a $500 million investment in our future, fueling cutting-edge research and proving that artificial intelligence can be harnessed safely as a powerful force for the public good.” Congressmember Tim Kennedy said, “For decades, the world has looked to New York State to lead the way in technological advancement. With this historic groundbreaking at UB, we continue that tradition by advancing research that benefits New Yorkers in a secure and responsible manner. As the next generation of researchers and entrepreneurs looks for where to call home, we’re keeping Western New York at the forefront of innovation.” State Senator Jeremy J. Zellner said, “Western New York has the talent and institutions to lead in the industries of tomorrow, and Empire AI puts us in a position to do just that,” said Senator Jeremy J. Zellner. “With its permanent home at the University at Buffalo, we are investing in groundbreaking research, economic opportunity, and Buffalo’s place in the future of technology. I thank Governor Hochul for ensuring our region is not watching the next technological revolution from the sidelines but helping lead it.” Assemblymember Bill Conrad said, “As we witness the lightning-speed advancement of artificial intelligence, we must consider how best to harness AI's grand potential for the advancement of humankind. Its future applications must be shaped by knowledgeable, responsible hands, and our state's consortium of universities, public and private, represent a world-renowned hub for that talent. I thank Governor Hochul for her foresightedness here, and I join in celebrating the partnerships that are solidifying UB's place in the realm of global research. Empire AI will establish New York State as a leader in supercomputing and a uniquely influential force in the shaping of AI's all-important future.” University at Buffalo President Caroline Attardo Genco said, “Today we break ground not only on a pioneering new facility, but on a lasting commitment to the people of Western New York and New York State. I am deeply grateful to Governor Kathy Hochul, whose vision and steadfast advocacy made this extraordinary resource a reality, and to our Empire AI partners for their invaluable collaboration. At UB, our researchers are already putting Empire AI to work on challenges in education and neuroscience, climate science and advanced manufacturing. As both the home of Empire AI and a neighbor invested in the future of our region, we embrace the responsibility that comes with those roles. The discoveries that begin here will improve lives, draw talent to our region and help our communities thrive for years to come.” New York University President Linda G. Mills said, “Governor Hochul has ensured that New York State is and will continue to be a leader in AI for years to come, contributing breakthroughs that will benefit the nation in ways we can only imagine today. New York University looks forward to its ongoing work with our university peers to drive scientific discovery—and has already deployed Empire AI’s world-class computing power to better understand the brain, to build more sustainable energy sources and novel materials, and to even improve AI itself.” CUNY Graduate Center President and Empire AI Board Treasurer Joshua Brumberg said, “The City University of New York’s participation in Empire AI has supercharged our researchers’ capabilities to solve pressing societal problems. It also allows us to conduct research for the public good and attracts to CUNY the best faculty and students who are excited to work in New York and gain access to Empire AI’s compute power.” Binghamton University President Anne D’Alleva said, “Empire AI is positioning New York, and especially the State University of New York, as the leader in safe and responsible AI that serves the public good. Binghamton University shares its congratulations with the University at Buffalo on the next phase of Empire AI Gamma. Our faculty and staff in the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research are looking forward to working with our partners at Buffalo and we thank Governor Hochul and the entire Empire AI team for its support of research and scholarship throughout the SUNY system.” Vice President for Research for the University of Rochester and Empire AI Board Member Steve Dewhurst said, “Empire AI has become an increasingly important resource for advancing research and innovation at the University of Rochester. Researchers across our institution are leveraging its capabilities to support a remarkable range of projects, spanning uses such as understanding brain-wide fluid flow, predicting the quantum dynamics of light-matter quasiparticles (polaritons), improving our ability to model climate change and much more. This breadth of use speaks to the transformative potential of Empire AI to accelerate scientific discovery and societal solutions by helping our researchers tackle complex challenges that traditional resources alone cannot address. We are deeply grateful to Governor Hochul and New York State for its vision and leadership in establishing Empire AI, and proud to be among the leading research institutions to benefit from the new Gamma facility, which will further expand the possibilities for research and discovery throughout the consortium.” Anne and Joel Ehrenkranz Dean at Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai Eric J. Nestler, MD, PhD said, “New York’s investment in Empire AI represents an important commitment to advancing scientific discovery through the responsible development and application of artificial intelligence. At Mount Sinai, we are already translating the potential of AI into meaningful advances in biomedical research, clinical care and medical education. Our work includes leveraging AI to accelerate drug discovery, developing sophisticated digital tools to support clinical decision-making across our hospitals and clinics, and integrating innovative AI capabilities into clinical workflows to help clinicians access and apply knowledge more effectively. As a member of the Empire AI consortium, we are proud to contribute our research expertise and collaborative spirit to this statewide effort. By bringing together leading academic institutions and providing researchers with unprecedented computing resources, New York is creating new opportunities to accelerate breakthroughs, improve human health and ensure that AI advances are developed and deployed safely, ethically and for the public good.” CUNY Chancellor Félix V. Matos Rodríguez said, “The groundbreaking of Empire AI’s permanent home marks an important new chapter in New York’s commitment to research and innovation for the public good. CUNY is proud to be part of this effort, which is expanding access to world-class computing resources and empowering researchers to tackle society’s most pressing challenges. As AI continues to transform our world, it is essential that its development remains responsible, equitable and focused on benefiting all New Yorkers.” University at Albany President Havidán Rodríguez said, “Artificial intelligence is already changing our world in countless ways. As one of the nation's most diverse public research universities, the University at Albany is committed to ensuring that our students and faculty have a seat at the table where this technology is being developed. Governor Hochul's Empire AI initiative is providing that opportunity to research universities that are focused on work that benefits the public good, like UAlbany. Together we are shaping the responsible development and trustworthy use of this technology that will dramatically reshape human knowledge, scientific exploration, and creative work in the future.” Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute President Martin A. Schmidt said, “Breaking ground on Empire AI’s permanent home marks an important milestone in strengthening New York’s capacity to lead in artificial intelligence research. By giving institutions access to advanced computing and shared expertise, Empire AI will accelerate progress in health, climate science and advanced manufacturing, while opening new opportunities at the intersection of AI and quantum science. RPI is proud to be a founding partner in this effort and grateful to Governor Hochul for her sustained leadership in advancing this collaboration.” Stony Brook University President Andrea Goldsmith said, “Stony Brook University is incredibly proud to drive forward Governor Hochul’s transformative vision to make New York a national model for AI-driven scientific research. Our exceptional researchers are rapidly advancing the frontiers of knowledge across scientific disciplines through the use of AI, and the addition of Empire AI’s supercomputing center will significantly expand their capability to make groundbreaking discoveries that benefit our communities, our great state, our country and the world.” Cornell University President Michael I. Kotlikoff said, “Cornell is proud to be part of the Empire AI consortium, which exemplifies what New York can do when its leading universities, government, and philanthropy join forces in service of the public good. Universities bring a distinct lens to AI, one grounded in long-term, open, and responsible inquiry. Empire AI is giving our faculty research teams access to unmatched computing power to take on questions in service of the greater good, from improving human health to building a more sustainable future, at a scale no single institution could access alone. We are grateful to Governor Hochul for her vision, leadership and investment in make New York a national model to demonstrate how public investment in academic AI research can accelerate discovery and benefit all New Yorkers.” Executive Vice President for Research at Columbia University and Empire AI Board Member Jeannette M. Wing said, “Columbia researchers are using Empire AI to measure NYC traffic volume to improve public safety, to enhance long-term climate resilience to floods and extreme heat in New York, and to better predict mental health behavioral outcomes like anxiety and depression. And unlike today’s AI models which stop learning once they are released, one Columbia research lab is using Empire AI to build agents that, like the human brain, keep learning from experience throughout their lifetimes. None of this work could be done without the computational capability of Empire AI.” New York's Growing Leadership in AI Science and Research and Safety The groundbreaking complements Governor Hochul's broader efforts to establish New York as a national center for scientific discovery and responsible artificial intelligence. Last week, Governor Hochul launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University. Supported by a historic $30 million philanthropic gift from a group of donors led by Empire AI Board Chair Tom Secunda, alongside an initial $25 million SUNY research investment, the center will bring together more than 80 scientists and researchers from institutions across New York. With Alpha and Beta already supporting researchers, the new Binghamton center advancing independent AI research, and construction of Gamma moving forward, Governor Hochul's original vision for Empire AI is becoming a permanent scientific resource designed to serve New Yorkers for generations. This announcement builds on Governor Hochul’s nation-leading AI safety agenda, which also includes implementation of New York’s RAISE Act. Under that new law, large frontier AI developers will be required to register with the state and comply with strict safety, transparency and reporting requirements — including New York’s strongest-in-the-nation requirement to report any critical safety incident within 72 hours. The Governor also established the first-in-the-nation Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust (DIGIT) to implement the RAISE Act and oversee large frontier AI Developers.
