University at Buffalo President Caroline Attardo Genco said, “Today we break ground not only on a pioneering new facility, but on a lasting commitment to the people of Western New York and New York State. I am deeply grateful to Governor Kathy Hochul, whose vision and steadfast advocacy made this extraordinary resource a reality, and to our Empire AI partners for their invaluable collaboration. At UB, our researchers are already putting Empire AI to work on challenges in education and neuroscience, climate science and advanced manufacturing. As both the home of Empire AI and a neighbor invested in the future of our region, we embrace the responsibility that comes with those roles. The discoveries that begin here will improve lives, draw talent to our region and help our communities thrive for years to come.”

New York University President Linda G. Mills said, “Governor Hochul has ensured that New York State is and will continue to be a leader in AI for years to come, contributing breakthroughs that will benefit the nation in ways we can only imagine today. New York University looks forward to its ongoing work with our university peers to drive scientific discovery—and has already deployed Empire AI’s world-class computing power to better understand the brain, to build more sustainable energy sources and novel materials, and to even improve AI itself.”

CUNY Graduate Center President and Empire AI Board Treasurer Joshua Brumberg said, “The City University of New York’s participation in Empire AI has supercharged our researchers’ capabilities to solve pressing societal problems. It also allows us to conduct research for the public good and attracts to CUNY the best faculty and students who are excited to work in New York and gain access to Empire AI’s compute power.”

Binghamton University President Anne D’Alleva said, “Empire AI is positioning New York, and especially the State University of New York, as the leader in safe and responsible AI that serves the public good. Binghamton University shares its congratulations with the University at Buffalo on the next phase of Empire AI Gamma. Our faculty and staff in the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research are looking forward to working with our partners at Buffalo and we thank Governor Hochul and the entire Empire AI team for its support of research and scholarship throughout the SUNY system.”

Vice President for Research for the University of Rochester and Empire AI Board Member Steve Dewhurst said, “Empire AI has become an increasingly important resource for advancing research and innovation at the University of Rochester. Researchers across our institution are leveraging its capabilities to support a remarkable range of projects, spanning uses such as understanding brain-wide fluid flow, predicting the quantum dynamics of light-matter quasiparticles (polaritons), improving our ability to model climate change and much more. This breadth of use speaks to the transformative potential of Empire AI to accelerate scientific discovery and societal solutions by helping our researchers tackle complex challenges that traditional resources alone cannot address. We are deeply grateful to Governor Hochul and New York State for its vision and leadership in establishing Empire AI, and proud to be among the leading research institutions to benefit from the new Gamma facility, which will further expand the possibilities for research and discovery throughout the consortium.”

Anne and Joel Ehrenkranz Dean at Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai Eric J. Nestler, MD, PhD said, “New York’s investment in Empire AI represents an important commitment to advancing scientific discovery through the responsible development and application of artificial intelligence. At Mount Sinai, we are already translating the potential of AI into meaningful advances in biomedical research, clinical care and medical education. Our work includes leveraging AI to accelerate drug discovery, developing sophisticated digital tools to support clinical decision-making across our hospitals and clinics, and integrating innovative AI capabilities into clinical workflows to help clinicians access and apply knowledge more effectively. As a member of the Empire AI consortium, we are proud to contribute our research expertise and collaborative spirit to this statewide effort. By bringing together leading academic institutions and providing researchers with unprecedented computing resources, New York is creating new opportunities to accelerate breakthroughs, improve human health and ensure that AI advances are developed and deployed safely, ethically and for the public good.”

CUNY Chancellor Félix V. Matos Rodríguez said, “The groundbreaking of Empire AI’s permanent home marks an important new chapter in New York’s commitment to research and innovation for the public good. CUNY is proud to be part of this effort, which is expanding access to world-class computing resources and empowering researchers to tackle society’s most pressing challenges. As AI continues to transform our world, it is essential that its development remains responsible, equitable and focused on benefiting all New Yorkers.”

University at Albany President Havidán Rodríguez said, “Artificial intelligence is already changing our world in countless ways. As one of the nation's most diverse public research universities, the University at Albany is committed to ensuring that our students and faculty have a seat at the table where this technology is being developed. Governor Hochul's Empire AI initiative is providing that opportunity to research universities that are focused on work that benefits the public good, like UAlbany. Together we are shaping the responsible development and trustworthy use of this technology that will dramatically reshape human knowledge, scientific exploration, and creative work in the future.”

Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute President Martin A. Schmidt said, “Breaking ground on Empire AI’s permanent home marks an important milestone in strengthening New York’s capacity to lead in artificial intelligence research. By giving institutions access to advanced computing and shared expertise, Empire AI will accelerate progress in health, climate science and advanced manufacturing, while opening new opportunities at the intersection of AI and quantum science. RPI is proud to be a founding partner in this effort and grateful to Governor Hochul for her sustained leadership in advancing this collaboration.”

Stony Brook University President Andrea Goldsmith said, “Stony Brook University is incredibly proud to drive forward Governor Hochul’s transformative vision to make New York a national model for AI-driven scientific research. Our exceptional researchers are rapidly advancing the frontiers of knowledge across scientific disciplines through the use of AI, and the addition of Empire AI’s supercomputing center will significantly expand their capability to make groundbreaking discoveries that benefit our communities, our great state, our country and the world.”

Cornell University President Michael I. Kotlikoff said, “Cornell is proud to be part of the Empire AI consortium, which exemplifies what New York can do when its leading universities, government, and philanthropy join forces in service of the public good. Universities bring a distinct lens to AI, one grounded in long-term, open, and responsible inquiry. Empire AI is giving our faculty research teams access to unmatched computing power to take on questions in service of the greater good, from improving human health to building a more sustainable future, at a scale no single institution could access alone. We are grateful to Governor Hochul for her vision, leadership and investment in make New York a national model to demonstrate how public investment in academic AI research can accelerate discovery and benefit all New Yorkers.”

Executive Vice President for Research at Columbia University and Empire AI Board Member Jeannette M. Wing said, “Columbia researchers are using Empire AI to measure NYC traffic volume to improve public safety, to enhance long-term climate resilience to floods and extreme heat in New York, and to better predict mental health behavioral outcomes like anxiety and depression. And unlike today’s AI models which stop learning once they are released, one Columbia research lab is using Empire AI to build agents that, like the human brain, keep learning from experience throughout their lifetimes. None of this work could be done without the computational capability of Empire AI.”
New York's Growing Leadership in AI Science and Research and Safety

The groundbreaking complements Governor Hochul's broader efforts to establish New York as a national center for scientific discovery and responsible artificial intelligence. Last week, Governor Hochul launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University. Supported by a historic $30 million philanthropic gift from a group of donors led by Empire AI Board Chair Tom Secunda, alongside an initial $25 million SUNY research investment, the center will bring together more than 80 scientists and researchers from institutions across New York.

With Alpha and Beta already supporting researchers, the new Binghamton center advancing independent AI research, and construction of Gamma moving forward, Governor Hochul's original vision for Empire AI is becoming a permanent scientific resource designed to serve New Yorkers for generations.

This announcement builds on Governor Hochul’s nation-leading AI safety agenda, which also includes implementation of New York’s RAISE Act. Under that new law, large frontier AI developers will be required to register with the state and comply with strict safety, transparency and reporting requirements — including New York’s strongest-in-the-nation requirement to report any critical safety incident within 72 hours. The Governor also established the first-in-the-nation Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust (DIGIT) to implement the RAISE Act and oversee large frontier AI Developers.

Kathy Hochul broke ground November 19, 2026, at the University at Buffalo on a supercomputing center that will house Empire AI Gamma, the consortium’s third phase.
The investment expands shared compute access for university researchers, but the stated funding figure applies to the broader initiative, not the building alone.
The Empire AI Research Computing Center will occupy 46,000 square feet on Service Center Road on UB’s North Campus.
The governor’s office describes Empire AI as a public-private initiative worth more than $500 million .
Its organizing principle is shared access: bringing public and private research institutions together around computing resources that, the state says, no single university could afford independently.
For the permanent center, SUNY Chancellor John B.
Research continues while the permanent home is built.
Hochul’s office says the permanent facility is expected to be completed by early 2028.

The facility, called Empire AI Gamma, is expected to be completed by early 2028, according to the governor’s office , and it matters to research offices because it is a state-funded alternative to each university buying its own AI computing.
New York State’s Empire AI has taken another step forward, with a groundbreaking on the University at Buffalo North Campus, where a permanent supercomputing center will be housed.
Empire AI is a $500 million public-private initiative involving higher education institutions throughout the state.
Governor Kathy Hochul was among those present for the ceremony.

“It's also worth emphasizing that at SUNY we are already on track to achieve a 40-percent reduction in carbon emissions by 2030, and this work at Empire AI actually builds on that effort because we will leverage electricity from renewable and clean sources, and we will use processes like heat capture to make sure that the heat that is produced by the supercomputer is actually recycled to heat other buildings at UB,” King said.

That good, the governor said, includes work by Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute to accurately diagnose lung cancer, work at Columbia University to create better weather tracking models, and at UB, speech therapy for children living with disabilities.
Tom Secunda, chair of Empire AI, says the technology and network changes the way research is conducted.
It also helps the academic sector do more with less.
He added it also strengthens New York's research ecosystem, by giving the state a means to attract and keep more world-class researchers.

That good, the governor said, includes work by Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute to accurately diagnose lung cancer, work at Columbia University to create better weather tracking models, and at UB, speech therapy for children living with disabilities.

extraction.body: Milestone Complements on New York’s Nation-Leading RAISE Act on Frontier AI Accountability and Launch of Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University to Advance Independent Research Into AI Safety and Security Governor Kathy Hochul today officially broke ground on the permanent home of Empire AI at the University at Buffalo, marking a major milestone in New York’s historic effort to lead artificial intelligence research for the public good. The groundbreaking launches the next phase of development for Empire AI Gamma, the full-scale supercomputing facility that will dramatically expand the computing power available to researchers at New York's leading public and private universities and establishing Empire AI as the most powerful academic AI research computer in the country. First announced by Governor Hochul in her 2024 State of the State address, Empire AI has grown into a more than $500 million public-private initiative that is already supporting groundbreaking research in medicine, climate science, advanced manufacturing and other fields, while establishing New York as a national model for responsible AI innovation. Today's groundbreaking comes just days after Governor Hochul launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University, a first-of-its-kind research initiative bringing together more than 80 scientists to independently study the safety, security and performance of advanced AI systems using Empire AI's computing infrastructure. Together, these investments are advancing the Governor's vision of a statewide AI research ecosystem that gives academic researchers the tools, infrastructure and expertise needed to accelerate scientific discovery and ensure artificial intelligence serves the public good. “Two years ago, we made a commitment to put New York at the forefront of the AI revolution — while ensuring safe and responsible AI development is a top priority — and today we are delivering on that promise,” Governor Hochul said. “Empire AI is already giving our brightest researchers the most powerful academic AI computing resources in the country, and now we're building the permanent home that will take this initiative to an entirely new level. From advancing medical breakthroughs to tackling climate change, we're proving that New York can lead the nation in artificial intelligence while building responsibly, creating opportunities and making sure this technology benefits all New Yorkers.” Building the Future of AI Research in New York Two years ago, we made a commitment to put New York at the forefront of the AI revolution — while ensuring safe and responsible AI development is a top priority — and today we are delivering on that promise.” Empire AI Board Chair Tom Secunda said, “Just two years ago, Empire AI was an ambitious idea, and today it is a national model for putting world-class computing power in the hands of academic researchers, with more than 1,500 registered users and hundreds of research projects already underway. Thanks to Governor Hochul's vision and leadership, New York has brought together government, universities and philanthropy to build a scientific resource that no single institution could create on its own. This groundbreaking takes that commitment to the next level, strengthening New York's leadership and helping shape the future of scientific discovery across the nation.” Rochester Institute of Technology President Bill Sanders said, “RIT has always believed that technology is most powerful when it is applied with purpose. This groundbreaking moves that vision forward on a statewide scale. extraction.body: Denmark's parliament has unanimously approved a security agreement with the United States, allowing for an expanded U.S. military presence in Greenland. The Folketing, Denmark's parliament, passed the agreement with a 109-0 vote on Thursday (November 19), as reported by Arctic Today . This decision marks the end of months of diplomatic tension between Denmark and the U.S. over President Donald Trump's interest in acquiring Greenland. The agreement, signed in New York on September 22, involves Denmark, Greenland, and the U.S. It supplements a 1951 defense accord and allows the U.S. to establish new military bases at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig in Greenland. The deal also permits the expansion of the Pituffik Space Base and the establishment of the Golden Dome missile defense shield, according to Al Jazeera . The agreement ensures that Greenland remains under Danish sovereignty while recognizing the island's right to self-determination. It also blocks non-NATO and non-EU states from gaining significant influence in sensitive sectors, preventing countries like China and Russia from strategic investments. Despite the smooth passage in Denmark, the agreement faced contention in Greenland's parliament, where it passed with 16 votes and seven abstentions earlier this month. The opposition party Naleraq criticized the deal, calling for a referendum and alleging that Greenland gains nothing from it. As reported by NBC5 , Greenland's Minister for Foreign Affairs, Múte B. Egede , accused Naleraq of leaking secret information, leading to a police report against the party. U.S. Ambassador to Denmark Ken Howery welcomed the agreement, stating it modernizes the partnership and strengthens security for the U.S., Denmark, Greenland, and NATO. He expressed optimism about deepening cooperation as the agreement is implemented. The agreement will remain in force even if Greenland gains independence, provided it joins NATO. It will officially take effect once the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs informs the U.S. that all procedures are complete.

Denmark’s Folketing unanimously ratified a security agreement with the United States covering Greenland on Thursday, with 109 members present voting in favour of the text without opposition or abstention. The agreement, signed in September and signed in New York on September 22, is aimed at bolstering security in the Arctic and North Atlantic and easing tensions over Donald Trump’s desire to annex the Arctic island. The deal supplements a 1951 accord on the US military presence in Greenland and allows the United States to build two military bases in Greenland.

The agreement also blocks countries outside the European Union and NATO from strategic sectors, in order to stop China or Russia from gaining influence over the territory, particularly through investments. The agreement is set to enter into force once the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs informs the US in a diplomatic note that procedures are complete.

The agreement remains in force even if Greenland gains full independence, and it reaffirms Danish sovereignty and the Greenlanders’ right to self-determination. The text is not subject to a vote by the US Senate because it is described as an executive agreement.

The ratification follows months of pressure tied to Donald Trump’s repeated calls for Greenland to become part of the United States and his refusal to rule out the use of military or economic force to seize control of the island. The dispute triggered a diplomatic crisis within NATO in January, forcing Denmark and Greenland into intensive negotiations that lasted for months before the agreement was approved by Greenland’s parliament earlier this month. Kenneth Howery, the U.S. ambassador to Denmark, welcomed the “strong support” in the Danish parliament for ratification of the deal “paving the way for it to enter into force.”

extraction.body: Denmark's parliament has unanimously approved a security agreement with the United States, allowing for an expanded U.S. military presence in Greenland. The Folketing, Denmark's parliament, passed the agreement with a 109-0 vote on Thursday (November 19), as reported by Arctic Today . This decision marks the end of months of diplomatic tension between Denmark and the U.S. over President Donald Trump's interest in acquiring Greenland. The agreement, signed in New York on September 22, involves Denmark, Greenland, and the U.S. It supplements a 1951 defense accord and allows the U.S. to establish new military bases at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig in Greenland. The deal also permits the expansion of the Pituffik Space Base and the establishment of the Golden Dome missile defense shield, according to Al Jazeera . The agreement ensures that Greenland remains under Danish sovereignty while recognizing the island's right to self-determination. It also blocks non-NATO and non-EU states from gaining significant influence in sensitive sectors, preventing countries like China and Russia from strategic investments. Despite the smooth passage in Denmark, the agreement faced contention in Greenland's parliament, where it passed with 16 votes and seven abstentions earlier this month. The opposition party Naleraq criticized the deal, calling for a referendum and alleging that Greenland gains nothing from it. As reported by NBC5 , Greenland's Minister for Foreign Affairs, Múte B. Egede , accused Naleraq of leaking secret information, leading to a police report against the party. U.S. Ambassador to Denmark Ken Howery welcomed the agreement, stating it modernizes the partnership and strengthens security for the U.S., Denmark, Greenland, and NATO. He expressed optimism about deepening cooperation as the agreement is implemented. The agreement will remain in force even if Greenland gains independence, provided it joins NATO. It will officially take effect once the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs informs the U.S. that all procedures are complete.

passages: Greenland is an autonomous territory of Denmark, but the deal is to remain in force even if Greenland gains full independence.

The US, Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September to resolve tensions after Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of ⁠the mineral-rich island, a self-governing Danish territory home to 57,000 people.
The Danish parliament ⁠has unanimously ratified a security agreement with the United States covering Greenland, aimed at bolstering security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
In early November, Greenland’s parliament had passed it by 16 votes, with seven abstentions.

It allows the US to build two military bases in Greenland and blocks countries outside the European Union and NATO from strategic sectors, in order to stop China or Russia from gaining influence over the territory, particularly through investments.
Thursday’s decision to approve the deal signed in September eases tensions over US President Donald Trump’s desire to annex the Arctic island.
The shortest route ‌from ‌Europe to North America runs via strategically located Greenland, where the northernmost US military base is located.

sources.title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says AI company isn't advocating for ban of open-weight models - CNBC
passages: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said on Monday that his company has "never advocated for a ban on open-weights models," an attempt to beat back criticism emerging across the tech industry that the AI lab is trying to exert excessive control over the future of artificial intelligence.

Amodei published his views in a blog post on Monday, after a coalition of tech companies, including Nvidia , Microsoft , Meta and Palantir , released a letter late last week urging policymakers to avoid "premature restrictions" on open-weight models, which users can download, modify and run on their own infrastructure.
Chief rival OpenAI also primarily builds closed models, but the company signed on in support of the open-weight letter after it was published, while Anthropic did not.

extraction.body: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said on Monday that his company has "never advocated for a ban on open-weights models," an attempt to beat back criticism emerging across the tech industry that the AI lab is trying to exert excessive control over the future of artificial intelligence. Amodei published his views in a blog post on Monday, after a coalition of tech companies, including Nvidia , Microsoft , Meta and Palantir , released a letter late last week urging policymakers to avoid "premature restrictions" on open-weight models, which users can download, modify and run on their own infrastructure. Chinese startups currently dominate the market, and some government officials have started to weigh whether those models should be banned or restricted in the U.S. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of proprietary models called Claude that it sells to businesses. Chief rival OpenAI also primarily builds closed models, but the company signed on in support of the open-weight letter after it was published, while Anthropic did not. "To summarize my and Anthropic's position, we have not and are not advocating for a ban on open-weights models as a category," Amodei wrote. "We should instead focus on keeping powerful chips out of authoritarian hands, stopping industrial-scale distillation, and requiring safety testing of all sufficiently capable models, open and closed." Distillation is an AI training method where a smaller, less capable model is built using outputs from a bigger model already on the market. Anthropic sent a letter to the U.S. Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs last month alleging that China's Alibaba , developer of the Qwen family of models, had carried out the "the largest known distillation attack" against it to date. In the Friday letter, the signatories said that concerns about unlawful distillation should be addressed through "targeted legal and commercial frameworks," an idea that Amodei agreed with on Monday. Amodei said he also agrees with other portions of the letter, namely that open-weight models give customers greater control, expand access to the AI economy and strengthen competition in some use cases. But he said he disagrees with the idea that open-weight models favor cyber defenders over attackers, or that they make it easier for users to develop safeguards. Even so, Amodei made it clear that he does not support banning open-weight models. "Protectionist bans would not address my most serious national security concerns," Amodei said. extraction.body: On the same day that Anthropic went public in the largest IPO on record, with investor enthusiasm for the AI lab through the roof, far away at the Slush startup conference in Helsinki, the topic du jour was open source everything. That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI , as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs. Fireworks runs AI models for other businesses. It specializes in open-weight models, which anyone can download, and helps customers tune them on their own data so they run faster and cheaper than the models of Anthropic, OpenAI, and other heavyweights, and are harder for rivals to copy. Customers have included Uber, Shopify, and Notion. Co-founder Chenyu Zhao and I spoke onstage toward the end of the day. Zhao and many others believe companies are gravitating toward platforms like his because frontier models are pricey and, in most cases, he says, unnecessary unless you need the very latest and greatest generalized intelligence. There are also growing concerns that frontier labs absorb too much of their customers’ know-how, even if only through the prompts used to get answers, a worry Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella raised in July . Fireworks has also gotten its first black eye, having disclosed two security incidents this fall. In one, hackers reached API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts; in the other, attackers breached its cloud provider, made their way into a development system, and nabbed customer data, including billing records and some datasets. Notion says AI chat transcripts from fewer than 1% of its workspaces were exposed, but it has disconnected from Fireworks. Uber says hackers stole the names, addresses, birth dates and driver’s license numbers of about 150,000 drivers through a vendor that TechCrunch identified as Fireworks . Fireworks will have to win back the confidence of customers like them. Fireworks, assigned a $17.5 billion valuation by its investors in summer, is reportedly in “ early talks ” for yet another round, though Zhao declined to comment. There’s money chasing everyone in the category, seems like. Rival companies Together AI and Baseten have announced massive rounds in recent months. On Wednesday, Palo Alto Networks said it will buy Applied Compute , which, like Fireworks, helps companies train and run custom AI models on their own data. The deal for the startup, founded just a year ago by former OpenAI researchers, is $4.5 billion, all of it in stock. Here’s some of what Zhao had to say. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. When you meet great co-founders, it’s obvious within five minutes that they’re really smart. I was sold after talking to Lin [Qiao] and Dima [Dzhulgakov]. It’s also important to find people who are genuinely nice, people you’ll enjoy working with. How do you describe Fireworks to a CEO who has never heard of it? I describe Fireworks as a specialized intelligence platform. OpenAI and Anthropic are building general intelligence. We use open models, which are often smaller, cheaper, and faster, and let companies add their own data to specialize them. That way you own your AI rather than being beholden to giant AI conglomerates. If you’re just using Opus or Sonnet, that’s not a differentiator. A few years ago I’d have said a year, a year and a half. Then came DeepSeek and a waterfall of fantastic open models. These days it’s at most six months behind, probably closer to three. If the models are so close behind, why are businesses slow to switch? Frontier models are a household brand, and before you find product-market fit, using the best model is low risk. But once you pass 10,000 or 100,000 users and you’re spending $10,000 to $100,000 a month on tokens, it’s time to think about open source. In July, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that companies using proprietary AI models pay twice , once in money and again in know-how. Do you think that warning had a material effect? We think we’ll live in a two-model world, with frontier and open models in parallel. You want the best intelligence for high-level planning, but you don’t need a frontier model for basic arithmetic. That’s why there’s so much interest in routing, and why people now think about cost per task, not just cost per token. Anthropic went public today. What do you think of its valuation? There’s one scenario in which it just continues to cement its place in this sort of oligopoly; there’s another where it starts to lose traction. On the record: I’ll probably call my broker tonight and buy a few shares. This is a long-term bet. In 10 years AI usage will be at a completely different scale, and that takes an incredible amount of capital, which is why these companies are going public. Fireworks has had a couple of security breaches recently. What do you tell customers? Every company is probably seeing an unprecedented frequency of attacks. For our incident, a lot of the motivation was LLM jacking: hunting through providers for API keys and secrets to sell tokens on illicit marketplaces. Our promise is zero data retention for inference traffic, and there’s no indication that has been compromised. Notion has disconnected from Fireworks. Did you lose other customers? How did that customer data get exposed, given your zero-retention promise? Notion was using batch prediction, where you upload a dataset that’s stored at rest, so it’s not a zero-retention product by nature. extraction.body: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said on Monday that his company has "never advocated for a ban on open-weights models," an attempt to beat back criticism emerging across the tech industry that the AI lab is trying to exert excessive control over the future of artificial intelligence. Amodei published his views in a blog post on Monday, after a coalition of tech companies, including Nvidia , Microsoft , Meta and Palantir , released a letter late last week urging policymakers to avoid "premature restrictions" on open-weight models, which users can download, modify and run on their own infrastructure. Chinese startups currently dominate the market, and some government officials have started to weigh whether those models should be banned or restricted in the U.S. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of proprietary models called Claude that it sells to businesses. Chief rival OpenAI also primarily builds closed models, but the company signed on in support of the open-weight letter after it was published, while Anthropic did not. "To summarize my and Anthropic's position, we have not and are not advocating for a ban on open-weights models as a category," Amodei wrote. "We should instead focus on keeping powerful chips out of authoritarian hands, stopping industrial-scale distillation, and requiring safety testing of all sufficiently capable models, open and closed." Distillation is an AI training method where a smaller, less capable model is built using outputs from a bigger model already on the market. Anthropic sent a letter to the U.S. Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs last month alleging that China's Alibaba , developer of the Qwen family of models, had carried out the "the largest known distillation attack" against it to date. In the Friday letter, the signatories said that concerns about unlawful distillation should be addressed through "targeted legal and commercial frameworks," an idea that Amodei agreed with on Monday. Amodei said he also agrees with other portions of the letter, namely that open-weight models give customers greater control, expand access to the AI economy and strengthen competition in some use cases. But he said he disagrees with the idea that open-weight models favor cyber defenders over attackers, or that they make it easier for users to develop safeguards. Even so, Amodei made it clear that he does not support banning open-weight models. "Protectionist bans would not address my most serious national security concerns," Amodei said. passages: On the same day that Anthropic went public in the largest IPO on record, with investor enthusiasm for the AI lab through the roof, far away at the Slush startup conference in Helsinki, the topic du jour was open source everything.
That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI , as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs.

Fireworks runs AI models for other businesses. It specializes in open-weight models, which anyone can download, and helps customers tune them on their own data so they run faster and cheaper than the models of Anthropic, OpenAI, and other heavyweights, and are harder for rivals to copy. Customers have included Uber, Shopify, and Notion. Co-founder Chenyu Zhao and I spoke onstage toward the end of the day.

Zhao and many others believe companies are gravitating toward platforms like his because frontier models are pricey and, in most cases, he says, unnecessary unless you need the very latest and greatest generalized intelligence. There are also growing concerns that frontier labs absorb too much of their customers’ know-how, even if only through the prompts used to get answers, a worry Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella raised in July .

Fireworks has also gotten its first black eye, having disclosed two security incidents this fall. In one, hackers reached API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts; in the other, attackers breached its cloud provider, made their way into a development system, and nabbed customer data, including billing records and some datasets.

Notion says AI chat transcripts from fewer than 1% of its workspaces were exposed, but it has disconnected from Fireworks. Uber says hackers stole the names, addresses, birth dates and driver’s license numbers of about 150,000 drivers through a vendor that TechCrunch identified as Fireworks . Fireworks will have to win back the confidence of customers like them.
Fireworks, assigned a $17.5 billion valuation by its investors in summer, is reportedly in “ early talks ” for yet another round, though Zhao declined to comment.

There’s money chasing everyone in the category, seems like. Rival companies Together AI and Baseten have announced massive rounds in recent months. On Wednesday, Palo Alto Networks said it will buy Applied Compute , which, like Fireworks, helps companies train and run custom AI models on their own data. The deal for the startup, founded just a year ago by former OpenAI researchers, is $4.5 billion, all of it in stock.
Here’s some of what Zhao had to say. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

When you meet great co-founders, it’s obvious within five minutes that they’re really smart. I was sold after talking to Lin [Qiao] and Dima [Dzhulgakov]. It’s also important to find people who are genuinely nice, people you’ll enjoy working with.
How do you describe Fireworks to a CEO who has never heard of it?

I describe Fireworks as a specialized intelligence platform. OpenAI and Anthropic are building general intelligence. We use open models, which are often smaller, cheaper, and faster, and let companies add their own data to specialize them. That way you own your AI rather than being beholden to giant AI conglomerates. If you’re just using Opus or Sonnet, that’s not a differentiator.
A few years ago I’d have said a year, a year and a half. Then came DeepSeek and a waterfall of fantastic open models. These days it’s at most six months behind, probably closer to three.
If the models are so close behind, why are businesses slow to switch?

Frontier models are a household brand, and before you find product-market fit, using the best model is low risk. But once you pass 10,000 or 100,000 users and you’re spending $10,000 to $100,000 a month on tokens, it’s time to think about open source.
In July, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that companies using proprietary AI models pay twice , once in money and again in know-how. Do you think that warning had a material effect?

We think we’ll live in a two-model world, with frontier and open models in parallel. You want the best intelligence for high-level planning, but you don’t need a frontier model for basic arithmetic. That’s why there’s so much interest in routing, and why people now think about cost per task, not just cost per token.

Anthropic went public today. What do you think of its valuation? There’s one scenario in which it just continues to cement its place in this sort of oligopoly; there’s another where it starts to lose traction.

On the record: I’ll probably call my broker tonight and buy a few shares. This is a long-term bet. In 10 years AI usage will be at a completely different scale, and that takes an incredible amount of capital, which is why these companies are going public.
Fireworks has had a couple of security breaches recently. What do you tell customers?

Every company is probably seeing an unprecedented frequency of attacks. For our incident, a lot of the motivation was LLM jacking: hunting through providers for API keys and secrets to sell tokens on illicit marketplaces. Our promise is zero data retention for inference traffic, and there’s no indication that has been compromised.
Notion has disconnected from Fireworks. Did you lose other customers?
How did that customer data get exposed, given your zero-retention promise?

Notion was using batch prediction, where you upload a dataset that’s stored at rest, so it’s not a zero-retention product by nature. We’re moving those services to an online flow so we keep data only as long as we need it.
Jensen Huang left Nvidia last week, and Nvidia has backed Fireworks since 2024. Does that affect you ?

sources.title: Meta’s Muse Is Collecting Information on Everyone in Your Life - Gizmodo
passages: “For any agent to be useful and actually help you achieve your goals, it needs to have context about you and those you interact with,” a Meta spokesperson told Gizmodo in an emailed statement.

“Muse gathers that based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share, which is how it remembers the person who just sent you an invoice is in fact the plumber who you previously hired to complete some work in your bathroom or which flowers your spouse said they liked best.”
In typical Meta fashion, the company’s popular new AI agent Muse reportedly keeps detailed, regularly updated files on the people in users’ lives.
The new details come just weeks after Meta launched Muse on Sept.
8 as a personal AI agent that can handle tasks like sending emails, booking travel, shopping, and tracking goals.
To do all that, users give Muse access to a wide range of their apps and accounts.
Muse has since climbed to the number-one spot on Apple’s U.S.
For instance, Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site in September, saying Meta had not notified the company in advance that the agent would access its online shop.
The company also raised concerns about how Muse handles customer credentials and account data.

Meta also recently patched a zero-day vulnerability in the Mac version of Muse that could allow malware already running on a user’s computer to hijack the agent and take advantage of permissions the user had previously granted it.
The spokesperson added that the information is stored in each user’s dedicated secure virtual machine, which Meta says cannot be accessed by other users’ agents.
Meta recently removed several accounts sharing AI-generated videos of coaches inappropriately touching and kissing young athletes.
Independent AI safety and security researcher Karan Joshi extracted a trove of Muse instructions and system prompts through the app’s regular chat interface and shared the findings with Wired.

Muse can also keep a history of the relationship, including events or milestones, as well as information about how close the user is to the person, what their relationship is built on, how they interact, and what the relationship appears to need at the moment.

extraction.body: In typical Meta fashion, the company’s popular new AI agent Muse reportedly keeps detailed, regularly updated files on the people in users’ lives. Nearly a month after its launch, researchers are digging into how Muse works. It turns out the AI agent will openly share internal files and instructions when users ask, offering a peek at how it operates. One of the somewhat unsettling details is an hourly process that instructs Muse to create and update “a page for every person in the user’s life,” Wired reports . Independent AI safety and security researcher Karan Joshi extracted a trove of Muse instructions and system prompts through the app’s regular chat interface and shared the findings with Wired. Separately, The Future Society published system instructions from an exported copy of a Muse virtual machine. “What it seemed like to me—from all these prompts, system skills data, and things that they’re feeding into Muse—is that they want to understand your relationships that you have with real people,” Joshi told Wired. “They’re trying to know you like a friend, which is honestly pretty creepy.” The new details come just weeks after Meta launched Muse on Sept. 8 as a personal AI agent that can handle tasks like sending emails, booking travel, shopping, and tracking goals. To do all that, users give Muse access to a wide range of their apps and accounts. Muse has since climbed to the number-one spot on Apple’s U.S. App Store chart for free iPhone apps. But privacy and security concerns have emerged almost immediately. For instance, Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site in September, saying Meta had not notified the company in advance that the agent would access its online shop. The company also raised concerns about how Muse handles customer credentials and account data. Meta also recently patched a zero-day vulnerability in the Mac version of Muse that could allow malware already running on a user’s computer to hijack the agent and take advantage of permissions the user had previously granted it. Now, we have a better idea of just how much Muse keeps track of about users and the people in their lives, even if those people don’t use Muse themselves. According to system instructions published by The Future Society, these relationship pages can include a person’s name, how they are connected to the Muse user, recurring topics such as an upcoming apartment move or savings goal, and important dates like birthdays and anniversaries. sources.title: Meta’s new Muse Charm device may cost $300
passages: Meta plans to charge $300 for Muse Charm, its upcoming Tamagotchi-like AI device that was teased at the company’s Connect event earlier this year, The Information has reported .
Indeed, $300 is arguably a pretty steep price for a product the size of a keychain, although it’s also a price point that’s in line with what other companies have been charging.
The wearable launched by Friend — the AI startup whose device lets you text and talk to an AI persona — is currently retailing for $250.

When reached for comment by TechCrunch, a Meta spokesperson didn’t deny the claims, merely providing the following statement: “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.”
It remains to be seen whether customers will bite or not.
AI wearables have had a rough go of it so far (here’s looking at you, Humane Ai pin ), but companies continue to iterate on the concept in an attempt to break through to a broader audience.

So far, Meta has made a relatively successful push into consumer AI, launching Muse — its agentic helper — along with a variety of cute avatars that users can use to give the system more of a personality.

extraction.body: In typical Meta fashion, the company’s popular new AI agent Muse reportedly keeps detailed, regularly updated files on the people in users’ lives. Nearly a month after its launch, researchers are digging into how Muse works. It turns out the AI agent will openly share internal files and instructions when users ask, offering a peek at how it operates. One of the somewhat unsettling details is an hourly process that instructs Muse to create and update “a page for every person in the user’s life,” Wired reports . Independent AI safety and security researcher Karan Joshi extracted a trove of Muse instructions and system prompts through the app’s regular chat interface and shared the findings with Wired. Separately, The Future Society published system instructions from an exported copy of a Muse virtual machine. “What it seemed like to me—from all these prompts, system skills data, and things that they’re feeding into Muse—is that they want to understand your relationships that you have with real people,” Joshi told Wired. “They’re trying to know you like a friend, which is honestly pretty creepy.” The new details come just weeks after Meta launched Muse on Sept. 8 as a personal AI agent that can handle tasks like sending emails, booking travel, shopping, and tracking goals. To do all that, users give Muse access to a wide range of their apps and accounts. Muse has since climbed to the number-one spot on Apple’s U.S. App Store chart for free iPhone apps. But privacy and security concerns have emerged almost immediately. For instance, Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site in September, saying Meta had not notified the company in advance that the agent would access its online shop. The company also raised concerns about how Muse handles customer credentials and account data. Meta also recently patched a zero-day vulnerability in the Mac version of Muse that could allow malware already running on a user’s computer to hijack the agent and take advantage of permissions the user had previously granted it. Now, we have a better idea of just how much Muse keeps track of about users and the people in their lives, even if those people don’t use Muse themselves. According to system instructions published by The Future Society, these relationship pages can include a person’s name, how they are connected to the Muse user, recurring topics such as an upcoming apartment move or savings goal, and important dates like birthdays and anniversaries. Muse can also keep a history of the relationship, including events or milestones, as well as information about how close the user is to the person, what their relationship is built on, how they interact, and what the relationship appears to need at the moment. “For any agent to be useful and actually help you achieve your goals, it needs to have context about you and those you interact with,” a Meta spokesperson told Gizmodo in an emailed statement. “Muse gathers that based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share, which is how it remembers the person who just sent you an invoice is in fact the plumber who you previously hired to complete some work in your bathroom or which flowers your spouse said they liked best.” The spokesperson added that the information is stored in each user’s dedicated secure virtual machine, which Meta says cannot be accessed by other users’ agents. sources.title: Meta’s AI agent Muse is mixing up conversations and could be exposing private data, report says
passages: Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.

“Employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products,” a Meta spokesperson said in an email to TechCrunch. “Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Launched in September, Muse is one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads.

One employee told colleagues that Muse had randomly sent an extra message in a chat about weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
Update 11/19/2026 12:05 PM PT: The article was updated to include Meta’s comment.

In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn’t belong to them.

passages: Meta launched its Muse AI agent with a promise that it was built from the ground up for privacy and security.A recent investigation and several reports reveal that the people testing the product internally were raising serious doubts about whether that promise was being met before and even after the product shipped.Meta Employees Expose Muse AI Privacy ConcernsReuters reviewed internal communications at Meta that showed employees raising significant concerns about Muse's handling of private data, including incidents where the AI agent appeared to be mixing up conversations between different user accounts.

Each Muse agent runs in its own cloud virtual machine, gated by a separate security process called Sentinel.Is Meta Muse a Security Liability?Based on the Reuters investigation, Claroc's research, and the Ars Technica reporting on internal Meta communications, Muse had experienced multiple distinct security and privacy failures by November 2026, two months after its US launch.The failures range from the DNS-accessible shared chat links, which exposed conversations that users believed were private, to internal testing that showed Muse reading Signal messages without direct user instruction, to employees reporting cross-account data confusion during testing.

Meta did not dispute that the internal posts existed.Separately, security firm Claroc discovered that the chat-sharing feature in Muse exposed shared conversations through publicly searchable DNS records.

Those internal posts revealed a pattern of safety issues that employees believed could expose private data, with some describing failure modes that made the product unreliable in real-world conditions.Employees testing Muse as recently as launch week flagged these concerns through internal channels, yet Meta proceeded with the September 2026 US launch as scheduled.

During controlled tests conducted by Reuters, Muse accessed private Signal messages on the device where it was installed, made possible by the broad Android notification permissions the app requests.Muse also sent employees unsolicited bank balance figures from an unidentified source during testing, raising concerns about where the financial data was originating from and how the agent was processing information it had not been directly prompted to retrieve.Employees also raised concerns about a human concierge feature that Meta had been developing alongside Muse.

Security researchers needed a single DNS query to surface thousands of previously shared chat links, all of which were accessible to anyone who found them, without any login requirement.The exposed conversations were created by users who had explicitly chosen to share them with specific recipients but did not expect that those links would be discoverable by third parties.

The internal chats reviewed by Ars Technica showed employees describing Muse behavior that they found alarming, and that conflicted directly with how the product had been marketed to the public.Frequently Asked QuestionsWhat Is Meta?Meta Platforms, Inc. is an American technology company headquartered in Menlo Park, California, and is the parent company of Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger, and Threads, as well as the developer of Meta AI, Muse, and the company's portfolio of AI products.

The sharing feature vulnerability was identified, reported to Meta through a bug bounty program, and patched.For users who want to minimize risk while using Muse, security researchers and IT experts recommend treating any AI agent with broad device permissions with caution, avoiding sharing conversations containing sensitive personal, financial, or business information through any AI tool's share feature, and monitoring the app's permission settings to understand what data Muse can access.

Meta is one of the most widely used technology companies in the world, with billions of users across its apps, and it generates revenue primarily through advertising across its social media platforms.What Is Meta Muse?Meta Muse is an AI agent developed by Meta and launched for US users in September 2026.

Organizations using Muse in business contexts should establish clear internal policies about which categories of information employees may submit to AI assistants and audit which tools are connected to business accounts.

A Meta spokesperson, Daniel Roberts, described the Reuters examples as isolated incidents and stated that the company prioritizes safety, conducts extensive internal testing, and follows strict rules. During controlled tests conducted by Reuters, Muse accessed private Signal messages on the device where it was installed, made possible by the broad Android notification permissions the app requests.Muse also sent employees unsolicited bank balance figures from an unidentified source during testing, raising concerns about where the financial data was originating from and how the agent was processing information it had not been directly prompted to retrieve.Employees also raised concerns about a human concierge feature that Meta had been developing alongside Muse. That feature, which involves Muse placing actual phone calls handled by human contractors when the AI cannot complete a task autonomously, prompted warnings from employees that it risked exposing sensitive user information to call center workers in ways that would undercut Muse's privacy-first positioning.Meta began testing the phone-calling capability with employees in August 2026 before gradually rolling it out to public Muse users in the days following launch.A separate disclosure from security researcher Patrick Wardle identified a vulnerability in Muse that put a user's dictated audio and account token at risk. The internal chats reviewed by Ars Technica showed employees describing Muse behavior that they found alarming, and that conflicted directly with how the product had been marketed to the public.Frequently Asked QuestionsWhat Is Meta?Meta Platforms, Inc. is an American technology company headquartered in Menlo Park, California, and is the parent company of Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger, and Threads, as well as the developer of Meta AI, Muse, and the company's portfolio of AI products. Founded by Mark Zuckerberg in 2004 as Facebook, the company rebranded as Meta in 2021 to reflect its focus on the development of the metaverse and augmented reality hardware through its Quest VR headset line. Meta is one of the most widely used technology companies in the world, with billions of users across its apps, and it generates revenue primarily through advertising across its social media platforms.What Is Meta Muse?Meta Muse is an AI agent developed by Meta and launched for US users in September 2026. Zuckerberg described Muse at launch as a personal AI assistant built from the ground up for privacy and security. The agent is designed to autonomously manage tasks across a user's digital life, including reading and composing emails, managing calendar events, handling financial tasks through connected payment accounts, making phone calls on behalf of the user, browsing the internet, and acting on information drawn from connected apps and devices. Muse operates through broad device permissions that allow it to access notifications, messages, and other data from other apps installed on the same device in order to provide context-aware assistance. Each Muse agent runs in its own cloud virtual machine, gated by a separate security process called Sentinel.Is Meta Muse a Security Liability?Based on the Reuters investigation, Claroc's research, and the Ars Technica reporting on internal Meta communications, Muse had experienced multiple distinct security and privacy failures by November 2026, two months after its US launch.The failures range from the DNS-accessible shared chat links, which exposed conversations that users believed were private, to internal testing that showed Muse reading Signal messages without direct user instruction, to employees reporting cross-account data confusion during testing. Meta described the incidents individually as isolated, but the volume and variety of issues raised by both internal employees and external researchers suggest a pattern rather than a series of unrelated anomalies.The severity varies: the shared chat exposure affected users across the platform broadly, while the Signal and bank balance issues were observed in controlled testing rather than as widespread public incidents.Is Meta Muse Safe to Use?Meta maintains that Muse is built with strong security foundations, that the incidents described are isolated, and that the company conducts extensive internal testing and follows strict internal rules. The sharing feature vulnerability was identified, reported to Meta through a bug bounty program, and patched.For users who want to minimize risk while using Muse, security researchers and IT experts recommend treating any AI agent with broad device permissions with caution, avoiding sharing conversations containing sensitive personal, financial, or business information through any AI tool's share feature, and monitoring the app's permission settings to understand what data Muse can access. coreStoryFacts.text: Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.

“Employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products,” a Meta spokesperson said in an email to TechCrunch. “Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Launched in September, Muse is one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads.

One employee told colleagues that Muse had randomly sent an extra message in a chat about weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
Update 11/19/2026 12:05 PM PT: The article was updated to include Meta’s comment.

In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn’t belong to them.

Meta launched its Muse AI agent in September 2026 with a promise that it was built from the ground up for privacy and security, but Reuters reviewed internal communications showing employees raising “significant concerns” about Muse’s handling of private data.

Reuters reported that internal posts described incidents where Muse appeared to be mixing up conversations between different user accounts, and employees flagged safety issues “as recently as launch week” while Meta proceeded with the September 2026 US launch as scheduled.
Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests employees said they never made and bank account balances that did not belong to them.

Muse had already been downloaded by more than 10 million people and Meta expected it to generate billions of dollars in revenue from AI, while La Nación described internal postings reviewed by Reuters as showing unsolicited actions including infiltrating encrypted personal messages and sending conversations that appeared destined for other people.

The Defense Watch said Reuters could not establish whether unfamiliar financial information represented actual exposure of another person’s data or information fabricated by the AI model, and the outlet described Meta’s position that many messages identified as possible account mix-ups were hallucinations and that some problems had already been addressed.

extraction.body: Not many of them made it in, but Chinese clouds no longer care The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) allowed Nvidia and AMD to sell hundreds of thousands of advanced GPUs to entities that the Department of War classifies as “Chinese military companies” that help Beijing to build its military. That news comes courtesy of Brian Mast, chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who asked BIS to provide information about NVIDIA’s and AMD’s applications for the export licenses required to sell advanced AI chips to China. The congressman on Thursday revealed requests to sell 3.4 million AI chips to China, and that BIS approved the sale of 879,000 items. BIS refused to authorize some giant deals for Nvidia, which applied to sell 610,000 chips to Alibaba and 508,000 to TikTok owner Bytedance. But the agency allowed many other sales, including to Alibaba and Tencent. Mast points out that both of those companies are on the Department of War’s List of Chinese Military Companies , the designation it uses for entities deemed to be a “military-civil fusion contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base.” That’s a polite way of saying that Washington thinks China relies on these companies to operate and improve its military, and therefore to challenge America’s national security. Advanced chips are essential when designing nuclear weapons, stealthy submarines, or advanced aircraft. Those applications are the core reason the US bans exports of advanced GPUs to China, so that the People’s Liberation Army can’t develop advanced weapons. The congressman also claims that some of Nvidia’s applications were attempts to sell its wares to “chip-smuggling fronts to facilitate their sales of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies.” The New York Times reports that some of those front entities are linked to Megaspeed, the outfit fronted by suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang, whose intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a key factor in his resignation. Megaspeed is accused of what the US calls “diversion” – claiming to buy chips for one reason while intending to either ship them to China or rent them exclusively to Chinese companies in ways that breach the spirit of export restrictions if not the letter of the law. One of the documents Mast shared says “Every Nvidia and AMD application stated that the proposed transfer posed a ‘low’ risk of diversion.” Mast’s point therefore appears to be that the BIS has authorized sales that go against the clear intent of established policy, and the national interest, and that Nvidia and AMD may have been a little too optimistic in their assessment of diversion risk. Earlier this week, Washington adopted a new policy that outlaws allowing remote access to advanced AI chips, in the hope it would stop diversion and dent China’s AI ambitions. Two Chinese tech giants, Tencent and Alibaba, have signaled the policy had immediate impact. Chinese web giant Tencent on Wednesday said that new ban will reduce the quantity of advanced compute capacity available to the company and mean its efforts to train models will slow. Alibaba offered similar sentiments on Thursday. Speaking on the company’s earnings call, CEO Eddie Wu said the new policy “will definitely have some impact on the long-term construction of Alibaba Cloud's data centers both domestically and globally.” “Based on our initial assessment, the long-term target of 20 gigawatts may be lowered, which will also lead to a reduction in our overall capital expenditure plan,” he said. But both Tencent and Alibaba don’t see the new policy as creating long-term problems, because both companies believe Chinese chipmakers will be making advanced AI hardware at scale in 2027 or 2028. Alibaba’s Wu predicted his company “will go through a phase of the largest investment in AI infrastructure” once Chinese chipmakers get up to speed. Once that happens, Nvidia and AMD may not even be able to sell chips to China through backdoors. And for what it’s worth, even after the two sultans of silicon went through the front door by asking BIS for permission, many of the approved orders never resulted in shipments. extraction.body: The Commerce Department approved applications to sell more than 3.4 million chips to the firms, lawmakers say [WASHINGTON] Lawmakers released confidential information on Thursday (Nov 19) showing that the Commerce Department had approved the sale of more than 800,000 advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies for the year, as of May 11, including several firms on a list of Chinese military companies maintained by the Pentagon. The department had received applications to sell more than 3.4 million of the chips to Chinese companies as at that date, lawmakers said. It approved 75,000 AI chips for Alibaba, a Chinese AI giant that The New York Times reported this week has ties with a military-linked laboratory . The release also showed that Nvidia had submitted an application in April to sell more than 40,000 of its advanced H200 chips to a company tied to Megaspeed and Alice Huang, the executive who US intelligence has concluded was a Chinese asset who had an affair with the former Nvidia CEO. The company – New Century Lettall Data Service – is part of a network of Chinese companies with ties to Megaspeed and Huang. Its historical ownership traces back in part to an investment firm controlled by Huang’s sister, where Kang Wei, whom Huang often introduced as her husband, was also executive director. The Commerce Department also approved 150,000 chips for Chinese tech conglomerate Tencent and its subsidiaries; 43,000 for Baidu, another Chinese AI firm; and 4,000 for BYD, a carmaker, the lawmakers said. They were Nvidia’s H200 chips and the equivalent from the chipmaker AMD, the MI325X. The lawmakers from the House Foreign Affairs Committee took special note of the Commerce Department’s approval of sales to the companies Maginfra, Beijing New Matrix Information Technologies and Aivres Systems. The committee cited reporting by The New York Times that had raised questions about those firms because of their ties to sanctioned entities and noted that many of the licence requests from Nvidia had listed the companies as entities that might install the systems in data centres. Two reports from The New York Times first raised concerns about the firms in September and October, saying that Aivres was the subsidiary of a sanctioned Chinese firm that had exported billions of dollars of advanced Nvidia chips to Megaspeed, the company at the centre of the Nvidia scandal. The New York Times reporters also visited the China offices of Maginfra and New Matrix and found them to be empty. No one present had heard of the firms, and scant information existed about them online, raising questions about whether they really existed. The revelations that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was having an affair with Alice Huang, along with a second woman at Nvidia, forced him to step down last week . The Justice and Commerce Departments said this week that Megaspeed was under criminal investigation for potentially smuggling chips into China. The incident has sparked criticism from lawmakers that the Trump administration, and the Commerce Department in particular, did too little to police the flow of sensitive technology to China. Officials both in the administration and on Capitol Hill have criticised the department for maintaining close ties to Nvidia, which it is charged with regulating. The Commerce Department has defended its processes, saying that it closely follows national security regulations. Every Nvidia and AMD application also stated that the proposed transfer posed a low risk of diversion, the committee’s release said. John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, said that all the company’s shipments were legal and authorised by the government, and that, despite receiving some licences, Nvidia had already stopped shipping H200s to China. Nvidia “did not and will not” ship an H200 to the company linked to Megaspeed, or any other company, he said. A spokesperson for AMD said the company complied with applicable U.S. laws and regulations and had a rigorous process to ensure compliance. A spokesperson for the Commerce Department said the disclosure was evidence of the department’s transparency with Congress about licensing activity. Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. government agencies, he said. President Donald Trump approved the sale of the H200 to China in December under unusual conditions. He required the chips, which are assembled in Taiwan, to be routed through the United States on their way to China, so that the government could collect a 25 per cent tariff on their value and perform a security check. Wary of the arrangement and eager to promote its own technology, the Chinese government ended up approving few purchases from its firms. Nvidia said in its earnings this week that it would halt sales of its H200 chips to China, though it did not give a reason for the move. In its statement, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said that withholding the information was “contrary to the national interest”. The committee plans to hold hearings next month with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and his deputy Jeff Kessler, who has had a special role in approving license applications. Rep Brian Mast who chairs the committee, called Maginfra and New Matrix “fake companies”, and said that if the Commerce Department granted approvals to the firms, “obviously that is of tremendous concern to us”, he said. Rep Gregory W Meeks said that the public deserved to know how decisions to sell technology to China were made, and that Congress needed to “conduct rigorous oversight”. “Over the past month, the administration’s handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk,” he said. The release also showed that Nvidia had submitted an application in April to sell more than 40,000 of its advanced H200 chips to a company tied to Megaspeed and Alice Huang, the executive who US intelligence has concluded was a Chinese asset who had an affair with the former Nvidia CEO.

The company – New Century Lettall Data Service – is part of a network of Chinese companies with ties to Megaspeed and Huang. Its historical ownership traces back in part to an investment firm controlled by Huang’s sister, where Kang Wei, whom Huang often introduced as her husband, was also executive director.

The Commerce Department also approved 150,000 chips for Chinese tech conglomerate Tencent and its subsidiaries; 43,000 for Baidu, another Chinese AI firm; and 4,000 for BYD, a carmaker, the lawmakers said.
They were Nvidia’s H200 chips and the equivalent from the chipmaker AMD, the MI325X.

The lawmakers from the House Foreign Affairs Committee took special note of the Commerce Department’s approval of sales to the companies Maginfra, Beijing New Matrix Information Technologies and Aivres Systems.

The committee cited reporting by The New York Times that had raised questions about those firms because of their ties to sanctioned entities and noted that many of the licence requests from Nvidia had listed the companies as entities that might install the systems in data centres.

Two reports from The New York Times first raised concerns about the firms in September and October, saying that Aivres was the subsidiary of a sanctioned Chinese firm that had exported billions of dollars of advanced Nvidia chips to Megaspeed, the company at the centre of the Nvidia scandal.

The New York Times reporters also visited the China offices of Maginfra and New Matrix and found them to be empty. No one present had heard of the firms, and scant information existed about them online, raising questions about whether they really existed.

The revelations that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was having an affair with Alice Huang, along with a second woman at Nvidia, forced him to step down last week . The Justice and Commerce Departments said this week that Megaspeed was under criminal investigation for potentially smuggling chips into China.
The incident has sparked criticism from lawmakers that the Trump administration, and the Commerce Department in particular, did too little to police the flow of sensitive technology to China.
Officials both in the administration and on Capitol Hill have criticised the department for maintaining close ties to Nvidia, which it is charged with regulating.

The Commerce Department has defended its processes, saying that it closely follows national security regulations. Every Nvidia and AMD application also stated that the proposed transfer posed a low risk of diversion, the committee’s release said.

John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, said that all the company’s shipments were legal and authorised by the government, and that, despite receiving some licences, Nvidia had already stopped shipping H200s to China.
Nvidia “did not and will not” ship an H200 to the company linked to Megaspeed, or any other company, he said.
A spokesperson for AMD said the company complied with applicable U.S. laws and regulations and had a rigorous process to ensure compliance.

A spokesperson for the Commerce Department said the disclosure was evidence of the department’s transparency with Congress about licensing activity. Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. government agencies, he said.

President Donald Trump approved the sale of the H200 to China in December under unusual conditions. He required the chips, which are assembled in Taiwan, to be routed through the United States on their way to China, so that the government could collect a 25 per cent tariff on their value and perform a security check.
Wary of the arrangement and eager to promote its own technology, the Chinese government ended up approving few purchases from its firms.
Nvidia said in its earnings this week that it would halt sales of its H200 chips to China, though it did not give a reason for the move.
In its statement, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said that withholding the information was “contrary to the national interest”.
The committee plans to hold hearings next month with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and his deputy Jeff Kessler, who has had a special role in approving license applications.

Rep Brian Mast who chairs the committee, called Maginfra and New Matrix “fake companies”, and said that if the Commerce Department granted approvals to the firms, “obviously that is of tremendous concern to us”, he said.
Rep Gregory W Meeks said that the public deserved to know how decisions to sell technology to China were made, and that Congress needed to “conduct rigorous oversight”.
“Over the past month, the administration’s handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk,” he said. NYTIMES
