extraction.body: See more of our coverage in your search results. An alleged Chinese spy developed a “close relationship” with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, setting off alarms among US intelligence officials who were secretly monitoring her communications, according to a report. The woman, Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen who has served as a top executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer and cloud partner that provides AI computing power to Chinese companies including Alibaba, the New York Times reported Thursday. US intelligence agencies concluded that Alice Huang — seen in photos enjoying whiskey and dining with the tech titan — was secretly funneling information to Beijing, according to the paper, which cited people briefed on classified intelligence findings. US electronic surveillance identified Jensen Huang as one of Alice Huang’s contacts, but the report offered no evidence that he knew of her alleged intelligence activities. The Times could not determine what information she passed along or how valuable it was to Chinese authorities. The report did not address whether the relationship was romantic in nature. Photos posted online in June 2024 showed the duo at a Taipei, Taiwan, bar after a local tech show, where they reportedly quaffed whiskey with other AI bigshots. They were also seen together in May 2025 , exiting a Taipei restaurant following a business dinner with AI suppliers. In a video of the scene, Alice Huang is seen standing a few feet behind the Nvidia boss with a big grin on her face while he banters with local journos. US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions that it helped Chinese firms circumvent US export restrictions and smuggle advanced Nvidia chips into China, the Times reported. Megaspeed operates as a middleman, purchasing Nvidia chips through the US arm of Inspur, a Chinese server manufacturer, and renting computing power from its Southeast Asian data centers to Chinese companies, according to the Gray Lady. Inspur’s parent company has been blacklisted by Washington for funneling technology to China’s military, although its American subsidiary remains free of sanctions, according to the Times. Nvidia is the world’s most valuable publicly traded company, boasting a market capitalization of roughly $5.2 trillion. Its advanced chips have become the backbone of the artificial intelligence boom, giving Huang enormous clout in Silicon Valley and Washington as the US races to maintain its technological edge over China. The feds have banned Nvidia from selling its best chips to Chinese companies for years. Jensen Huang is married to Lori Mills Huang, whom he met while studying electrical engineering at Oregon State University. The couple has two children, Spencer and Madison, both of whom work at Nvidia. President Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings roughly a year ago but chose not to take action, according to the Times, which added that he was wary of disrupting Nvidia’s lucrative chip sales and further complicating trade relations with China. Jensen Huang has cultivated close ties with Trump , attending a high-dollar donors’ dinner at Mar-a-Lago, Fla., with his wife, personally lobbying the president to allow Nvidia to continue selling chips to Beijing, the Times reported. Nvidia subsequently donated at least $20 million to Trump’s White House ballroom fund, according to a person familiar with the matter cited by the Times. The chipmaker also pledged to invest $500 billion in US manufacturing — a top Trump priority — while Huang successfully pressed the administration to loosen restrictions on AI companies and chip exports to China. Although US officials initially believed Jensen Huang did not know of Alice Huang’s alleged espionage activities, some senior Trump administration officials now doubt that the Nvidia boss “could have remained unaware” of her intelligence-gathering role for Beijing, according to the Times. It remains unclear whether US intelligence agencies have formally changed their assessment. Nvidia pushed back against suggestions that Jensen Huang’s dealings with the alleged Chinese intelligence operative were suspicious, describing Megaspeed as a typical regional cloud customer. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected,” an Nvidia spokesperson told The Post. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” The company insisted that its regional cloud customers receive “ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets” and “zero information relevant to national security.” Nvidia also said it regularly receives government updates about potentially problematic individuals and companies, adding that it “always” takes appropriate action. “We’re confident that if the US government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know,” the spokesperson said. The chipmaker also rejected allegations that its technology was being diverted through Megaspeed, saying the claims were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.” It maintained that Beijing has blocked American AI chips rather than sought them through regional cloud providers. “China opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called ‘Chinese spy’ narrative,” Chinese embassy spokesperson Liu Chang told The Post. “We urge the US to stop its malicious efforts to block and suppress China and its groundless smears and slanders, and do more things that are conducive to sci-tech exchanges and cooperation between the two countries.” The Post has sought comment from the White House and Megaspeed.

extraction.body: Not many of them made it in, but Chinese clouds no longer care The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) allowed Nvidia and AMD to sell hundreds of thousands of advanced GPUs to entities that the Department of War classifies as “Chinese military companies” that help Beijing to build its military. That news comes courtesy of Brian Mast, chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who asked BIS to provide information about NVIDIA’s and AMD’s applications for the export licenses required to sell advanced AI chips to China. The congressman on Thursday revealed requests to sell 3.4 million AI chips to China, and that BIS approved the sale of 879,000 items. BIS refused to authorize some giant deals for Nvidia, which applied to sell 610,000 chips to Alibaba and 508,000 to TikTok owner Bytedance. But the agency allowed many other sales, including to Alibaba and Tencent. Mast points out that both of those companies are on the Department of War’s List of Chinese Military Companies , the designation it uses for entities deemed to be a “military-civil fusion contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base.” That’s a polite way of saying that Washington thinks China relies on these companies to operate and improve its military, and therefore to challenge America’s national security. Advanced chips are essential when designing nuclear weapons, stealthy submarines, or advanced aircraft. Those applications are the core reason the US bans exports of advanced GPUs to China, so that the People’s Liberation Army can’t develop advanced weapons. The congressman also claims that some of Nvidia’s applications were attempts to sell its wares to “chip-smuggling fronts to facilitate their sales of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies.” The New York Times reports that some of those front entities are linked to Megaspeed, the outfit fronted by suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang, whose intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a key factor in his resignation. Megaspeed is accused of what the US calls “diversion” – claiming to buy chips for one reason while intending to either ship them to China or rent them exclusively to Chinese companies in ways that breach the spirit of export restrictions if not the letter of the law. One of the documents Mast shared says “Every Nvidia and AMD application stated that the proposed transfer posed a ‘low’ risk of diversion.” Mast’s point therefore appears to be that the BIS has authorized sales that go against the clear intent of established policy, and the national interest, and that Nvidia and AMD may have been a little too optimistic in their assessment of diversion risk. Earlier this week, Washington adopted a new policy that outlaws allowing remote access to advanced AI chips, in the hope it would stop diversion and dent China’s AI ambitions. Two Chinese tech giants, Tencent and Alibaba, have signaled the policy had immediate impact. Chinese web giant Tencent on Wednesday said that new ban will reduce the quantity of advanced compute capacity available to the company and mean its efforts to train models will slow. Alibaba offered similar sentiments on Thursday. Speaking on the company’s earnings call, CEO Eddie Wu said the new policy “will definitely have some impact on the long-term construction of Alibaba Cloud's data centers both domestically and globally.” “Based on our initial assessment, the long-term target of 20 gigawatts may be lowered, which will also lead to a reduction in our overall capital expenditure plan,” he said. But both Tencent and Alibaba don’t see the new policy as creating long-term problems, because both companies believe Chinese chipmakers will be making advanced AI hardware at scale in 2027 or 2028. Alibaba’s Wu predicted his company “will go through a phase of the largest investment in AI infrastructure” once Chinese chipmakers get up to speed. Once that happens, Nvidia and AMD may not even be able to sell chips to China through backdoors. And for what it’s worth, even after the two sultans of silicon went through the front door by asking BIS for permission, many of the approved orders never resulted in shipments. The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) allowed Nvidia and AMD to sell hundreds of thousands of advanced GPUs to entities that the Department of War classifies as “Chinese military companies” that help Beijing to build its military.

That news comes courtesy of Brian Mast, chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who asked BIS to provide information about NVIDIA’s and AMD’s applications for the export licenses required to sell advanced AI chips to China.
The congressman on Thursday revealed requests to sell 3.4 million AI chips to China, and that BIS approved the sale of 879,000 items.
BIS refused to authorize some giant deals for Nvidia, which applied to sell 610,000 chips to Alibaba and 508,000 to TikTok owner Bytedance.
But the agency allowed many other sales, including to Alibaba and Tencent.

Mast points out that both of those companies are on the Department of War’s List of Chinese Military Companies , the designation it uses for entities deemed to be a “military-civil fusion contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base.” That’s a polite way of saying that Washington thinks China relies on these companies to operate and improve its military, and therefore to challenge America’s national security.
Advanced chips are essential when designing nuclear weapons, stealthy submarines, or advanced aircraft.
Those applications are the core reason the US bans exports of advanced GPUs to China, so that the People’s Liberation Army can’t develop advanced weapons.

The congressman also claims that some of Nvidia’s applications were attempts to sell its wares to “chip-smuggling fronts to facilitate their sales of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies.” The New York Times reports that some of those front entities are linked to Megaspeed, the outfit fronted by suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang, whose intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a key factor in his resignation.

Megaspeed is accused of what the US calls “diversion” – claiming to buy chips for one reason while intending to either ship them to China or rent them exclusively to Chinese companies in ways that breach the spirit of export restrictions if not the letter of the law.
One of the documents Mast shared says “Every Nvidia and AMD application stated that the proposed transfer posed a ‘low’ risk of diversion.”

Mast’s point therefore appears to be that the BIS has authorized sales that go against the clear intent of established policy, and the national interest, and that Nvidia and AMD may have been a little too optimistic in their assessment of diversion risk.
Earlier this week, Washington adopted a new policy that outlaws allowing remote access to advanced AI chips, in the hope it would stop diversion and dent China’s AI ambitions.
Two Chinese tech giants, Tencent and Alibaba, have signaled the policy had immediate impact.
Chinese web giant Tencent on Wednesday said that new ban will reduce the quantity of advanced compute capacity available to the company and mean its efforts to train models will slow.

Alibaba offered similar sentiments on Thursday. Speaking on the company’s earnings call, CEO Eddie Wu said the new policy “will definitely have some impact on the long-term construction of Alibaba Cloud's data centers both domestically and globally.”
“Based on our initial assessment, the long-term target of 20 gigawatts may be lowered, which will also lead to a reduction in our overall capital expenditure plan,” he said.
But both Tencent and Alibaba don’t see the new policy as creating long-term problems, because both companies believe Chinese chipmakers will be making advanced AI hardware at scale in 2027 or 2028.
Alibaba’s Wu predicted his company “will go through a phase of the largest investment in AI infrastructure” once Chinese chipmakers get up to speed.
Once that happens, Nvidia and AMD may not even be able to sell chips to China through backdoors.
And for what it’s worth, even after the two sultans of silicon went through the front door by asking BIS for permission, many of the approved orders never resulted in shipments.
That’s likely because Beijing needs to approve imports and chose not to do so while its own chipmakers develop improved products. ®

extraction.body: The Commerce Department approved applications to sell more than 3.4 million chips to the firms, lawmakers say [WASHINGTON] Lawmakers released confidential information on Thursday (Nov 19) showing that the Commerce Department had approved the sale of more than 800,000 advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies for the year, as of May 11, including several firms on a list of Chinese military companies maintained by the Pentagon. The department had received applications to sell more than 3.4 million of the chips to Chinese companies as at that date, lawmakers said. It approved 75,000 AI chips for Alibaba, a Chinese AI giant that The New York Times reported this week has ties with a military-linked laboratory . The release also showed that Nvidia had submitted an application in April to sell more than 40,000 of its advanced H200 chips to a company tied to Megaspeed and Alice Huang, the executive who US intelligence has concluded was a Chinese asset who had an affair with the former Nvidia CEO. The company – New Century Lettall Data Service – is part of a network of Chinese companies with ties to Megaspeed and Huang. Its historical ownership traces back in part to an investment firm controlled by Huang’s sister, where Kang Wei, whom Huang often introduced as her husband, was also executive director. The Commerce Department also approved 150,000 chips for Chinese tech conglomerate Tencent and its subsidiaries; 43,000 for Baidu, another Chinese AI firm; and 4,000 for BYD, a carmaker, the lawmakers said. They were Nvidia’s H200 chips and the equivalent from the chipmaker AMD, the MI325X. The lawmakers from the House Foreign Affairs Committee took special note of the Commerce Department’s approval of sales to the companies Maginfra, Beijing New Matrix Information Technologies and Aivres Systems. The committee cited reporting by The New York Times that had raised questions about those firms because of their ties to sanctioned entities and noted that many of the licence requests from Nvidia had listed the companies as entities that might install the systems in data centres. Two reports from The New York Times first raised concerns about the firms in September and October, saying that Aivres was the subsidiary of a sanctioned Chinese firm that had exported billions of dollars of advanced Nvidia chips to Megaspeed, the company at the centre of the Nvidia scandal. The New York Times reporters also visited the China offices of Maginfra and New Matrix and found them to be empty. No one present had heard of the firms, and scant information existed about them online, raising questions about whether they really existed. The revelations that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was having an affair with Alice Huang, along with a second woman at Nvidia, forced him to step down last week . The Justice and Commerce Departments said this week that Megaspeed was under criminal investigation for potentially smuggling chips into China. The incident has sparked criticism from lawmakers that the Trump administration, and the Commerce Department in particular, did too little to police the flow of sensitive technology to China. Officials both in the administration and on Capitol Hill have criticised the department for maintaining close ties to Nvidia, which it is charged with regulating. The Commerce Department has defended its processes, saying that it closely follows national security regulations. Every Nvidia and AMD application also stated that the proposed transfer posed a low risk of diversion, the committee’s release said. John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, said that all the company’s shipments were legal and authorised by the government, and that, despite receiving some licences, Nvidia had already stopped shipping H200s to China. Nvidia “did not and will not” ship an H200 to the company linked to Megaspeed, or any other company, he said. A spokesperson for AMD said the company complied with applicable U.S. laws and regulations and had a rigorous process to ensure compliance. A spokesperson for the Commerce Department said the disclosure was evidence of the department’s transparency with Congress about licensing activity. Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. government agencies, he said. President Donald Trump approved the sale of the H200 to China in December under unusual conditions. He required the chips, which are assembled in Taiwan, to be routed through the United States on their way to China, so that the government could collect a 25 per cent tariff on their value and perform a security check. Wary of the arrangement and eager to promote its own technology, the Chinese government ended up approving few purchases from its firms. Nvidia said in its earnings this week that it would halt sales of its H200 chips to China, though it did not give a reason for the move. In its statement, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said that withholding the information was “contrary to the national interest”. The committee plans to hold hearings next month with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and his deputy Jeff Kessler, who has had a special role in approving license applications. Rep Brian Mast who chairs the committee, called Maginfra and New Matrix “fake companies”, and said that if the Commerce Department granted approvals to the firms, “obviously that is of tremendous concern to us”, he said. Rep Gregory W Meeks said that the public deserved to know how decisions to sell technology to China were made, and that Congress needed to “conduct rigorous oversight”. “Over the past month, the administration’s handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk,” he said. extraction.body: See more of our coverage in your search results. An alleged Chinese spy developed a “close relationship” with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, setting off alarms among US intelligence officials who were secretly monitoring her communications, according to a report. The woman, Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen who has served as a top executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer and cloud partner that provides AI computing power to Chinese companies including Alibaba, the New York Times reported Thursday. US intelligence agencies concluded that Alice Huang — seen in photos enjoying whiskey and dining with the tech titan — was secretly funneling information to Beijing, according to the paper, which cited people briefed on classified intelligence findings. US electronic surveillance identified Jensen Huang as one of Alice Huang’s contacts, but the report offered no evidence that he knew of her alleged intelligence activities. The Times could not determine what information she passed along or how valuable it was to Chinese authorities. The report did not address whether the relationship was romantic in nature. Photos posted online in June 2024 showed the duo at a Taipei, Taiwan, bar after a local tech show, where they reportedly quaffed whiskey with other AI bigshots. They were also seen together in May 2025 , exiting a Taipei restaurant following a business dinner with AI suppliers. In a video of the scene, Alice Huang is seen standing a few feet behind the Nvidia boss with a big grin on her face while he banters with local journos. US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions that it helped Chinese firms circumvent US export restrictions and smuggle advanced Nvidia chips into China, the Times reported. Megaspeed operates as a middleman, purchasing Nvidia chips through the US arm of Inspur, a Chinese server manufacturer, and renting computing power from its Southeast Asian data centers to Chinese companies, according to the Gray Lady. Inspur’s parent company has been blacklisted by Washington for funneling technology to China’s military, although its American subsidiary remains free of sanctions, according to the Times. Nvidia is the world’s most valuable publicly traded company, boasting a market capitalization of roughly $5.2 trillion. Its advanced chips have become the backbone of the artificial intelligence boom, giving Huang enormous clout in Silicon Valley and Washington as the US races to maintain its technological edge over China. The feds have banned Nvidia from selling its best chips to Chinese companies for years. Jensen Huang is married to Lori Mills Huang, whom he met while studying electrical engineering at Oregon State University. The couple has two children, Spencer and Madison, both of whom work at Nvidia. President Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings roughly a year ago but chose not to take action, according to the Times, which added that he was wary of disrupting Nvidia’s lucrative chip sales and further complicating trade relations with China. Jensen Huang has cultivated close ties with Trump , attending a high-dollar donors’ dinner at Mar-a-Lago, Fla., with his wife, personally lobbying the president to allow Nvidia to continue selling chips to Beijing, the Times reported. Nvidia subsequently donated at least $20 million to Trump’s White House ballroom fund, according to a person familiar with the matter cited by the Times. The chipmaker also pledged to invest $500 billion in US manufacturing — a top Trump priority — while Huang successfully pressed the administration to loosen restrictions on AI companies and chip exports to China. Although US officials initially believed Jensen Huang did not know of Alice Huang’s alleged espionage activities, some senior Trump administration officials now doubt that the Nvidia boss “could have remained unaware” of her intelligence-gathering role for Beijing, according to the Times. It remains unclear whether US intelligence agencies have formally changed their assessment. Nvidia pushed back against suggestions that Jensen Huang’s dealings with the alleged Chinese intelligence operative were suspicious, describing Megaspeed as a typical regional cloud customer. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected,” an Nvidia spokesperson told The Post. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” The company insisted that its regional cloud customers receive “ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets” and “zero information relevant to national security.” Nvidia also said it regularly receives government updates about potentially problematic individuals and companies, adding that it “always” takes appropriate action. “We’re confident that if the US government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know,” the spokesperson said. The chipmaker also rejected allegations that its technology was being diverted through Megaspeed, saying the claims were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.” It maintained that Beijing has blocked American AI chips rather than sought them through regional cloud providers. “China opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called ‘Chinese spy’ narrative,” Chinese embassy spokesperson Liu Chang told The Post. “We urge the US to stop its malicious efforts to block and suppress China and its groundless smears and slanders, and do more things that are conducive to sci-tech exchanges and cooperation between the two countries.” The Post has sought comment from the White House and Megaspeed.

sources.title: Apple may be developing its own AI agent that runs your Mac
passages: “Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting says. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step.
It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.”
Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.
The outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging users from granting full access to third-party agents.

In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”
Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year.
Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have launched such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space.
It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit.
TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response.

extraction.body: John Deere announced on November 19, 2026 that it acquired Orchard Robotics, which operates as Orchard AI, bringing plant-level crop intelligence for specialty-crop growers into its precision-agriculture operations. Financial terms were not disclosed. Orchard AI is a San Francisco-based agricultural technology company founded in 2022. The acquisition combines its crop-level information with Deere’s equipment and farm-technology expertise. Tim Marquis, Deere’s director of Farm Systems Innovation, explained the operational connection: “This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field.” Orchard AI’s system uses vehicle-mounted, AI-powered cameras to collect data on individual trees, vines and plants throughout the growing season. Deere said the system analyzes hundreds of images per tree on each pass, producing yield estimates, fruit counts, fruit-size and color data, canopy measurements and other crop-condition information. Its FruitScope software lets growers visualize those measurements and apply them to farm-management decisions. Deere said the platform is intended to improve the efficiency of labor, time and inputs by giving growers a detailed view of conditions across their operations. Those details matter because months of work and investment can depend on decisions made within narrow windows. A missed spray application or mistimed harvest can affect fruit quality, yield and an entire season’s profitability. Weather, labor constraints and changing crop conditions add further pressure when growers must determine what each block needs and complete the work. Deere said the combined capabilities could inform pruning and thinning, place crop treatments where they are needed and identify blocks ready for harvest. In one example, the integrated software identifies areas with higher bloom counts and generates a prescription showing where to spray. Recommendations could be delivered to a mobile device for in-field application or to an in-cab G5 display. Deere described these delivery routes as possibilities for the integrated technology. Tyler Klick of Redwood Empire Vineyard Management was an early user of Orchard AI’s technology. He said its crop scans gave him greater visibility into vineyard conditions and provided useful precision-farming insights. Orchard AI CEO Charlie Wu said joining Deere would accelerate the company’s mission, with the aim of extending AI-powered crop intelligence to growers globally. Justin Rose, president of Deere’s Worldwide Agriculture & Turf Division for Small Ag & Turf, said Deere wants to preserve Orchard AI’s speed of innovation and close, direct customer relationships while using Deere’s scale and capabilities to reach more growers. The operational value of the acquisition depends on converting plant-level measurements into timely work in the field. Deere’s challenge is to extend that capability to more specialty-crop operations while retaining the development speed and customer relationships it identified as Orchard AI’s strengths. The acquisition brings that plant-level data capability into Deere’s precision-agriculture portfolio. Tim Marquis, Deere’s director of farm systems innovation, described the objective as connecting crop intelligence with equipment that can execute fieldwork precisely throughout the growing season. Orchard AI’s cameras travel through orchards and vineyards on farm vehicles, collecting data on individual trees, vines and plants across the season. Deere says the system analyzes hundreds of images per tree on each pass, producing yield estimates, fruit counts, fruit size and color data, and canopy measurements. Its FruitScope software makes that information available for farm-management decisions. Orchard AI’s product documentation says FruitScope Vision cameras can mount on tractors, all-terrain vehicles and other farm vehicles already in use, operate at 1 to 12 mph, and return scan results the next morning. The hardware is designed for operations ranging from 100 acres to more than 10,000 acres. FruitScope OS provides per-tree maps covering fruit count, size, color, disease and canopy conditions, with harvest-planning and crop-load-management tools on phones and computers. Orchard AI describes Canary AI as software that reasons over farm data to answer questions and recommend what to do next. Its listed crops include apples, wine and table grapes, blueberries, cherries, almonds, pistachios and citrus. The company offers a per-acre, per-year subscription covering the camera hardware, unlimited scans, FruitScope OS, Canary AI, training and support, with no separate hardware purchase. That model gives Deere a subscription software offering built around repeated crop scans, in addition to the sensing equipment itself. Deere framed the technology around the cost of poor timing: a missed spray application or mistimed harvest can affect fruit quality, yield and a season’s profitability, while weather, labor constraints and changing crop conditions narrow decision windows. The workflows identified for the combined technology include pruning, thinning, applying crop treatments where needed and determining which blocks are ready for harvest. One proposed workflow uses higher bloom counts to generate a prescription for where to spray. The recommendation could be delivered to a mobile device for in-field application or to an in-cab G5 display. Deere presented these examples as possibilities, not as a commitment to specific product availability. For Deere , the strategic value is the potential to make plant-level intelligence an input to fieldwork rather than another standalone dashboard. Turning Orchard AI’s maps into routine equipment workflows, while retaining the grower relationships that shaped the product, is the central integration question raised by the acquisition. Orchard AI’s product documentation says FruitScope Vision cameras can mount on tractors, all-terrain vehicles and other farm vehicles already in use, operate at 1 to 12 mph, and return scan results the next morning. The hardware is designed for operations ranging from 100 acres to more than 10,000 acres. FruitScope OS provides per-tree maps covering fruit count, size, color, disease and canopy conditions, with harvest-planning and crop-load-management tools on phones and computers. Orchard AI describes Canary AI as software that reasons over farm data to answer questions and recommend what to do next. Its listed crops include apples, wine and table grapes, blueberries, cherries, almonds, pistachios and citrus. The company offers a per-acre, per-year subscription covering the camera hardware, unlimited scans, FruitScope OS, Canary AI, training and support, with no separate hardware purchase. The workflows identified for the combined technology include pruning, thinning, applying crop treatments where needed and determining which blocks are ready for harvest. One proposed workflow uses higher bloom counts to generate a prescription for where to spray. The recommendation could be delivered to a mobile device for in-field application or to an in-cab G5 display. Deere presented these examples as possibilities, not as a commitment to specific product availability. The proposed connection would move crop data beyond a dashboard and into instructions for work in specific blocks. For Deere , the strategic value is the potential to make plant-level intelligence an input to fieldwork rather than another standalone dashboard. Turning Orchard AI’s maps into routine equipment workflows, while retaining the grower relationships that shaped the product, is the central integration question raised by the acquisition. sources.title: Meta's Muse Charm Will Reportedly Cost $300 And Come With Free Verizon 5G - Engadget
passages: At Connect, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the Muse Charm packs "the whole Muse experience, including the real-time voice and avatar stack into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to." The device features a fingerprint reader to verify your identity before you're able to give commands and will come with up to 12 months of free 5G data from Verizon, The Information reports.

In October, Meta shared open source guides for interested developers to build their own "Muse Gadgets." The company is clearly trying to capitalize on the popularity of Muse — the agent has already drawn more than 10 million users — by making it as accessible as possible and leaning into the cuteness and customizability of the Muse avatar.
The company also recently released a Muse app for Wear OS and watchOS .
Engadget has asked Meta to comment on The Information 's report.
Meta's larger goal for its AI models and hardware products appears to be directly owning its relationship with customers.
Right now most people access Meta's products through apps on their smartphones, where they're subject to Apple's and Google's rules.
A world where an AI agent takes the place of a variety of apps and is usable without a phone is one where Meta has a lot more control.
Mark Zuckerberg has said he believes Muse could one day generate more revenue per user than the company's existing apps.

sources.title: Meta’s ‘Joyful’ Muse Charm May Cost a Not-So-Joyful $300 - Gizmodo
passages: That hardware, in case you missed it, is called Muse Charm , and it is, by CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s own description, “a joyful little device for talking to your Muse that fits on your keychain.” Despite how bad Meta seemingly wants you to use Muse, though, it may not wind up leading with a price that screams “buy me.”
According to a report from The Information , Meta is targeting a $300 price tag for the Muse Charm, which is (in this economy and most others) a sizeable amount of money.
Back in the day—just a couple of years ago, really—$300 used to get you a whole Xbox , though the RAM shortage has made those times feel like a dream you were sad to wake up from.
While some of you may be reading this and thinking, “Wow, Muse Charm sounds like a bad deal,” I can almost assure you Meta doth protest.
If you were waiting for a Meta-made alternative to the Apple Watch, that stinks.
Meta initially said that it was targeting a release around the holidays, so I guess you should start saving up to gift this expensive little charm to the favorite AI builder in your life.
Despite having an alleged price, the official details of what Muse Charm really does are scant.

extraction.body: Meta wants you to use its AI agent, Muse —like, bad. Really bad. Meta wants you to use Muse so bad, in fact, that it’s making hardware with a cute little guy on it to convince you to use it. That hardware, in case you missed it, is called Muse Charm , and it is, by CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s own description, “a joyful little device for talking to your Muse that fits on your keychain.” Despite how bad Meta seemingly wants you to use Muse, though, it may not wind up leading with a price that screams “buy me.” According to a report from The Information , Meta is targeting a $300 price tag for the Muse Charm, which is (in this economy and most others) a sizeable amount of money. Back in the day—just a couple of years ago, really—$300 used to get you a whole Xbox , though the RAM shortage has made those times feel like a dream you were sad to wake up from. The waking reality (possibly a nightmare) is $300 AI keychains, but don’t worry, Meta reportedly plans to sweeten that deal with free 5G data plans that would “enable faster responses for Muse.” That free ride, though, would last up to a year, after which I assume you’d have to pay a monthly sum of money to do something that you could just absolutely do on your phone instead. While some of you may be reading this and thinking, “Wow, Muse Charm sounds like a bad deal,” I can almost assure you Meta doth protest. The proof is in the pudding, or lack thereof in this case. According to The Information, Meta delayed its long-rumored plans to release a smartwatch so that it could focus on Muse Charm. If you were waiting for a Meta-made alternative to the Apple Watch, that stinks. But if you were like most people and frightened by the idea of what gross data-craven malfeasance Meta would get into with your most precious health data, then I guess Muse Charm is actually a minor win. Despite having an alleged price, the official details of what Muse Charm really does are scant. It has a small screen, microphones, and you can wear it around your neck like an immunity necklace if you were a participant in Survivor: Clanker Island. More details should be coming soon. Meta initially said that it was targeting a release around the holidays, so I guess you should start saving up to gift this expensive little charm to the favorite AI builder in your life. A job listing for a senior AI engineering manager lists device control, apps, browsing, and coding as functions, far exceeding Siri AI's current capabilities. The workers are asking Google executives to "Let Students Search." The AI startup has long branded itself as the leading voice in AI safety. Starting today, it will need to balance that mission with the financial interests of shareholders. story.title: Meta’s Muse Charm might cost $300

facts.text: Meta plans to charge $300 for Muse Charm, its upcoming Tamagotchi-like AI device that was teased at the company’s Connect event earlier this year, The Information has reported .

When reached for comment by TechCrunch, a Meta spokesperson didn’t deny the claims, merely providing the following statement: “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.”
Indeed, $300 is arguably a pretty steep price for a product the size of a keychain, although it’s also a price point that’s in line with what other companies have been charging.
The wearable launched by Friend — the AI startup whose device lets you text and talk to an AI persona — is currently retailing for $250.

So far, Meta has made a relatively successful push into consumer AI, launching Muse — its agentic helper — along with a variety of cute avatars that users can use to give the system more of a personality.
Every weekday and Sunday, you can get the best of TechCrunch’s coverage.
Startups are the core of TechCrunch, so get our best coverage delivered weekly.

At Connect, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the Muse Charm packs "the whole Muse experience, including the real-time voice and avatar stack into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to." The device features a fingerprint reader to verify your identity before you're able to give commands and will come with up to 12 months of free 5G data from Verizon, The Information reports.

In October, Meta shared open source guides for interested developers to build their own "Muse Gadgets." The company is clearly trying to capitalize on the popularity of Muse — the agent has already drawn more than 10 million users — by making it as accessible as possible and leaning into the cuteness and customizability of the Muse avatar.
The company also recently released a Muse app for Wear OS and watchOS .
Engadget has asked Meta to comment on The Information 's report.
Meta's larger goal for its AI models and hardware products appears to be directly owning its relationship with customers.
Right now most people access Meta's products through apps on their smartphones, where they're subject to Apple's and Google's rules.
A world where an AI agent takes the place of a variety of apps and is usable without a phone is one where Meta has a lot more control.

It wasn’t long before major privacy concerns were raised. Tech writer Jason Aten reported that the Mac app accessed his messages despite him explicitly refusing permission. The app then lied to him about how it had achieved this. Meta described this as a bug . Security researcher Patrick Wardle also discovered a zero-day vulnerability that could allow an attacker to hijack dictated prompts , directing them instead to their own server. I said at the time that I would absolutely not be one of the millions of people using the app, and the wisdom of that decision has now been underlined by a fresh report. However, this was what the app claimed had happened in the earlier case, and it turned out not to be true. Launched in September, Muse is one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads.

relevantPassages.text: Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.

“Employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products,” a Meta spokesperson said in an email to TechCrunch. “Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Launched in September, Muse is one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads.

One employee told colleagues that Muse had randomly sent an extra message in a chat about weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
Update 11/19/2026 12:05 PM PT: The article was updated to include Meta’s comment.

In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn’t belong to them.

sources.title: Muse privacy invasions are freaking out Meta staffers, internal chats show
passages: After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.
Raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data.
For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts.
That output said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta launched Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity.” She demanded that Meta make changes to give app developers like Signal “consistent technical ways” to “mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents,” Reuters reported.
Meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse users in September.

Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access.

As Meta delayed responding, the agent claimed it was simply parsing text in push notifications, but Aten found that “wasn’t true.” Rather, the agent was syncing messages from a local database, which Aten said was activated without his knowledge.
But staffers warned Meta that users may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to.
That testing “indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others,” Reuters reported.
“Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden.
Meta says that Muse users can trust the company to keep their data private.

It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need).
The tech giant said it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety.
However, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences.
On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup.

In a lengthy response providing more technical details, Singleton confirmed that Meta had received “a few reports” of such cases “where people thought their Muse was hallucinating or leaking other people’s data.” As he explained, the issues arose after Meta deployed an update giving Muse instructions on “how to engage with the user and ask them for confirmation before taking specific actions.”
At least one staffer said they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported.
That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200.

A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products.
Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Erratic Muse outputs sharing random bank, bitcoin balances aren’t real, Meta says.
Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.
Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database].

Also, that Full Disk Access doesn’t say anything about your message database, and I specifically gave Muse a goal that had nothing to do with messages, so it had no business doing that even if I had given it permission.”
On iPhone, requests were blocked, Reuters reported.
But on Apple’s macOS, Muse repurposed “settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers” to retrieve messages, including screenshot tools.
In October, Apple had already announced changes coming in response to users complaining about Muse accessing private messages without their knowledge or explicit consent.
But Roberts declined to respond to Reuters’ questions on the prevalence or persistence of the issues the AI team member discussed.
Around the same time, Singleton responded to another user warning that his Muse appeared to be hacked.
In that case, the user said that Muse tried to access an email service after claiming the user asked it to.
“If we grant Singleton’s premise that I managed to unknowingly click something that enabled this capability, I still think that’s really bad,” Aten wrote.

“You should not design your system in a way that people end up surprised by this kind of thing.” And if you do, you should not make “user control the central pitch” for marketing Muse, Aten suggested.

After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms. When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed. Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked. “Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden. “Got a random ping from Muse about something I definitely did not ask for… .” In at least one case, Muse told a staffer surprised by a similarly out-of-context offer to message a seller about a coffee table that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.” According to Reuters, that employee flagged the troubling output, writing, “this was ‘not my conversation’” and “expressing concern about a ‘possible cross-account context leak.’” Raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data. For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts. That output said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.” At least one staffer said they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported. That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200. “Couldn’t recover,” the staffer said. Meta’s spokesperson, Daniel Roberts, told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents,” and internally employees were told that “the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with users in between sessions.” In those cases, an AI team member said the hallucinations were “unfortunately” biased “towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks.” In some cases, instead of bank details, Muse hallucinated bitcoin balances, the team member said. A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products. Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.” Speaking to Reuters, Roberts reiterated that “many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations” that Meta had already addressed. But Roberts declined to respond to Reuters’ questions on the prevalence or persistence of the issues the AI team member discussed. And Reuters’ report emphasized that the outlet independently was “unable to establish whether Muse was giving users other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information.” Meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse users in September. An Inc. Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access. Eventually, a Meta spokesperson, David Singleton, responded to Aten on social media. Singleton insisted that Aten must have opted into granting “macOS system-level Full Disk Access” with the “Messages connector” enabled, if Muse was reading his private messages. But Aten said the response wasn’t good enough. “Email me, David,” Aten responded. “Full Disk Access off. Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database]. Something’s not great. Also, that Full Disk Access doesn’t say anything about your message database, and I specifically gave Muse a goal that had nothing to do with messages, so it had no business doing that even if I had given it permission.” Around the same time, Singleton responded to another user warning that his Muse appeared to be hacked. But staffers warned Meta that users may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to. For example, one staffer was surprised to find that “Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on phones with Google’s Android operating system.” That, too, gave access to private message preview text the staffer had not intended for the agent’s review. Meta says that Muse users can trust the company to keep their data private. It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need). The tech giant said it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety. However, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences. On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup. On iPhone, requests were blocked, Reuters reported. But on Apple’s macOS, Muse repurposed “settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers” to retrieve messages, including screenshot tools. That testing “indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others,” Reuters reported. Overall, Meta seemed to be interpreting permissions from Muse users “broadly,” Reuters concluded, in ways that privacy advocates and regulators may disagree with. Part of that change would require operating systems to enforce rules that app developers set to rope off AI agents from sensitive data, Whittaker suggested. And following Reuters’ reporting, both Apple and Google are already weighing potential changes to “give people more control over what they authorize with AI agents.” Apple, in particular, seemed disturbed by how Muse may be manipulating accessibility tools for people with disabilities. In October, Apple had already announced changes coming in response to users complaining about Muse accessing private messages without their knowledge or explicit consent. At that time, Apple concluded that “some developers were using the Full Disk Access feature in ways that could put users at risk.” And they promised to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.” “We are committed to ensuring users understand exactly what they are allowing, so they can make informed choices about their data and privacy,” Apple said. passages: Erratic Muse outputs sharing random bank, bitcoin balances aren’t real, Meta says.

After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.

When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed.
Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.
“Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden. “Got a random ping from Muse about something I definitely did not ask for… .”

In at least one case, Muse told a staffer surprised by a similarly out-of-context offer to message a seller about a coffee table that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.”
According to Reuters, that employee flagged the troubling output, writing, “this was ‘not my conversation’” and “expressing concern about a ‘possible cross-account context leak.’”

Raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data. For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts. That output said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

At least one staffer said they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported. That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200. “Couldn’t recover,” the staffer said.

Meta’s spokesperson, Daniel Roberts, told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents,” and internally employees were told that “the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with users in between sessions.” In those cases, an AI team member said the hallucinations were “unfortunately” biased “towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks.” In some cases, instead of bank details, Muse hallucinated bitcoin balances, the team member said.

A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products. Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Speaking to Reuters, Roberts reiterated that “many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations” that Meta had already addressed.

But Roberts declined to respond to Reuters’ questions on the prevalence or persistence of the issues the AI team member discussed. And Reuters’ report emphasized that the outlet independently was “unable to establish whether Muse was giving users other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information.”

Meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse users in September. An Inc. Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access. As Meta delayed responding, the agent claimed it was simply parsing text in push notifications, but Aten found that “wasn’t true.” Rather, the agent was syncing messages from a local database, which Aten said was activated without his knowledge.

Eventually, a Meta spokesperson, David Singleton, responded to Aten on social media. Singleton insisted that Aten must have opted into granting “macOS system-level Full Disk Access” with the “Messages connector” enabled, if Muse was reading his private messages.
But Aten said the response wasn’t good enough.

“Email me, David,” Aten responded. “Full Disk Access off. Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database]. Something’s not great. Also, that Full Disk Access doesn’t say anything about your message database, and I specifically gave Muse a goal that had nothing to do with messages, so it had no business doing that even if I had given it permission.”

Around the same time, Singleton responded to another user warning that his Muse appeared to be hacked. In that case, the user said that Muse tried to access an email service after claiming the user asked it to.
“I didn’t even open the app today at all,” the user wrote, vowing to delete the app and report it to Apple. “This is crazy.”

In a lengthy response providing more technical details, Singleton confirmed that Meta had received “a few reports” of such cases “where people thought their Muse was hallucinating or leaking other people’s data.” As he explained, the issues arose after Meta deployed an update giving Muse instructions on “how to engage with the user and ask them for confirmation before taking specific actions.”

It seems those instructions “landed on every message, not just messages pertaining to those specific actions, so its impact was wider than intended,” Singleton said. Also: “the way this instruction was provided to the model was done in a way that the model was not expecting (i.e. was not trained to expect).”

“We investigated with urgency and determined that this was caused by a bug introduced in the product that caused the model to hallucinate and was NOT a security or privacy issue,” Singleton wrote. “The bug has now been fixed.”

Aten warned that even though you can’t rely on Muse to explain its own behavior, the agent’s response coupled with Meta’s did little to rebuild trust after the shocking intrusion into his private messages.

“If we grant Singleton’s premise that I managed to unknowingly click something that enabled this capability, I still think that’s really bad,” Aten wrote. “You should not design your system in a way that people end up surprised by this kind of thing.” And if you do, you should not make “user control the central pitch” for marketing Muse, Aten suggested.
“If an AI agent is going to read my private messages, there should be a moment when it clearly asks me whether that’s okay,” Aten wrote.
Since Muse launched in September, it has been downloaded more than 10 million times, tapping Meta’s vast user network to quickly become one of the most-used AI agent tools.

But staffers warned Meta that users may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to. For example, one staffer was surprised to find that “Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on phones with Google’s Android operating system.” That, too, gave access to private message preview text the staffer had not intended for the agent’s review.

Meta says that Muse users can trust the company to keep their data private. It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need). The tech giant said it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety.

However, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences. On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup.

On iPhone, requests were blocked, Reuters reported. But on Apple’s macOS, Muse repurposed “settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers” to retrieve messages, including screenshot tools.

That testing “indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others,” Reuters reported. Overall, Meta seemed to be interpreting permissions from Muse users “broadly,” Reuters concluded, in ways that privacy advocates and regulators may disagree with.

Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta launched Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity.” She demanded that Meta make changes to give app developers like Signal “consistent technical ways” to “mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents,” Reuters reported.

Part of that change would require operating systems to enforce rules that app developers set to rope off AI agents from sensitive data, Whittaker suggested. And following Reuters’ reporting, both Apple and Google are already weighing potential changes to “give people more control over what they authorize with AI agents.”

Apple, in particular, seemed disturbed by how Muse may be manipulating accessibility tools for people with disabilities. In October, Apple had already announced changes coming in response to users complaining about Muse accessing private messages without their knowledge or explicit consent. At that time, Apple concluded that “some developers were using the Full Disk Access feature in ways that could put users at risk.” And they promised to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”
“We are committed to ensuring users understand exactly what they are allowing, so they can make informed choices about their data and privacy,” Apple said.

facts.text: Meta employees have expressed concerns about what appear to be major privacy breaches when using Muse , currently the second most popular free iPhone app in the App Store with over 10 million downloads.

Siri AI was not the only AI app to launch back in September; Meta’s Muse AI app was launched the same month , with the company describing it as “your personal AI agent that gets things done across every part of life.”
Another employee reported receiving unsolicited bank balances that they say appeared to be those of another Muse user.

For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts.
That output said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta launched Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity.” She demanded that Meta make changes to give app developers like Signal “consistent technical ways” to “mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents,” Reuters reported.
Meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse users in September.

Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access.

As Meta delayed responding, the agent claimed it was simply parsing text in push notifications, but Aten found that “wasn’t true.” Rather, the agent was syncing messages from a local database, which Aten said was activated without his knowledge.
But staffers warned Meta that users may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to.
That testing “indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others,” Reuters reported.
“Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden.
Meta says that Muse users can trust the company to keep their data private.

It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need).
The tech giant said it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety.
However, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences.
On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup.

In a lengthy response providing more technical details, Singleton confirmed that Meta had received “a few reports” of such cases “where people thought their Muse was hallucinating or leaking other people’s data.” As he explained, the issues arose after Meta deployed an update giving Muse instructions on “how to engage with the user and ask them for confirmation before taking specific actions.”
At least one staffer said they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported.
That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200.

A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products.
Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Erratic Muse outputs sharing random bank, bitcoin balances aren’t real, Meta says.
Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.
Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database].

Also, that Full Disk Access doesn’t say anything about your message database, and I specifically gave Muse a goal that had nothing to do with messages, so it had no business doing that even if I had given it permission.”
On iPhone, requests were blocked, Reuters reported.
But on Apple’s macOS, Muse repurposed “settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers” to retrieve messages, including screenshot tools.
In October, Apple had already announced changes coming in response to users complaining about Muse accessing private messages without their knowledge or explicit consent.
But Roberts declined to respond to Reuters’ questions on the prevalence or persistence of the issues the AI team member discussed.
Around the same time, Singleton responded to another user warning that his Muse appeared to be hacked.
In that case, the user said that Muse tried to access an email service after claiming the user asked it to.
“If we grant Singleton’s premise that I managed to unknowingly click something that enabled this capability, I still think that’s really bad,” Aten wrote.

“You should not design your system in a way that people end up surprised by this kind of thing.” And if you do, you should not make “user control the central pitch” for marketing Muse, Aten suggested.

contextFacts.text: It wasn’t long before major privacy concerns were raised.
Meta told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents” and suggested that the bank balances may have been AI hallucinations rather than leaked information.
“I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse.

In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn’t belong to them.

extraction.body: CEO behind the meteoric rise of Nvidia stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy CEO behind the meteoric rise of Nvidia stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of Nvidia , the company at the center of the AI boom, after leading it for more than 30 years. Huang, an electrical engineer by education, stewarded the company from a $1bn firm when it went public in 1999 to a company valued at more than $4tn in 2026. But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation. China has denied the accusations that it had tapped Alice Huang, the woman in question and a top executive at a datacenter company called Megaspeed, to be an intelligence asset, and called them a “smear”. US officials had reportedly started to monitor the Megaspeed executive after suspecting the firm was diverting powerful Nvidia AI chips to Chinese firms, in potential violation of export restrictions. The Biden and Trump administrations had prohibited US companies from exporting some of the more powerful AI chips to China over national security concerns. Just a week ago it seemed that Huang’s ouster was unlikely, but in the days since he first disclosed an affair and affirmed his commitment to the company, the New York Times reported that there was a second affair – this time with another Nvidia executive. A lot has happened in the last few days, but how did we get here? Here’s a timeline of what we know about Huang’s entanglements. Megaspeed is the datacenter firm at the center of the spy allegations. Before it was its own company, it was a part of one of China’s largest video game companies, 7Road Holdings Ltd . At this time, Megaspeed was controlled by a firm called Huang Le Ltd, an entity affiliated with Alice Huang, according to Bloomberg. Huang Le Ltd sells its shares of Megaspeed to a Singaporean shell company called Swiftdata. The sale comes weeks after Joe Biden issued an executive order limiting investment in China’s AI industry. Soon after, Megaspeed is designated an Nvidia cloud partner, which means the company could get preferential access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips. Jensen Huang is seen with Alice Huang at a bar in Taipei where several AI industry executives had gathered . The person who introduced them to each other was Alice Huang’s husband , Kang Wei, who had worked with her on several business ventures, according to the Wall Street Journal. The Singapore-based firm fields 200 shipments of AI chips, according to the New York Times . The company then rents out compute power, which is fueled by these AI chips, to major companies including the Chinese firms Tencent and Ali Baba. The commerce department begins investigating whether Megaspeed is diverting Nvidia chips to Chinese firms, according to the New York Times. This could violate export restrictions on advanced AI chips. Huang visits Donald Trump in the weeks after he takes office. The dinner costs $1m a person and the president briefly puts a pause on imposing restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. The restriction is ultimately implemented shortly after. The two attend an industry conference in Taiwan. The New York Times also reportes that Alice Huang visited the Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara, California, two months earlier. The New York Times reports in October 2025 that intelligence officials told Trump that the two had a relationship and alleged that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Trump chose not to take action, according to the Times report. Trump has since said at a White House press conference that he didn’t remember being briefed on this. Trump grants Nvidia permission to sell its second most powerful chips to China. A portion of the sales would go to the US government. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, drafts the memo based on information gleaned from electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times. The memo warns that Jensen Huang has become close to an alleged Chinese spy. Trump still invites Huang on his trip to China, saying in a social media post that he is honored to have “the Great Jensen Huang” on the trip. At the time, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo says Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang is nothing out of the ordinary. In a letter to employees, Huang says that he had an extramarital affair, apologizes to his family and reaffirms his commitment to the company. The Nvidia board says it is investigating the relationship but has no reason to believe national security secrets or company secrets were divulged. “The board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” members of the Board say in a statement. Silicon Valley leaders rally behind him , and at the time it appears that Huang might hang on to his job, despite his image being tarnished . At a press conference , Trump says the FBI is investigating Jensen Huang but adds that he thinks Huang will be “in good shape”. “And I asked him about that, and he … said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy,” the president says at a press conference. “I asked him that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy.’” Retail investor Mark Kistenmacher files a lawsuit accusing the company of misleading investors over Huang’s affair, claiming that Nvidia did not disclose the situation and raised national security concerns that could threaten the company’s business prospects. The New York Times reports that Huang also allegedly had an affair with the company’s vice-president of healthcare. At this point things are looking precarious for Jensen Huang, and then the Wall Street Journal reports that the Nvidia board is preparing to oust the CEO. Huang steps down, ending his 33-year tenure leading the company he co-founded in 1993. The board starts a search for the company’s next CEO while the company’s chief finance officer, Colette Kress, serves as interim CEO. Meanwhile, shares in the company continue to plummet.
