extraction.body: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. Nvidia reported its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, which beat Wall Street expectations with $115.8 billion in revenue, up 103% year-over-year. Despite the unknowns the company faces without Huang involved, interim CEO Colette Kress said that full-year revenue is also on track to exceed expectations. The company also plans to raise its outlook for the 2028 fiscal year, indicating confidence that this unexpected leadership change won’t get in the way of its trajectory. “We have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap,” Kress said. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual. We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones affirmed that the company is not considering reinstating Huang. Kress also said that Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country. Jensen Huang posted his first public statement since he admitted to having an extramarital affair more than a week earlier. “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote. Many of Huang’s colleagues in the tech industry, including Elon Musk, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey , and Y Combinator President and CEO Garry Tan, have called for his return. Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an… More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia. Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.” Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making. In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy. “Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales,” the letter states. Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993. Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26. “Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.” The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed. After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed . An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.”

But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security.

U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.)

Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported.

The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.

By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee.

The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities.
As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.

The company also plans to raise its outlook for the 2028 fiscal year, indicating confidence that this unexpected leadership change won’t get in the way of its trajectory.

“We have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap,” Kress said. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual. We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.”

Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones affirmed that the company is not considering reinstating Huang. Kress also said that Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country.
Jensen Huang posted his first public statement since he admitted to having an extramarital affair more than a week earlier.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.
Many of Huang’s colleagues in the tech industry, including Elon Musk, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey , and Y Combinator President and CEO Garry Tan, have called for his return.

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an…
More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia.
Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.”

Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making.

In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy.

“Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993.
Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26.

“Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.”
The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed.

Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo.

A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service.
Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born.

But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation. China has denied the accusations that it had tapped Alice Huang, the woman in question and a top executive at a datacenter company called Megaspeed, to be an intelligence asset, and called them a “smear”. US officials had reportedly started to monitor the Megaspeed executive after suspecting the firm was diverting powerful Nvidia AI chips to Chinese firms, in potential violation of export restrictions. The Biden and Trump administrations had prohibited US companies from exporting some of the more powerful AI chips to China over national security concerns. Just a week ago it seemed that Huang’s ouster was unlikely, but in the days since he first disclosed an affair and affirmed his commitment to the company, the New York Times reported that there was a second affair – this time with another Nvidia executive. Before it was its own company, it was a part of one of China’s largest video game companies, 7Road Holdings Ltd . At this time, Megaspeed was controlled by a firm called Huang Le Ltd, an entity affiliated with Alice Huang, according to Bloomberg. Huang Le Ltd sells its shares of Megaspeed to a Singaporean shell company called Swiftdata. The sale comes weeks after Joe Biden issued an executive order limiting investment in China’s AI industry. Soon after, Megaspeed is designated an Nvidia cloud partner, which means the company could get preferential access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips. Jensen Huang is seen with Alice Huang at a bar in Taipei where several AI industry executives had gathered . The person who introduced them to each other was Alice Huang’s husband , Kang Wei, who had worked with her on several business ventures, according to the Wall Street Journal. The Singapore-based firm fields 200 shipments of AI chips, according to the New York Times . The company then rents out compute power, which is fueled by these AI chips, to major companies including the Chinese firms Tencent and Ali Baba. This could violate export restrictions on advanced AI chips. Huang visits Donald Trump in the weeks after he takes office. The dinner costs $1m a person and the president briefly puts a pause on imposing restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. The restriction is ultimately implemented shortly after. At the time, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo says Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang is nothing out of the ordinary. The Nvidia board says it is investigating the relationship but has no reason to believe national security secrets or company secrets were divulged. “The board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” members of the Board say in a statement. Silicon Valley leaders rally behind him , and at the time it appears that Huang might hang on to his job, despite his image being tarnished . At a press conference , Trump says the FBI is investigating Jensen Huang but adds that he thinks Huang will be “in good shape”. “And I asked him about that, and he … said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy,” the president says at a press conference. “I asked him that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy.’” Retail investor Mark Kistenmacher files a lawsuit accusing the company of misleading investors over Huang’s affair, claiming that Nvidia did not disclose the situation and raised national security concerns that could threaten the company’s business prospects. At this point things are looking precarious for Jensen Huang, and then the Wall Street Journal reports that the Nvidia board is preparing to oust the CEO. Huang steps down, ending his 33-year tenure leading the company he co-founded in 1993. The board starts a search for the company’s next CEO while the company’s chief finance officer, Colette Kress, serves as interim CEO. Meanwhile, shares in the company continue to plummet.

extraction.body: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. Nvidia reported its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, which beat Wall Street expectations with $115.8 billion in revenue, up 103% year-over-year. Despite the unknowns the company faces without Huang involved, interim CEO Colette Kress said that full-year revenue is also on track to exceed expectations. The company also plans to raise its outlook for the 2028 fiscal year, indicating confidence that this unexpected leadership change won’t get in the way of its trajectory. “We have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap,” Kress said. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual. We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones affirmed that the company is not considering reinstating Huang. Kress also said that Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country. Jensen Huang posted his first public statement since he admitted to having an extramarital affair more than a week earlier. “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote. Many of Huang’s colleagues in the tech industry, including Elon Musk, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey , and Y Combinator President and CEO Garry Tan, have called for his return. Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an… More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia. Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.” Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making. In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy. “Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales,” the letter states. Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993. Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26. “Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.” The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed. After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed . An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.”

The controversy has drawn attention from US lawmakers, prompted an independent investigation by Nvidia's board and reportedly raised questions about Huang's future at the company.
Here is how the events unfolded, from the initial investigations into a Singapore-based business to the latest developments surrounding the Nvidia chief.
October 2025: Chip smuggling investigation The controversy has its roots in investigations into Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company and Nvidia customer.
In October 2025, authorities in the US and Singapore began investigating the company over suspicions that it was helping Chinese businesses obtain Nvidia chips despite American export restrictions.
According to reports, Megaspeed had been renting computing capacity to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other companies.

Concerns grew after a US Commerce Department official visiting one of its data centres in Malaysia in 2024 reportedly discovered Nvidia equipment still packed in boxes, raising questions about whether the hardware was being shipped elsewhere rather than deployed for cloud computing.
Huang had also been seen socialising with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang in Taiwan as early as 2024.
Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is not related to the Nvidia CEO.

2025: Trump reportedly briefed on Huang's relationship US President Donald Trump was reportedly briefed towards the end of 2025 about intelligence findings concerning Alice Huang and her relationship with the Nvidia chief.
However, the president did not take action following the briefing, according to the New York Times.
Huang has been an ally of Trump and has repeatedly argued that the US government should allow Nvidia to expand its business in China.
May 2026: Secret memo raises concerns about suspected Chinese spy The matter took another turn in spring 2026 when a confidential memo circulated among Trump administration officials.
The document reportedly identified Alice Huang as a suspected Chinese intelligence operative working for China's Ministry of State Security.
According to reports, Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the preparation of the memo.
It warned policymakers about her alleged relationship with Huang and the potential implications for American national security.

October 29, 2026: Huang's relationship with Alice Huang becomes public The controversy became public when the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, who was already under investigation by American authorities.
Nvidia pushed back against suggestions that their interactions were unusual.
Company spokesperson John Rizzo said meetings with customers were part of Huang's responsibilities as chief executive, adding that he interacted with thousands of customer executives every year.
He also said Nvidia would expect the US government to inform the company if it believed someone posed a threat to American industry.
November 5, 2026: Republican lawmakers seek answers from Huang Three Republican committee chairmen asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing with members of their committees.

The lawmakers included John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.
Their letter highlighted concerns about China's access to sensitive American technology and information.
They said Congress needed to establish whether US national security had been compromised through potential Chinese infiltration.

November 8, 2026: Huang apologises for affair as Nvidia, FDA launches investigation Huang addressed the controversy directly in a letter to Nvidia employees, admitting that he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologising to his family and colleagues.
Although he did not identify Alice Huang by name, he acknowledged the national security concerns raised in media reports.

Huang also confirmed that Nvidia's board had initiated an independent investigation, pledging to cooperate fully and reiterating his commitment to protecting the company and American national security.
The admission had an immediate impact on investor sentiment, with Nvidia shares falling more than 5 per cent the following day.
US President Donald Trump also weighed in on the controversy on November 8.
Despite acknowledging that he did not know all the details, Trump described Huang as a 'fine person' and said he believed the Nvidia chief should remain in charge of the company.
November 9-10, 2026: More about Alice Huang's business network Further reporting shed light on the business connections between Alice Huang, her family and Nvidia's chip supply chain.
According to reports, Alice Huang and her family had established a network of businesses across China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia processors.
One of these was Shanghai Century Litong, a Chinese company founded in 2023 that reportedly became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips.
The Information reported that the company had facilitated purchases worth $7.5 billion, including chips restricted under US export controls.
Separately, Bloomberg reported that Nvidia's head lawyer, Tim Teter, had intervened during a 2025 US government investigation into suspected chip smuggling involving Megaspeed.

facts.text: Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of Nvidia , the company at the center of the AI boom, after leading it for more than 30 years.
At this point things are looking precarious for Jensen Huang, and then the Wall Street Journal reports that the Nvidia board is preparing to oust the CEO.
In a letter to employees, Huang says that he had an extramarital affair, apologizes to his family and reaffirms his commitment to the company.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, drafts the memo based on information gleaned from electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times.
Jensen Huang is seen with Alice Huang at a bar in Taipei where several AI industry executives had gathered .

Retail investor Mark Kistenmacher files a lawsuit accusing the company of misleading investors over Huang’s affair, claiming that Nvidia did not disclose the situation and raised national security concerns that could threaten the company’s business prospects.
Here’s a timeline of what we know about Huang’s entanglements.
Soon after, Megaspeed is designated an Nvidia cloud partner, which means the company could get preferential access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips.
The two attend an industry conference in Taiwan.
Trump grants Nvidia permission to sell its second most powerful chips to China.
The dinner costs $1m a person and the president briefly puts a pause on imposing restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China.
The restriction is ultimately implemented shortly after.
U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.
This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times.
Jensen Huang posted his first public statement since he admitted to having an extramarital affair more than a week earlier.
Nvidia reported its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, which beat Wall Street expectations with $115.8 billion in revenue, up 103% year-over-year.
Despite the unknowns the company faces without Huang involved, interim CEO Colette Kress said that full-year revenue is also on track to exceed expectations.
The company also plans to raise its outlook for the 2028 fiscal year, indicating confidence that this unexpected leadership change won’t get in the way of its trajectory.

Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him.
Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report.
Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.
Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said .
As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.

The chairmen of the House Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and the House Intelligence Committee formally requested a closed-door briefing from Jensen Huang, with the request reported around November 5, 2026.
No public response from Huang or Nvidia was identified in the cited reporting at that time.
During 2024 and into 2025 , media reports said Jensen Huang and Alice Huang were photographed or observed socializing in Taiwan, where Jensen Huang was born.
The memo allegedly stated she had been recruited to gather information about Jensen Huang .
It also alleged she was tasked with influencing Nvidia’s commercial position on advanced chip sales to China.
Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led it since.
Alice Huang , also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen and former senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data-center company that rents computing capacity built on Nvidia processors.
Nvidia responded by characterizing Jensen Huang’s interactions with her as ordinary customer-related contact.

Public reporting has not established what information Alice Huang allegedly obtained, whether any Nvidia proprietary information was transferred, or whether export-control violations involving Megaspeed occurred.

Congressional committees have requested access to Jensen Huang ; no hearing date has been announced, and until investigators publish conclusions or authorities bring formal charges, the espionage allegations remain unproven.

In October 2025 , U.S. and Singapore authorities reportedly examined whether Megaspeed had helped Chinese firms, including Alibaba, obtain Nvidia processors in potential violation of U.S. export restrictions.

The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public.
Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday.
Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November.

Earlier this week, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang after the longtime Nvidia boss and co-founder issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return, as some tech leaders including Elon Musk campaigned on his behalf.

passages: California Attorney General Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia on Thursday as part of a probe of whether the company's advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China i n contravention of U.S. export restrictions, his office said.
The probe comes a week after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang , a suspected Chinese spy.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," the attorney general said.

"My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law," Bonta said.
Nvidia shares are down 22% in the nine trading days since Huang admitted to an extramarital affair.
The stock is on pace for its seventh straight weekly loss, shedding 38% of its value over that stretch.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bonta's subpoena.

The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public.
Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.

Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November.

California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta on Thursday subpoenaed the AI chip manufacturer Nvidia — asking whether its advanced chips or other confidential information went to China and whether it had misled investors and the public on the issue.
Nvidia, which is based in Santa Clara, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The subpoena follows Nvidia co-founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang's resignation after it was revealed he was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and after Bonta's office sued OpenAI — another AI company — over similar claims that it had misled the public about its advanced AI capabilities.
Bonta's office said information gleaned from the subpoenas "will help the California Department of Justice evaluate whether Nvidia's actions violated California law."

Bonta said both Nvidia's and Jensen's conduct raises "bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," and his office intends to determine whether it did so.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said.

The shake-up at Nvidia has rattled markets . It has also raised questions about the company's handling of its AI chips, whether it facilitated those chips being smuggled to China, and whether the U.S. Commerce Department was complicit or incompetent in failing to prevent such diversions despite its stated interest in preventing the powerful chips — crucial for supporting AI models — from getting into Chinese hands.

Democrats on the House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committees in particular are investigating whether the administration's response to Nvidia's chip business was improperly influenced by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick — whose family has holdings in the company.

"Did Trump's Commerce Secretary compromise our national security so that his family firm could profit from hundreds of millions of dollars invested in Nvidia?" Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee asked on social media Thursday.

The Democrats' questions hold extra weight since their party won control of both chambers of Congress in this month's midterm elections, which will give them greater investigative and subpoena powers come January.

In a Commerce statement shared by Lutnick on Monday, the department acknowledged an ongoing, years-long investigation into the Singaporean company Megaspeed and allegations it may have skirted export rules governing Nvidia's powerful AI chips. It credited that investigation to its own "excellent work" under Lutnick.

The department noted that the investigation involved an interview of former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman with whom Nvidia's Huang acknowledged having an affair and who U.S. intelligence officials suspect may be a Chinese spy.

The Commerce statement said it and the Justice Department "have an extremely strong track record of bringing semiconductor smugglers to justice" and "will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred."
Megaspeed has said that Alice Huang left the company in 2025 and that it is conducting its own internal investigation .

The explanations have reassured few, and criticism has not been limited to Democrats. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also blamed the Commerce Department for failing to blacklist Megaspeed over possible export violations.

Harvey C. Jones, Nvidia's chairman, has said the company's board unanimously accepted Jensen Huang's resignation and does not intend to reinstate him — despite calls for exactly that from President Trump and other administration allies.

"While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company's employees, customers, partners, and shareholders," Jones said. Colette Kress, Nvidia's executive vice president and chief financial officer, is now serving as interim CEO.

On Tuesday, the company announced third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year prior. The company's reporting has raised additional questions, as it stopped reporting Singapore revenue separately just as scrutiny of Megaspeed was arising.

In a post on X on Tuesday, Jensen Huang said he "did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA," had "made serious mistakes" in his personal life and "created problems for" the company's board.

But he also said he had received many messages from supporters encouraging him to return as CEO, which he would consider if the board wanted him to help the company as it "navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics."
This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

passages: Nvidia faces a California investigation into both possible transfers of advanced chips or confidential information to China and what it told investors about those risks.
Attorney General Rob Bonta issued the company an investigative subpoena on November 19, 2026, seeking information to assess whether its conduct violated state law.
The investigation is not a finding that any transfer occurred or that Nvidia misled investors; its outcome could clarify how California applies securities law to export-control risks.
Bonta is examining the company’s communications as well as the underlying conduct.
His statement frames the investor question around California corporate securities law, rather than treating possible chip diversion as the only issue.
Bonta described the conduct of Nvidia and Huang as raising “bright red flags,” including about possible misleading statements to investors.
The subpoena is part of an ongoing investigation.
His office said the information sought would help the California Department of Justice evaluate whether Nvidia’s actions violated California law , the Los Angeles Times reported.
His stated investigative questions also cover confidential information —not just the physical movement of chips—and whether actions by Nvidia or Jensen Huang resulted in China obtaining either.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC’s request for comment on the subpoena.

California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta on Thursday subpoenaed the AI chip manufacturer Nvidia — asking whether its advanced chips or other confidential information went to China and whether it had misled investors and the public on the issue.
Nvidia, which is based in Santa Clara, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The subpoena follows Nvidia co-founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang's resignation after it was revealed he was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and after Bonta's office sued OpenAI — another AI company — over similar claims that it had misled the public about its advanced AI capabilities.
Bonta's office said information gleaned from the subpoenas "will help the California Department of Justice evaluate whether Nvidia's actions violated California law."

Bonta said both Nvidia's and Jensen's conduct raises "bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," and his office intends to determine whether it did so.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said.

The shake-up at Nvidia has rattled markets . It has also raised questions about the company's handling of its AI chips, whether it facilitated those chips being smuggled to China, and whether the U.S. Commerce Department was complicit or incompetent in failing to prevent such diversions despite its stated interest in preventing the powerful chips — crucial for supporting AI models — from getting into Chinese hands.

Democrats on the House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committees in particular are investigating whether the administration's response to Nvidia's chip business was improperly influenced by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick — whose family has holdings in the company.

"Did Trump's Commerce Secretary compromise our national security so that his family firm could profit from hundreds of millions of dollars invested in Nvidia?" Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee asked on social media Thursday.

The Democrats' questions hold extra weight since their party won control of both chambers of Congress in this month's midterm elections, which will give them greater investigative and subpoena powers come January.

In a Commerce statement shared by Lutnick on Monday, the department acknowledged an ongoing, years-long investigation into the Singaporean company Megaspeed and allegations it may have skirted export rules governing Nvidia's powerful AI chips. It credited that investigation to its own "excellent work" under Lutnick.

The department noted that the investigation involved an interview of former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman with whom Nvidia's Huang acknowledged having an affair and who U.S. intelligence officials suspect may be a Chinese spy.

The Commerce statement said it and the Justice Department "have an extremely strong track record of bringing semiconductor smugglers to justice" and "will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred."
Megaspeed has said that Alice Huang left the company in 2025 and that it is conducting its own internal investigation .

The explanations have reassured few, and criticism has not been limited to Democrats. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also blamed the Commerce Department for failing to blacklist Megaspeed over possible export violations.

Harvey C. Jones, Nvidia's chairman, has said the company's board unanimously accepted Jensen Huang's resignation and does not intend to reinstate him — despite calls for exactly that from President Trump and other administration allies.

"While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company's employees, customers, partners, and shareholders," Jones said. Colette Kress, Nvidia's executive vice president and chief financial officer, is now serving as interim CEO.

On Tuesday, the company announced third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year prior. The company's reporting has raised additional questions, as it stopped reporting Singapore revenue separately just as scrutiny of Megaspeed was arising.

In a post on X on Tuesday, Jensen Huang said he "did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA," had "made serious mistakes" in his personal life and "created problems for" the company's board.

But he also said he had received many messages from supporters encouraging him to return as CEO, which he would consider if the board wanted him to help the company as it "navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics."
This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

passages: Apple appears to be developing its own in-house AI agent.
While we picked up on this development via Mark Gurman at Bloomberg , the news actually comes direct from the company this time.
Apple has an open job listing for a senior engineering manager of agentic AI that was posted earlier this week.

The description states: "As a senior leader in this org, you will own the technical direction and delivery of our agent platform and the AI capabilities built on it." It includes both general computer use and more technical coding tasks as falling within the future AI agent's purview, with the goal of being "capable, reliable and safe."
Apple, on the other hand, has been a bit more cautious when it comes to agents.
It recently warned developers that working with agentic AI "could put users at risk" by unwittingly allowing Full Disk Access.
Privacy is a frequent buzzword in Apple's recent software launches, so it will be interesting to see how the company walks the line whenever it unveils its own service.
But other businesses not directly working in artificial intelligence are also embracing the agentic path.

extraction.body: Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That’s according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant. An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhone maker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks. Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same. Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which you can use to ask questions about what’s on your screen, as well as perform actions across apps. It looks like Apple is planning to give Siri more agentic capabilities, as a report from Bloomberg suggests the company could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs. This lines up with the company’s new job listing, which says the engineer will work closely with teams across its Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions. “People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service,” the job listing says. “We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.” With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update, Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.

Apple is hiring for an AI assistant designed to do computer work on a user’s behalf , not just answer questions. Bloomberg identified job listings describing software that would browse websites, control apps and write code. The November 19 disclosure offers a detailed view of the company’s ambitions, but not a finished product.

One opening seeks a senior engineering manager to oversee an agent that can use a computer, according to TechCrunch’s account of Bloomberg’s reporting. The role’s title, “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” places the work around an assistant that takes actions. Apple’s description says the team is building the foundation for that system.

The proposed assistant would move among several ways of getting work done. Alongside websites and apps, the listing names commands, software code and outside services. It also gives the agent responsibility for choosing which tool to use at each step , rather than describing a single-purpose tool for browsing or programming.
A passage reproduced by 9to5Mac sets out the intended experience in unusually direct language:

Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step.

The scope extends beyond taking one action at a time. Apple describes agents that would plan and execute multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code and APIs—the interfaces software uses to call other software. Those agents could also coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way, giving parts of the work to other agents.

Privacy is part of the stated goal, too. The listing says the agent would do its work “privately” and with the polish users expect from Apple. That wording describes an intended quality of the system, not a demonstrated privacy safeguard or a technical explanation of how the proposed assistant would handle information.

Bloomberg reported that Apple has considered introducing the service as soon as the end of 2027 , according to TechCrunch. But the same account describes progress as remaining in the early stages. That makes the date a reported possibility, not an announced delivery commitment.

facts.text: Apple appears to be developing its own in-house AI agent.
While we picked up on this development via Mark Gurman at Bloomberg , the news actually comes direct from the company this time.
Apple has an open job listing for a senior engineering manager of agentic AI that was posted earlier this week.

The description states: "As a senior leader in this org, you will own the technical direction and delivery of our agent platform and the AI capabilities built on it." It includes both general computer use and more technical coding tasks as falling within the future AI agent's purview, with the goal of being "capable, reliable and safe."
Apple, on the other hand, has been a bit more cautious when it comes to agents.
It recently warned developers that working with agentic AI "could put users at risk" by unwittingly allowing Full Disk Access.
Privacy is a frequent buzzword in Apple's recent software launches, so it will be interesting to see how the company walks the line whenever it unveils its own service.
But other businesses not directly working in artificial intelligence are also embracing the agentic path.

“We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.” With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update, Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.
That’s according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant.
An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhone maker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks.

Bloomberg reported that Apple has considered launching it as soon as the end of 2027, but that timing is tentative, not a product commitment.
The immediate development is a search for an engineering leader; the listings describe intended capabilities and privacy goals, not a released system or verified safeguards.
The role’s title, “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” places the work around an assistant that takes actions.
Apple’s description says the team is building the foundation for that system.

California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta on Thursday subpoenaed the AI chip manufacturer Nvidia — asking whether its advanced chips or other confidential information went to China and whether it had misled investors and the public on the issue.
Nvidia, which is based in Santa Clara, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The subpoena follows Nvidia co-founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang's resignation after it was revealed he was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and after Bonta's office sued OpenAI — another AI company — over similar claims that it had misled the public about its advanced AI capabilities.
Bonta's office said information gleaned from the subpoenas "will help the California Department of Justice evaluate whether Nvidia's actions violated California law."

Bonta said both Nvidia's and Jensen's conduct raises "bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," and his office intends to determine whether it did so.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said.

The shake-up at Nvidia has rattled markets . It has also raised questions about the company's handling of its AI chips, whether it facilitated those chips being smuggled to China, and whether the U.S. Commerce Department was complicit or incompetent in failing to prevent such diversions despite its stated interest in preventing the powerful chips — crucial for supporting AI models — from getting into Chinese hands.

Democrats on the House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committees in particular are investigating whether the administration's response to Nvidia's chip business was improperly influenced by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick — whose family has holdings in the company.

"Did Trump's Commerce Secretary compromise our national security so that his family firm could profit from hundreds of millions of dollars invested in Nvidia?" Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee asked on social media Thursday.

The Democrats' questions hold extra weight since their party won control of both chambers of Congress in this month's midterm elections, which will give them greater investigative and subpoena powers come January.

In a Commerce statement shared by Lutnick on Monday, the department acknowledged an ongoing, years-long investigation into the Singaporean company Megaspeed and allegations it may have skirted export rules governing Nvidia's powerful AI chips. It credited that investigation to its own "excellent work" under Lutnick.

The department noted that the investigation involved an interview of former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman with whom Nvidia's Huang acknowledged having an affair and who U.S. intelligence officials suspect may be a Chinese spy.

The Commerce statement said it and the Justice Department "have an extremely strong track record of bringing semiconductor smugglers to justice" and "will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred."
Megaspeed has said that Alice Huang left the company in 2025 and that it is conducting its own internal investigation .

The explanations have reassured few, and criticism has not been limited to Democrats. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also blamed the Commerce Department for failing to blacklist Megaspeed over possible export violations.

Harvey C. Jones, Nvidia's chairman, has said the company's board unanimously accepted Jensen Huang's resignation and does not intend to reinstate him — despite calls for exactly that from President Trump and other administration allies.

"While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company's employees, customers, partners, and shareholders," Jones said. Colette Kress, Nvidia's executive vice president and chief financial officer, is now serving as interim CEO.

On Tuesday, the company announced third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year prior. The company's reporting has raised additional questions, as it stopped reporting Singapore revenue separately just as scrutiny of Megaspeed was arising.

In a post on X on Tuesday, Jensen Huang said he "did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA," had "made serious mistakes" in his personal life and "created problems for" the company's board.

But he also said he had received many messages from supporters encouraging him to return as CEO, which he would consider if the board wanted him to help the company as it "navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics."
This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta on Thursday subpoenaed the AI chip manufacturer Nvidia — asking whether its advanced chips or other confidential information went to China and whether it had misled investors and the public on the issue. Nvidia, which is based in Santa Clara, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The subpoena follows Nvidia co-founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang's resignation after it was revealed he was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and after Bonta's office sued OpenAI — another AI company — over similar claims that it had misled the public about its advanced AI capabilities. Bonta's office said information gleaned from the subpoenas "will help the California Department of Justice evaluate whether Nvidia's actions violated California law." Bonta said both Nvidia's and Jensen's conduct raises "bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," and his office intends to determine whether it did so. "Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said. The shake-up at Nvidia has rattled markets . It has also raised questions about the company's handling of its AI chips, whether it facilitated those chips being smuggled to China, and whether the U.S. Commerce Department was complicit or incompetent in failing to prevent such diversions despite its stated interest in preventing the powerful chips — crucial for supporting AI models — from getting into Chinese hands. Democrats on the House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committees in particular are investigating whether the administration's response to Nvidia's chip business was improperly influenced by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick — whose family has holdings in the company. "Did Trump's Commerce Secretary compromise our national security so that his family firm could profit from hundreds of millions of dollars invested in Nvidia?" Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee asked on social media Thursday. The Democrats' questions hold extra weight since their party won control of both chambers of Congress in this month's midterm elections, which will give them greater investigative and subpoena powers come January. In a Commerce statement shared by Lutnick on Monday, the department acknowledged an ongoing, years-long investigation into the Singaporean company Megaspeed and allegations it may have skirted export rules governing Nvidia's powerful AI chips. It credited that investigation to its own "excellent work" under Lutnick. The department noted that the investigation involved an interview of former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman with whom Nvidia's Huang acknowledged having an affair and who U.S. intelligence officials suspect may be a Chinese spy. The Commerce statement said it and the Justice Department "have an extremely strong track record of bringing semiconductor smugglers to justice" and "will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred." Megaspeed has said that Alice Huang left the company in 2025 and that it is conducting its own internal investigation . The explanations have reassured few, and criticism has not been limited to Democrats. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also blamed the Commerce Department for failing to blacklist Megaspeed over possible export violations. Harvey C. Jones, Nvidia's chairman, has said the company's board unanimously accepted Jensen Huang's resignation and does not intend to reinstate him — despite calls for exactly that from President Trump and other administration allies. "While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company's employees, customers, partners, and shareholders," Jones said. Colette Kress, Nvidia's executive vice president and chief financial officer, is now serving as interim CEO. On Tuesday, the company announced third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year prior. The company's reporting has raised additional questions, as it stopped reporting Singapore revenue separately just as scrutiny of Megaspeed was arising. California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta on Thursday subpoenaed the AI chip manufacturer Nvidia — asking whether its advanced chips or other confidential information went to China and whether it had misled investors and the public on the issue.
Nvidia, which is based in Santa Clara, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The subpoena follows Nvidia co-founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang's resignation after it was revealed he was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and after Bonta's office sued OpenAI — another AI company — over similar claims that it had misled the public about its advanced AI capabilities.
Bonta's office said information gleaned from the subpoenas "will help the California Department of Justice evaluate whether Nvidia's actions violated California law."

Bonta said both Nvidia's and Jensen's conduct raises "bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," and his office intends to determine whether it did so.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said.

The shake-up at Nvidia has rattled markets . It has also raised questions about the company's handling of its AI chips, whether it facilitated those chips being smuggled to China, and whether the U.S. Commerce Department was complicit or incompetent in failing to prevent such diversions despite its stated interest in preventing the powerful chips — crucial for supporting AI models — from getting into Chinese hands.

Democrats on the House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committees in particular are investigating whether the administration's response to Nvidia's chip business was improperly influenced by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick — whose family has holdings in the company.

"Did Trump's Commerce Secretary compromise our national security so that his family firm could profit from hundreds of millions of dollars invested in Nvidia?" Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee asked on social media Thursday.

The Democrats' questions hold extra weight since their party won control of both chambers of Congress in this month's midterm elections, which will give them greater investigative and subpoena powers come January.

In a Commerce statement shared by Lutnick on Monday, the department acknowledged an ongoing, years-long investigation into the Singaporean company Megaspeed and allegations it may have skirted export rules governing Nvidia's powerful AI chips. It credited that investigation to its own "excellent work" under Lutnick.

The department noted that the investigation involved an interview of former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman with whom Nvidia's Huang acknowledged having an affair and who U.S. intelligence officials suspect may be a Chinese spy.

The Commerce statement said it and the Justice Department "have an extremely strong track record of bringing semiconductor smugglers to justice" and "will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred."
Megaspeed has said that Alice Huang left the company in 2025 and that it is conducting its own internal investigation .

The explanations have reassured few, and criticism has not been limited to Democrats. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also blamed the Commerce Department for failing to blacklist Megaspeed over possible export violations.

Harvey C. Jones, Nvidia's chairman, has said the company's board unanimously accepted Jensen Huang's resignation and does not intend to reinstate him — despite calls for exactly that from President Trump and other administration allies.

"While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company's employees, customers, partners, and shareholders," Jones said. Colette Kress, Nvidia's executive vice president and chief financial officer, is now serving as interim CEO.

On Tuesday, the company announced third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year prior. The company's reporting has raised additional questions, as it stopped reporting Singapore revenue separately just as scrutiny of Megaspeed was arising.

In a post on X on Tuesday, Jensen Huang said he "did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA," had "made serious mistakes" in his personal life and "created problems for" the company's board.

But he also said he had received many messages from supporters encouraging him to return as CEO, which he would consider if the board wanted him to help the company as it "navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics."
This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

The approvals for 879,000 chip shipments by the Commerce Department included 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD, all on the Pentagon’s list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies, the committee noted.

The unusual release of chip export licensing data comes as the administration of President Donald Trump faces heightened scrutiny following news about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy , which has fuelled renewed calls in Washington for a tougher stance on China.
Companies had sought permission to ship 3.4 million of them to China total during the period, committee documents show.
It was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipment of the chips, which included Nvidia’s H200 and AMD’s equivalent MI325X.

News surrounding Huang has turned a spotlight on instances of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialling up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech ​threats.

The Commerce Department said its approach to H200 licensing “is based on a rule published in the Federal Register in January 2026, which imposes significant additional national security-related requirements on license applicants in order to qualify for case-by-case consideration rather than a presumption of denial.”

Chris McGuire, a former US official and expert on the US-China technology battle, said: “The fact that over 30% of the AI chips sent to China were shipped to companies that the Department of War has designated as Chinese military companies is astonishing, and calls into question whether Commerce conducted any serious national security review before approving these licenses.”
Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were “subject to strict conditions and limited volumes.”
It added that “despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China.”
AMD said it “complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations.”
Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu, BYD, the Commerce Department and the Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Former US President Joe Biden had restricted Chinese access to the prized chips over fears that they would supercharge China’s military and erode the US lead in artificial intelligence.

But Trump in December gave the green light for Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to China, rolling back Biden-era restrictions and drawing fierce criticism from China hawks across the US political spectrum.
Despite the approvals, questions swirled as to whether the AI chips were actually reaching Chinese shores.
