sources.title: Google will launch Android app verification requirement globally in January 2027
passages: Google announced Android developer verification last year , and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the company is forging ahead .
It began blocking the installation of unregistered apps in some countries this fall, and the system is expanding globally soon.
Google says it will start rolling out the requirement in all regions in January 2027, and it urges devs who still haven’t registered their apps to do so soon.
In September, Google launched verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand.
It says that verification will reach all devices within “several months.”
So far, Google is getting what it wanted from this initiative, with “millions” of non-Play apps already registered.
The company says this accounts for more than 99 percent of global Android app installs.

The verifier system service has already been rolled out to Google-certified devices running Android 8 Oreo or higher, which accounts for just about every Android device in the world outside of China and Russia.
Google has also partnered with the biggest third-party app stores to enforce verification: Galaxy Store, Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Transsion, and Vivo.
The system-level verifier is responsible for blocking installs, but these stores will only list verified apps once Google flips the switch.
As Google moves toward full verification enforcement, it has created guides for developers and app distributors to outline all the salient points.
These guides suggest Google expects verification to be fully online by March 1, 2027.
The apps you download from the Play Store all come from verified developers, and Google’s new requirement expands that requirement to apps from third-party sources.
Once developer verification is live in your region, you won’t be able to sideload apps unless the developer has registered with Google, which is framed as a security measure .
Verification requires providing government identification and paying a $25 fee, which will allegedly make it harder for nefarious actors to distribute malware and scammy apps.
Google also relented and created an opt-out system for users who don’t want their installations limited.
The so-called “ advanced flow ” will let you install whatever you want regardless of verification status, but it’s not a simple toggle.
The option will be buried, and there will be plenty of scary warnings about the risks.
You’ll also have to wait 24 hours to fully activate the feature.
This setting is already live, so you can tell your phone to ignore verification right now.
Google has gotten a lot of feedback since announcing this change, and it has listened to some of it.
Google initially planned to limit this to 25 total installs, but that has since been increased to 50 installs.
There’s also now an API that developers can use to streamline registering new application packages.
Sideloading an app may also require a Google server connection.
Only popular app IDs will be cached on devices for verification purposes.
For others, your phone will have to check with Google before installing.
These will be edge cases, certainly, but still very annoying ones.
Google says almost all developers have already gotten on board with verification.

sources.title: Google to Enforce Android App Verification Worldwide Starting January 2027 - BigGo Finance
passages: Google will begin enforcing its Android developer verification requirement across all regions in January 2027, extending to third-party app sources a rule that until now applied mainly to software distributed through the Play Store.
The company said the system will reach all eligible devices within a few months of the rollout, with its own developer documentation pointing to full coverage by March 1, 2027.
Separately, Google is tightening rules for large-screen devices.

Beginning in April 2027, apps must meet the company's "Tier 3 - Adaptive ready" standard, meaning they fill the display without letterboxing or compatibility modes and preserve state such as scroll position, text input and media playback through rotation, folding and resizing.
Listings will also need three foldable screenshots, which developers can submit now.
Once added, BigGo Finance appears first in Google Search Top Stories, so you get the broadest, most up-to-the-minute, and most comprehensive global financial news first.
A system-level verifier has been pushed to Google-certified devices running Android 8 Oreo or later, which covers nearly every Android handset in circulation outside China and Russia.
Once verification goes live in a market, that service blocks installation of any app whose developer has not registered with Google.
Google tested the program first in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand beginning in September, and is now preparing the wider launch.
It says millions of non-Play apps have already been registered, representing more than 99 percent of global Android installs.
Google has adjusted the program in response to criticism.
Hobbyists can register a free account to distribute apps to a limited audience, with the cap raised from an initial 25 installs to 50.
A new API is available to speed the registration of application packages.
The company also built an opt-out path for users who want no installation limits, though it is deliberately hard to find, comes wrapped in warnings about risk, and takes 24 hours to activate.
Even with those concessions, the requirement shifts significant control toward Google.
Developers in sanctioned countries cannot complete identity verification and would be cut off from distribution.
Some sideloads may also depend on a live connection to Google's servers, since only widely used app IDs are cached on handsets for offline checks.
The verification mandate hands Google a gatekeeping role over software installed outside its store, a position that draws antitrust scrutiny in several jurisdictions.
For independent developers, the $25 fee and ID requirement add friction, while the free hobbyist tier and the package-registration API soften the burden for small projects.
Users who rely on sideloaded software face the sharpest change: without registration, apps simply will not install unless they navigate the buried advanced flow.
The parallel foldable rules raise the bar for app quality on premium hardware, but they also add compliance work for smaller studios already stretched across form factors.
Third-party storefronts are being folded into the system as well.
Google has agreements with Samsung's Galaxy Store, along with Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Transsion and Vivo, under which those platforms will list only verified apps once enforcement takes effect.
Note: Foldable deadlines are a separate Google Play policy track from developer verification.

passages: Google will begin enforcing Android developer verification worldwide in January 2027, Matthew Forsythe, director of product management for Android app safety, wrote on the Android Developers Blog on Nov.
Certified Android devices will only install apps from developers who have verified their identity and registered their apps, a requirement that until now applied in four countries [1] [2] .
Google announced developer verification in August 2025 and switched it on for participating stores in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand on Sept.

Registering an app takes less than ten minutes, according to the company [1] .
Google listed changes made after developer feedback.

Limited distribution accounts, launched in August for students and hobbyists who want to share apps without paying the registration fee or verifying a government ID, can now share with 50 authorized devices instead of 20 [1] .

The global rollout starts with seven app distributors: Google Play, Samsung's Galaxy Store, Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Transsion and Vivo.
That includes apps sideloaded from websites or third-party stores, which is why critics call the rules a limit on Android's openness [3] .

coreStoryFacts.text: Google announced Android developer verification last year , and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the company is forging ahead .
It began blocking the installation of unregistered apps in some countries this fall, and the system is expanding globally soon.
Google says it will start rolling out the requirement in all regions in January 2027, and it urges devs who still haven’t registered their apps to do so soon.
In September, Google launched verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand.
It says that verification will reach all devices within “several months.”
So far, Google is getting what it wanted from this initiative, with “millions” of non-Play apps already registered.
The company says this accounts for more than 99 percent of global Android app installs.

The verifier system service has already been rolled out to Google-certified devices running Android 8 Oreo or higher, which accounts for just about every Android device in the world outside of China and Russia.
Google has also partnered with the biggest third-party app stores to enforce verification: Galaxy Store, Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Transsion, and Vivo.
The system-level verifier is responsible for blocking installs, but these stores will only list verified apps once Google flips the switch.
As Google moves toward full verification enforcement, it has created guides for developers and app distributors to outline all the salient points.
These guides suggest Google expects verification to be fully online by March 1, 2027.
The apps you download from the Play Store all come from verified developers, and Google’s new requirement expands that requirement to apps from third-party sources.
Once developer verification is live in your region, you won’t be able to sideload apps unless the developer has registered with Google, which is framed as a security measure .
Verification requires providing government identification and paying a $25 fee, which will allegedly make it harder for nefarious actors to distribute malware and scammy apps.
Google also relented and created an opt-out system for users who don’t want their installations limited.
The so-called “ advanced flow ” will let you install whatever you want regardless of verification status, but it’s not a simple toggle.
The option will be buried, and there will be plenty of scary warnings about the risks.
You’ll also have to wait 24 hours to fully activate the feature.
This setting is already live, so you can tell your phone to ignore verification right now.
Google has gotten a lot of feedback since announcing this change, and it has listened to some of it.

There’s also now an API that developers can use to streamline registering new application packages.
Sideloading an app may also require a Google server connection.

The apps you download from the Play Store all come from verified developers, and Google’s new requirement expands that requirement to apps from third-party sources. Once developer verification is live in your region, you won’t be able to sideload apps unless the developer has registered with Google, which is framed as a security measure . Verification requires providing government identification and paying a $25 fee, which will allegedly make it harder for nefarious actors to distribute malware and scammy apps.

In September, Google launched verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. Apparently, nothing exploded, so the company is now ready to expand. sources.title: Google to Enforce Android App Verification Worldwide Starting January 2027 - BigGo Finance
passages: Google will begin enforcing its Android developer verification requirement across all regions in January 2027, extending to third-party app sources a rule that until now applied mainly to software distributed through the Play Store.
The company said the system will reach all eligible devices within a few months of the rollout, with its own developer documentation pointing to full coverage by March 1, 2027.
Separately, Google is tightening rules for large-screen devices.

Beginning in April 2027, apps must meet the company's "Tier 3 - Adaptive ready" standard, meaning they fill the display without letterboxing or compatibility modes and preserve state such as scroll position, text input and media playback through rotation, folding and resizing.
Listings will also need three foldable screenshots, which developers can submit now.
Once added, BigGo Finance appears first in Google Search Top Stories, so you get the broadest, most up-to-the-minute, and most comprehensive global financial news first.
A system-level verifier has been pushed to Google-certified devices running Android 8 Oreo or later, which covers nearly every Android handset in circulation outside China and Russia.
Once verification goes live in a market, that service blocks installation of any app whose developer has not registered with Google.
Google tested the program first in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand beginning in September, and is now preparing the wider launch.
It says millions of non-Play apps have already been registered, representing more than 99 percent of global Android installs.
Google has adjusted the program in response to criticism.
Hobbyists can register a free account to distribute apps to a limited audience, with the cap raised from an initial 25 installs to 50.
A new API is available to speed the registration of application packages.
The company also built an opt-out path for users who want no installation limits, though it is deliberately hard to find, comes wrapped in warnings about risk, and takes 24 hours to activate.
Even with those concessions, the requirement shifts significant control toward Google.
Developers in sanctioned countries cannot complete identity verification and would be cut off from distribution.
Some sideloads may also depend on a live connection to Google's servers, since only widely used app IDs are cached on handsets for offline checks.
The verification mandate hands Google a gatekeeping role over software installed outside its store, a position that draws antitrust scrutiny in several jurisdictions.
For independent developers, the $25 fee and ID requirement add friction, while the free hobbyist tier and the package-registration API soften the burden for small projects.
Users who rely on sideloaded software face the sharpest change: without registration, apps simply will not install unless they navigate the buried advanced flow.
The parallel foldable rules raise the bar for app quality on premium hardware, but they also add compliance work for smaller studios already stretched across form factors.
Third-party storefronts are being folded into the system as well.
Google has agreements with Samsung's Galaxy Store, along with Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Transsion and Vivo, under which those platforms will list only verified apps once enforcement takes effect.
Note: Foldable deadlines are a separate Google Play policy track from developer verification.

facts.text: Google announced Android developer verification last year , and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the company is forging ahead .
It began blocking the installation of unregistered apps in some countries this fall, and the system is expanding globally soon.
Google says it will start rolling out the requirement in all regions in January 2027, and it urges devs who still haven’t registered their apps to do so soon.
In September, Google launched verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand.
It says that verification will reach all devices within “several months.”
So far, Google is getting what it wanted from this initiative, with “millions” of non-Play apps already registered.
The company says this accounts for more than 99 percent of global Android app installs.

The verifier system service has already been rolled out to Google-certified devices running Android 8 Oreo or higher, which accounts for just about every Android device in the world outside of China and Russia.
Google has also partnered with the biggest third-party app stores to enforce verification: Galaxy Store, Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Transsion, and Vivo.
The system-level verifier is responsible for blocking installs, but these stores will only list verified apps once Google flips the switch.
As Google moves toward full verification enforcement, it has created guides for developers and app distributors to outline all the salient points.
These guides suggest Google expects verification to be fully online by March 1, 2027.
The apps you download from the Play Store all come from verified developers, and Google’s new requirement expands that requirement to apps from third-party sources.
Once developer verification is live in your region, you won’t be able to sideload apps unless the developer has registered with Google, which is framed as a security measure .
Verification requires providing government identification and paying a $25 fee, which will allegedly make it harder for nefarious actors to distribute malware and scammy apps.
Google also relented and created an opt-out system for users who don’t want their installations limited.
The so-called “ advanced flow ” will let you install whatever you want regardless of verification status, but it’s not a simple toggle.
The option will be buried, and there will be plenty of scary warnings about the risks.
You’ll also have to wait 24 hours to fully activate the feature.
This setting is already live, so you can tell your phone to ignore verification right now.
Google has gotten a lot of feedback since announcing this change, and it has listened to some of it.
Google initially planned to limit this to 25 total installs, but that has since been increased to 50 installs.
There’s also now an API that developers can use to streamline registering new application packages.
Sideloading an app may also require a Google server connection.
Only popular app IDs will be cached on devices for verification purposes.
For others, your phone will have to check with Google before installing.
These will be edge cases, certainly, but still very annoying ones.
Google says almost all developers have already gotten on board with verification.

Google will begin enforcing its Android developer verification requirement across all regions in January 2027, extending to third-party app sources a rule that until now applied mainly to software distributed through the Play Store.
The company said the system will reach all eligible devices within a few months of the rollout, with its own developer documentation pointing to full coverage by March 1, 2027.
Separately, Google is tightening rules for large-screen devices.

Beginning in April 2027, apps must meet the company's "Tier 3 - Adaptive ready" standard, meaning they fill the display without letterboxing or compatibility modes and preserve state such as scroll position, text input and media playback through rotation, folding and resizing.
Listings will also need three foldable screenshots, which developers can submit now.

A system-level verifier has been pushed to Google-certified devices running Android 8 Oreo or later, which covers nearly every Android handset in circulation outside China and Russia.
Once verification goes live in a market, that service blocks installation of any app whose developer has not registered with Google.
Google tested the program first in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand beginning in September, and is now preparing the wider launch.
It says millions of non-Play apps have already been registered, representing more than 99 percent of global Android installs.
Google has adjusted the program in response to criticism.
Hobbyists can register a free account to distribute apps to a limited audience, with the cap raised from an initial 25 installs to 50.
A new API is available to speed the registration of application packages.
The company also built an opt-out path for users who want no installation limits, though it is deliberately hard to find, comes wrapped in warnings about risk, and takes 24 hours to activate.
Even with those concessions, the requirement shifts significant control toward Google.
Developers in sanctioned countries cannot complete identity verification and would be cut off from distribution.
Some sideloads may also depend on a live connection to Google's servers, since only widely used app IDs are cached on handsets for offline checks.
The verification mandate hands Google a gatekeeping role over software installed outside its store, a position that draws antitrust scrutiny in several jurisdictions.
For independent developers, the $25 fee and ID requirement add friction, while the free hobbyist tier and the package-registration API soften the burden for small projects.
Users who rely on sideloaded software face the sharpest change: without registration, apps simply will not install unless they navigate the buried advanced flow.
The parallel foldable rules raise the bar for app quality on premium hardware, but they also add compliance work for smaller studios already stretched across form factors.
Third-party storefronts are being folded into the system as well.
Google has agreements with Samsung's Galaxy Store, along with Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Transsion and Vivo, under which those platforms will list only verified apps once enforcement takes effect.
Note: Foldable deadlines are a separate Google Play policy track from developer verification.

Registering an app takes less than ten minutes, according to the company [1] .
Google listed changes made after developer feedback.

Limited distribution accounts, launched in August for students and hobbyists who want to share apps without paying the registration fee or verifying a government ID, can now share with 50 authorized devices instead of 20 [1] .
An advanced flow lets experienced users install unregistered apps if they accept the risk, while Google keeps what it calls guardrails against social engineering scams for other users [1] .
The global rollout starts with seven app distributors: Google Play, Samsung's Galaxy Store, Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Transsion and Vivo.
That includes apps sideloaded from websites or third-party stores, which is why critics call the rules a limit on Android's openness [3] .
Google also published a guide for developers who distribute through open-source registries such as F-Droid, and a separate guide for app distributors [1] .

sources.title: Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you
passages: The tech giant is a little late to the game with this launch, as other leading AI model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have already been offering agentic features in their desktop applications for some time.

Meanwhile, Google only this week announced the broader rollout of Gemini’s “Tasks,” the in-app feature that allows the AI to work more as an agent, helping users sign into websites, make online purchases, or book appointments.

Google on Thursday announced that it is bringing computer use to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing its AI to complete tasks on users’ behalf, navigating native Mac apps, and browsing websites in the background.
The feature is initially available in English in the U.S. and requires the Gemini app for Mac and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription.
The company didn’t say when it would expand to other markets or platforms.

Google also only recently began admitting early testers to try its revamped “CC” AI agent, announced in September , which is designed to help families stay organized across email, calendars, chats, and tasks.

After the user instructs the AI what they want to do, they’ll see the agent working in a live preview in their chat, while still keeping their screen and cursor free to continue working on other things.

Google suggests the feature could be useful for tedious tasks and other workflows, like filling out forms, repeating the same task over and over across a batch of files, organizing files into folders based on specific criteria, creating slideshows from files or information in online dashboards, and more.

Google is upgrading the Gemini app on Mac with a computer use feature that lets the assistant click, type, navigate menus, and fill out forms across local desktop apps and the web. Gemini runs in an “isolated background window with a live preview right in your chat,” while the main screen and cursor remain free for other work. Google says users can stop Gemini at any time with one click, and Google also says users choose what apps Gemini uses. Google is rolling out computer use in US English starting today for Google AI Plus, Pro, and Ultra subscribers, and the feature is described as handling multi-step tasks that span desktop apps and websites that do not connect to each other. Google says Gemini can perform actions instead of simply helping users prepare them, and the assistant will navigate menus, click buttons, enter information, and move between apps to finish a task. Google also says Gemini works in a separate virtual screen, leaving the main display and cursor available for other work, and Google says users can stop the task at any time. AppleInsider highlights that Google requires users to enable macOS Accessibility and Screen & System Audio Recording permissions before Gemini can operate Mac apps, and AppleInsider also notes that Gemini requests permission before controlling individual apps. Apple is tightening Mac permissions in macOS 27.3 developer beta 2 on November 16, and Apple’s changes include options to require approval each time and display an indicator when one app controls another. Apple will add clearer macOS warnings and app permission controls around this. Google’s examples for computer use include speeding up creative workflows by batching color-grade photos in design software or setting up complex 3D scenes, and Google also points to skipping manual form entry by extracting weights, dimensions, and addresses from local PDFs. Google also describes turning live data into ready-to-present decks by pulling metrics and screenshots from live dashboards across multiple regions and building a presentation in Google Slides. Google warns that Gemini can access active sessions in native Mac apps and read or interact with multifactor authentication codes visible in desktop or messaging apps, and Google warns that untrusted content in one app could redirect Gemini into taking actions in another app it has permission to use. Google also warns that Gemini can attempt to create temporary backups when its on-demand backup setting is enabled, but Google warns that some apps do not support backups and certain changes cannot be undone, with backups expiring after 24 hours or when the user submits another prompt, whichever comes first. AppleInsider foregrounds security risks while Crypto Briefing foregrounds user control as the selling point. facts.text: The tech giant is a little late to the game with this launch, as other leading AI model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have already been offering agentic features in their desktop applications for some time.

Meanwhile, Google only this week announced the broader rollout of Gemini’s “Tasks,” the in-app feature that allows the AI to work more as an agent, helping users sign into websites, make online purchases, or book appointments.

Google on Thursday announced that it is bringing computer use to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing its AI to complete tasks on users’ behalf, navigating native Mac apps, and browsing websites in the background.
The feature is initially available in English in the U.S. and requires the Gemini app for Mac and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription.
The company didn’t say when it would expand to other markets or platforms.

Google also only recently began admitting early testers to try its revamped “CC” AI agent, announced in September , which is designed to help families stay organized across email, calendars, chats, and tasks.

After the user instructs the AI what they want to do, they’ll see the agent working in a live preview in their chat, while still keeping their screen and cursor free to continue working on other things.

Google suggests the feature could be useful for tedious tasks and other workflows, like filling out forms, repeating the same task over and over across a batch of files, organizing files into folders based on specific criteria, creating slideshows from files or information in online dashboards, and more.

Shares of AMD fell Thursday after the investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging the company "has its own China problem." The Commerce Department signed off on selling more than 879,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, a number that's now driving urgent calls on Capitol Hill for a complete overhaul of America's semiconductor export regime.
It's a no-win situation for chipmakers: sell to China and face Congressional fury, or leave billions in revenue on the table to appease Washington.
Brian Mast dropped the bombshell figure during hearings this week, revealing an approval volume that far exceeds what most lawmakers believed was flowing to China under current restrictions.
Kress delivered better-than-expected earnings in her first quarterly report as interim CEO, but the China export controversy has overshadowed those results.
Nvidia just completed its fastest product ramp ever with the H200, shipping thousands of units weekly before the China halt kicked in.
For chipmakers, the calculus is shifting from maximizing China revenue to minimizing Washington blowback - a change that will reshape the global AI hardware market for years to come.
The sheer volume of approved chip exports - nearly a million advanced processors - has blindsided members of Congress who believed existing controls were far more restrictive.

Wall Street is now pricing in the reality that Nvidia's China business - once a growth engine - has become a political liability that could trigger regulatory crackdowns extending far beyond voluntary sales halts.
The company's MI300 series chips were included in the approved exports, and CEO Lisa Su now faces the same pressure Kress does to voluntarily restrict sales beyond what regulations require.
Now Congress has hard numbers showing just how many chips were cleared for export before that voluntary halt, and members from both parties are furious.
Some of those chips are now sitting in Chinese data centers, a fact that's driving the urgency behind Mast's legislative effort.

The Florida Republican is now leading a bipartisan effort to pass legislation that would shift the burden of proof in export licensing, requiring chipmakers to demonstrate that sales won't enhance Chinese military or surveillance capabilities rather than forcing the government to prove they will.

Brian Mast revealed today, igniting a Congressional push for legislation to dramatically tighten export controls. The disclosure comes as lawmakers scramble to contain fallout from the Jensen Huang scandal that's already reshaped Nvidia's leadership and sent shockwaves through the semiconductor industry. The sheer volume of approved chip exports - nearly a million advanced processors - has blindsided members of Congress who believed existing controls were far more restrictive. The Commerce Department signed off on selling more than 879,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, a number that's now driving urgent calls on Capitol Hill for a complete overhaul of America's semiconductor export regime. Brian Mast dropped the bombshell figure during hearings this week, revealing an approval volume that far exceeds what most lawmakers believed was flowing to China under current restrictions. Nvidia is still reeling from the departure of founder Jensen Huang amid a widening scandal, and interim CEO Colette Kress just announced the company would halt H200 chip sales to China entirely - a dramatic reversal that came despite White House approval. Now Congress has hard numbers showing just how many chips were cleared for export before that voluntary halt, and members from both parties are furious. The 879,000 figure represents approved sales from multiple chipmakers, with both Nvidia and AMD products included in the Commerce Department's green-lit shipments. Each chip represents compute capability that Beijing can deploy for applications Washington would rather it didn't have. Mast, who chairs a key subcommittee overseeing technology exports, didn't mince words about what the number means. The Florida Republican is now leading a bipartisan effort to pass legislation that would shift the burden of proof in export licensing, requiring chipmakers to demonstrate that sales won't enhance Chinese military or surveillance capabilities rather than forcing the government to prove they will. It's a fundamental restructuring of how America polices its most strategic technology exports. The legislative push arrives as Nvidia's stock has whipsawed investors through one of the most turbulent periods in the company's history. Kress delivered better-than-expected earnings in her first quarterly report as interim CEO, but the China export controversy has overshadowed those results. Wall Street is now pricing in the reality that Nvidia's China business - once a growth engine - has become a political liability that could trigger regulatory crackdowns extending far beyond voluntary sales halts. passages: The US Commerce Department approved the export of more than 879,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD to Chinese companies between December 2025 and May 2026, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said.Chinese companies had sought licences to ship about 3.4 million such chips during the period, with approvals covering 75,000 chips for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD, Reuters reported, citing the committee's disclosure.All four companies are on a Pentagon list of Chinese firms alleged to have ties to China's military.The licences covered Nvidia's H200 chips and AMD's comparable MI325X accelerators.

It was not immediately clear how many of the approved chips were ultimately shipped to China.The disclosure comes as the Trump administration faces mounting scrutiny over its China chip policy and efforts to prevent advanced US technology from reaching Chinese companies.

It was not immediately clear how many of the approved chips were ultimately shipped to China.The disclosure comes as the Trump administration faces mounting scrutiny over its China chip policy and efforts to prevent advanced US technology from reaching Chinese companies. Nvidia said the licences were subject to strict conditions and limited volumes and that, despite receiving some approvals, it has since stopped shipping H200 chips to China.The approvals followed a policy shift by the Trump administration. In December 2025, Trump allowed Nvidia's H200 and similar chips to be exported to approved Chinese customers, reversing the tougher approach adopted under former President Joe Biden. The Commerce Department subsequently moved to a case-by-case review of H200 and AMD MI325X export applications, subject to security requirements including customer screening and safeguards against diversion.The latest disclosure also comes amid a broader US crackdown on Chinese access to American AI computing.Earlier this week, the administration introduced rules aimed at preventing Chinese companies from accessing advanced US chips remotely through data centres in third countries, while imposing additional licensing requirements on chip exports to countries including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil because of concerns over diversion to China.The measures followed scrutiny of Singapore-based Megaspeed, which US authorities are investigating over suspected diversion of Nvidia chips to China. The case has also triggered a public dispute within the Trump administration over whether the Commerce Department moved quickly enough to restrict the company.

extraction.body: The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee. Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies," according to the documents. From December through May, companies had made 3.4 million requests for sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices . "Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents. Spokespersons for Nvidia and AMD said their companies comply with U.S. export control laws. Nvidia argued it was following the Commerce Department regulations that were in effect at the time. A spokesperson from the Bureau of Industry and Security said it shared information with Congress on both approvals and denials of licenses for Nvidia's H200 and comparable chips. "Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. Government agencies," the spokesperson said. "The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China," Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told CNBC. On Tuesday, Nvidia reported $2.4 billion in quarterly revenue from H200 and related chip sales in China. In total, customers based in China and Hong Kong made up about 9.5% of all revenue. "AMD complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations," AMD said through a spokesperson. The approval of 879,000 AI chips is "not that many," Bernstein Senior Analyst Stacy Rasgon told CNBC, adding that this news is not surprising. "It doesn't sound to me like they're approving everything they got willy nilly," Rasgon said of the Commerce Department. With 879,000 approvals out of 3.4 million requested AI chip sales, he added, "There was a process in place, and it sounds like they approved about one out of every four." Despite a rapid succession of China export controls on AI chips that started under the Biden administration in 2022, Nvidia and AMD both re-engineered some chips to comply and be sold legally in China. And in December, Trump said Nvidia could ship H200s, its older generation Hopper chips, to "approved customers in China" if the U.S. got a 25% cut of sales. The U.S. then licensed Nvidia H200 sales to Alibaba , Tencent, ByteDance and other Chinese companies, although sales were limited because Beijing didn't approve large-scale imports, chip analyst Patrick Moorhead of Moor Insights & Strategy told CNBC last week. H200 sales numbers remained low due to those restrictions on China's end. Nvidia said H200 shipments to China made up less than 1% of data center revenue for the quarter that ended in July. "In the grand context of the size of this market and how much they're shipping, it's a rounding error. It's tiny," Rasgon told CNBC. The committee cited the Export Control Reform Act as justification for releasing the data. The panel said the law allows it to declassify and release export data if it "determines that the withholding of the following information is contrary to the national interest." The license requests released by the Foreign Affairs Committee include requests to sell to major firms including ByteDance, Tesla (Shanghai) and Baidu . The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang 's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China. In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries. "The license information we are disclosing today will help inform the American public about how BIS has handled licenses for Nvidia H200 and equivalent AMD chips to China. The public has the right to know how these decisions were made," Meeks said. Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS — Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions. "Both are fake companies. If BIS approved the sale of these chips to these firms, obviously that is of tremendous concern to us — especially given that President Trump made clear last year that the sale of any AI chips to China will have very real national security conditions," Mast said at the Thursday meeting. Maginfra and New Matrix did not reply to requests for comment. Shares of AMD fell Thursday after the investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging the company "has its own China problem." The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers." CNBC did not independently verify this information. Fallout from the Huang scandal on Capitol Hill has intensified in the last week, as lawmakers question the degree to which the former head of Nvidia's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy could have jeopardized national security and American AI dominance. Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels Dec. 2. Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., announced on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had also agreed to testify. Lutnick has come under fire over his relationship to Huang and for his failure to take action on Megaspeed , the Singaporean company where Alice Huang , with whom the former Nvidia CEO had an affair, was an executive until 2025. U.S. investigators suspect Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips to China. Amid that criticism, the Commerce Department on Monday issued an interim final rule to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia's advancing computing power from data centers in third countries. The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release.

Brian Mast revealed today, igniting a Congressional push for legislation to dramatically tighten export controls. The disclosure comes as lawmakers scramble to contain fallout from the Jensen Huang scandal that's already reshaped Nvidia's leadership and sent shockwaves through the semiconductor industry. The sheer volume of approved chip exports - nearly a million advanced processors - has blindsided members of Congress who believed existing controls were far more restrictive. The Commerce Department signed off on selling more than 879,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, a number that's now driving urgent calls on Capitol Hill for a complete overhaul of America's semiconductor export regime. Brian Mast dropped the bombshell figure during hearings this week, revealing an approval volume that far exceeds what most lawmakers believed was flowing to China under current restrictions. Nvidia is still reeling from the departure of founder Jensen Huang amid a widening scandal, and interim CEO Colette Kress just announced the company would halt H200 chip sales to China entirely - a dramatic reversal that came despite White House approval. Now Congress has hard numbers showing just how many chips were cleared for export before that voluntary halt, and members from both parties are furious. The 879,000 figure represents approved sales from multiple chipmakers, with both Nvidia and AMD products included in the Commerce Department's green-lit shipments. Each chip represents compute capability that Beijing can deploy for applications Washington would rather it didn't have. Mast, who chairs a key subcommittee overseeing technology exports, didn't mince words about what the number means. The Florida Republican is now leading a bipartisan effort to pass legislation that would shift the burden of proof in export licensing, requiring chipmakers to demonstrate that sales won't enhance Chinese military or surveillance capabilities rather than forcing the government to prove they will. It's a fundamental restructuring of how America polices its most strategic technology exports. The legislative push arrives as Nvidia's stock has whipsawed investors through one of the most turbulent periods in the company's history. Kress delivered better-than-expected earnings in her first quarterly report as interim CEO, but the China export controversy has overshadowed those results. Wall Street is now pricing in the reality that Nvidia's China business - once a growth engine - has become a political liability that could trigger regulatory crackdowns extending far beyond voluntary sales halts. Many of these 879,000 chips were approved and shipped while the Huang scandal was already unfolding behind closed doors. Commerce Department officials were apparently clearing massive export licenses even as intelligence agencies were raising red flags about how previous chip shipments were being used. What's changed is the political willingness to let those exports continue. The Huang scandal transformed the debate from a technical discussion about compute thresholds and end-use verification into a raw political fight about whether America is funding its own strategic competitor. The bill would create a presumption of denial for AI chip exports to China, require annual audits of all approved licenses, and impose criminal penalties on executives who knowingly facilitate diversions to military end users. Lawmakers who once trusted the export licensing process now see it as dangerously permissive, and they're moving fast to slam the door shut. For chipmakers, the calculus is shifting from maximizing China revenue to minimizing Washington blowback - a change that will reshape the global AI hardware market for years to come. What happens next depends on how quickly Congress can pass new restrictions and whether the industry will accept them or fight back.

sources.title: US cleared nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips for Chinese firms, including Alibaba, Tencent, in six months
passages: The US Commerce Department approved the export of more than 879,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD to Chinese companies between December 2025 and May 2026, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said.Chinese companies had sought licences to ship about 3.4 million such chips during the period, with approvals covering 75,000 chips for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD, Reuters reported, citing the committee's disclosure.All four companies are on a Pentagon list of Chinese firms alleged to have ties to China's military.The licences covered Nvidia's H200 chips and AMD's comparable MI325X accelerators.

It was not immediately clear how many of the approved chips were ultimately shipped to China.The disclosure comes as the Trump administration faces mounting scrutiny over its China chip policy and efforts to prevent advanced US technology from reaching Chinese companies.

Nvidia said the licences were subject to strict conditions and limited volumes and that, despite receiving some approvals, it has since stopped shipping H200 chips to China.The approvals followed a policy shift by the Trump administration. In December 2025, Trump allowed Nvidia's H200 and similar chips to be exported to approved Chinese customers, reversing the tougher approach adopted under former President Joe Biden. The Commerce Department subsequently moved to a case-by-case review of H200 and AMD MI325X export applications, subject to security requirements including customer screening and safeguards against diversion.The latest disclosure also comes amid a broader US crackdown on Chinese access to American AI computing.Earlier this week, the administration introduced rules aimed at preventing Chinese companies from accessing advanced US chips remotely through data centres in third countries, while imposing additional licensing requirements on chip exports to countries including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil because of concerns over diversion to China.The measures followed scrutiny of Singapore-based Megaspeed, which US authorities are investigating over suspected diversion of Nvidia chips to China. The case has also triggered a public dispute within the Trump administration over whether the Commerce Department moved quickly enough to restrict the company.

Russia is reportedly comfortable with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine postwar. Kushner says Russia agreed to a multilateral format involving Europe for Ukraine talks.

U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said Russia is “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine, after Trump held rare three-way talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Kushner’s remarks came as European leaders spoke at Berlin’s summit of Ukraine’s allies known as the Coalition of the Willing, where UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, “Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position.” Putin addressed multilateral peace talks in Shenzhen, telling reporters the Americans were “insistently” asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part, while also saying Russia wanted to clarify “what Europe will bring to these talks.”

Kushner told reporters that the U.S. president came away from Shenzhen believing that “peace is achievable,” and he said Moscow was now “comfortable” with Ukraine having security guarantees based on Nato’s Article Five. The BBC reported that Zelensky made clear Putin had spurned every proposal so far, saying, “Putin has always said no.”
Thousands of POWs will return home in coming weeks

Kushner insisted in Berlin that Russia had committed to maintaining a “multilateral” format of negotiations on Ukraine with the participation of European representatives. Kushner said, “Most importantly, Russia has agreed to its involvement in a multilateral format with the Europeans, because we have explained to the Russians that Europe is an essential actor,” framing Europe as part of the negotiating process. Putin questioned the need to include a European negotiating team and suggested instead that they visit Moscow to explain in person why they should participate, because Europe, in his view, has no interest in achieving peace.

The BBC said Putin told the summit question of multilateral peace talks that Russia was not against the idea but wanted to clarify “what Europe will bring to these talks,” and he added that “every day” Russia heard European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. The BBC also reported that Merz said, “A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace,” as he argued that Europe could enter “serious discussions on European security” only alongside a first peace agreement with Ukraine.

The Berlin summit brought together more than 40 European leaders to coordinate support for Ukraine and work toward postwar security guarantees, with Zelensky expecting the next meeting to take a four-way format. Zelensky said Ukraine would hold separate talks with senior U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on the timing and format of the next round of peace negotiations, and he said he expected Europe to be included alongside the U.S. and Russia. Kushner claimed that security guarantees for Ukraine had not been on the table before he and Witkoff became involved, and he said Trump approved drafting them when the two envoys raised the issue.

The PBS report tied the diplomacy to battlefield developments, saying a third Ukrainian aerial attack in four days on the key Kerch Bridge halted rail traffic across the span and that officials assessed damage after earlier strikes shut down the road section. PBS reported that Russia’s air defenses intercepted 53 Ukrainian drones over 10 Russian regions during the night, while Ukrainian authorities said Russia launched anti-ship missiles and 98 drones at Ukraine with hits recorded at 18 locations.

Speaking at a press conference after talks with European allies in Berlin, Kushner said US President Donald Trump was open to providing Ukraine with security assurances modelled on Article 5 of the Nato treaty.
The discussions came amid heightened tensions following Ukraine's third aerial attack in four days on the strategically important Kerch Bridge, which connects Russia with Crimea.

extraction.body: With diplomatic efforts to resolve the conflict intensifying ahead of its fifth anniversary, Russia is “comfortable” with Nato-like security guarantees for Ukraine as part of a possible agreement to end the war, US envoy Jared Kushner said on Thursday. Speaking at a press conference after talks with European allies in Berlin, Kushner said US President Donald Trump was open to providing Ukraine with security assurances modelled on Article 5 of the Nato treaty. However, any such arrangement would have to serve American interests. "From America's perspective, giving an Article Five-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal. And I think that that's something that President Trump is open to, but obviously it has to be in America's interest to do that," he said. Another US envoy, Steve Witkoff, said Trump had discussed Ukraine and efforts to secure a peaceful end to the war during his trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping earlier on Thursday. Kushner and Witkoff met European allies in Berlin to discuss continued support for Ukraine and possible steps towards ending the conflict. The discussions came amid heightened tensions following Ukraine's third aerial attack in four days on the strategically important Kerch Bridge, which connects Russia with Crimea. Train services were suspended as Russian authorities assessed the damage but resumed later on Thursday afternoon, according to Russia's state news agency RIA Novosti. The Ukrainian attacks appeared aimed at embarrassing Putin while he was meeting Trump and Xi in China. The latest attack took place hours before the Berlin discussions involving Kushner, Witkoff, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and more than 40 European leaders. European governments supporting Ukraine's war effort have expressed concerns that Trump's direct engagement with Putin could leave them sidelined in decisions concerning the future of the conflict. Trump also joined the Berlin discussions by phone following his meeting with Putin, Kushner said. Europe pledges continued support for Ukraine British Prime Minister Andy Burnham reiterated Europe's commitment to supporting Ukraine, saying the backing would continue for as long as necessary. For as long as it takes, we will be there at the side of Ukraine and we will not falter," Burnham told reporters after co-chairing the Berlin talks. Kushner said Trump wanted European countries to be involved in efforts to negotiate a peace agreement, adding that the positions of Washington and its European allies were becoming "much closer". "We want to make sure that everything we're doing is unified, and I also want to be able to reiterate that President Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side. He's not looking to impose anything unilaterally," Kushner told reporters. He added that Trump had called into the Berlin meeting to brief participants on his discussions in Shenzhen with Xi and Putin. The proposed Article 5-style security assurances have emerged as an important element of the discussions on ending the war. Nato's Article 5 provides for collective defence, under which an armed attack against one member is considered an attack against all. Kushner's remarks indicate that Washington is discussing security arrangements for Ukraine with Moscow and European partners as part of the wider diplomatic effort to settle.

Speaking at a press conference after talks with European allies in Berlin, Kushner said US President Donald Trump was open to providing Ukraine with security assurances modelled on Article 5 of the Nato treaty.
However, any such arrangement would have to serve American interests.
"From America's perspective, giving an Article Five-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal.
And I think that that's something that President Trump is open to, but obviously it has to be in America's interest to do that," he said.

Another US envoy, Steve Witkoff, said Trump had discussed Ukraine and efforts to secure a peaceful end to the war during his trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping earlier on Thursday.
Kushner and Witkoff met European allies in Berlin to discuss continued support for Ukraine and possible steps towards ending the conflict.
The discussions came amid heightened tensions following Ukraine's third aerial attack in four days on the strategically important Kerch Bridge, which connects Russia with Crimea.
Train services were suspended as Russian authorities assessed the damage but resumed later on Thursday afternoon, according to Russia's state news agency RIA Novosti.
The Ukrainian attacks appeared aimed at embarrassing Putin while he was meeting Trump and Xi in China.
The latest attack took place hours before the Berlin discussions involving Kushner, Witkoff, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and more than 40 European leaders.
European governments supporting Ukraine's war effort have expressed concerns that Trump's direct engagement with Putin could leave them sidelined in decisions concerning the future of the conflict.
Trump also joined the Berlin discussions by phone following his meeting with Putin, Kushner said.
Europe pledges continued support for Ukraine British Prime Minister Andy Burnham reiterated Europe's commitment to supporting Ukraine, saying the backing would continue for as long as necessary.
For as long as it takes, we will be there at the side of Ukraine and we will not falter," Burnham told reporters after co-chairing the Berlin talks.
Kushner said Trump wanted European countries to be involved in efforts to negotiate a peace agreement, adding that the positions of Washington and its European allies were becoming "much closer".
"We want to make sure that everything we're doing is unified, and I also want to be able to reiterate that President Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side.
He's not looking to impose anything unilaterally," Kushner told reporters.
He added that Trump had called into the Berlin meeting to brief participants on his discussions in Shenzhen with Xi and Putin.
The proposed Article 5-style security assurances have emerged as an important element of the discussions on ending the war.
Nato's Article 5 provides for collective defence, under which an armed attack against one member is considered an attack against all.
Kushner's remarks indicate that Washington is discussing security arrangements for Ukraine with Moscow and European partners as part of the wider diplomatic effort to settle.

extraction.body: On November 19, 2026, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (“HHS”) Office for Civil Rights (“OCR”) published the “ HIPAA Privacy Rule: Changes to Support Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement and Reduce Regulatory Burdens ” (the “Final Rule”). Finalizing many, though not all, of the proposals in OCR’s January 21, 2021, Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (the “2021 NPRM”), the Final Rule modifies the HIPAA Privacy Rule, making significant changes to the individual right of access, expanding the permissions for care coordination and case management, streamlining Notice of Privacy Practices (“NPP”) requirements, and revising certain provisions affecting business associates, among other modifications. OCR explains that the Final Rule targets Privacy Rule standards that “may impede the nationwide transition to value-based health care by limiting or discouraging individual access or care coordination and case management or posing other unnecessary burdens,” with the goal of promoting “the essential sharing of individuals’ protected health information (PHI) for care coordination and individual engagement while continuing to protect its privacy and security.” OCR frames the Final Rule as part of the Trump Administration’s “Make America Healthy Again” agenda and its broader effort to build a “digital health ecosystem” in which patients can view, manage, use and share their health information through apps and other tools, situating it alongside related federal initiatives, including the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ Digital Health Tech Ecosystem initiative, ONC health IT certification work, and HHS’s crackdown on information blocking. Consistent with OCR’s historical approach, the amendments to the Privacy Rule are generally technology neutral. The Final Rule makes several key changes to the Privacy Rule’s right of access: OCR identifies facilitating care coordination and case management as a central aim of the Final Rule, and the Final Rule makes two targeted changes in this area. First, it amends the definition of “health care operations” at 45 C.F.R. § 164.501 to confirm that the definition encompasses both population-based and individual-focused care coordination and case management, a clarification especially significant for health plans. OCR explains that some covered entities had read the existing definition to reach only population-based activities, which would have excluded individual-level care coordination and case management; the Final Rule confirms that health plans and covered health care providers may use and disclose PHI for care coordination and case management, whether individual-level or population-based. Second, the Final Rule adds 45 C.F.R. § 164.506(c)(6), which expressly permits covered entities to disclose PHI to social services agencies, community-based organizations, home and community-based services (“HCBS”) providers, or similar third parties that provide health or human services to specific individuals, for purposes of individual-level care coordination and case management of the individual. The Final Rule makes two notable changes in this area. First, it amends 45 C.F.R. § 164.502(a)(4)(ii) to codify OCR’s longstanding interpretation that a business associate must disclose PHI as required by its business associate agreement, including, where specified in the business associate agreement, to the individual or the individual’s designee to fulfill the covered entity’s obligations with respect to the right of access and right to direct. OCR advises that covered entities and their business associates should address in their business associate agreements which party will be responsible for responding to such requests. Even where a covered entity delegates that responsibility to a business associate, the covered entity remains ultimately responsible for ensuring the individual receives the requested PHI, and contractual arrangements cannot be used to circumvent that obligation. Second, the Final Rule excludes Telecommunications Relay Services (“TRS”) providers from the definition of “business associate.” TRS enables people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or deaf-blind, or who have a speech disability to communicate by telephone. A longstanding OCR FAQ already provides that a covered entity using TRS to communicate with such individuals does not need a business associate agreement with the TRS provider, but it does not address covered entity workforce members who themselves rely on TRS to share PHI with colleagues or outside persons as needed to perform their duties. The Final Rule closes that gap by excluding TRS providers from the definition of “business associate” at 45 C.F.R. § 160.103 and expressly permitting a regulated entity to disclose PHI to a TRS Communications Assistant as necessary to conduct covered functions. Health care providers with a direct treatment relationship no longer need to obtain an individual’s written acknowledgment that they received the NPP, or document a good faith effort to obtain one, and OCR has eliminated the associated 6-year NPP document retention requirement. The Final Rule also revises NPP content requirements to better explain individuals’ rights and how to exercise them, including by informing individuals of their right to discuss the NPP with a contact person or office designated by the covered entity. It also, among other revisions to NPP requirements, removes the provision that excepted inmates of correctional institutions from the right to receive a copy of the NPP. Covered entities will therefore need to update their NPPs. The Final Rule extends the existing permission to use or disclose PHI of members of the Armed Forces to command authorities for mission readiness to all Uniformed Services, adding the U.S. Public Health Service (“USPHS”) Commissioned Corps and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (“NOAA”) Commissioned Corps to the six branches of the Armed Forces. It also makes a number of technical, non-substantive corrections to the Privacy Rule. Effective and Compliance Dates; Transition Period Effective and compliance dates. The Final Rule takes effect on January 19, 2027, with compliance required by July 19, 2027. Transition period for business associate agreements. The Final Rule modifies the transition provisions at 45 C.F.R. § 164.532(e) to allow regulated entities to continue to operate under certain existing business associate agreements (including subcontractor business associate agreements) for up to one year after the effective date of the Final Rule. If, prior to November 19, 2026, a regulated entity had an existing, compliant business associate agreement in place, and the agreement is not renewed or modified from January 19, 2027, until July 19, 2027, OCR deems such business associate agreement compliant with the modifications to the Privacy Rule until the earlier of (1) the date the business associate agreement is renewed or modified on or after July 19, 2027, or (2) January 18, 2028. This transition period covers only the updating of the business associate agreements themselves; it does not affect any other HIPAA compliance obligations. For example, as of the Final Rule’s compliance date, a business associate that responds to individual requests for access on behalf of a covered entity must respond to such requests as soon as practicable, but no later than 15 calendar days after receiving the request irrespective of whether its business associate agreement with the covered entity has been modified to reflect such requirement. With approximately 240 days between publication and the general compliance date, covered entities and business associates should begin their compliance review now. Priority areas for covered entities include (1) auditing access request workflows against the new 15 calendar day response period, (2) posting the required fee schedule, (3) revising NPPs to satisfy the updated content requirements and to extend the right to receive NPPs to inmates, and (4) updating or creating new policies and procedures and workforce training materials to address the regulatory changes. All covered entities with business associate agreements (and business associates with subcontractor business associate agreements) should review and revise such agreements to ensure compliance with the modified right of access provisions.

extraction.body: Federal regulators have finalized substantial changes to the HIPAA Privacy Rule aimed at giving patients faster and easier access to their health records - including through third-party applications - while reducing obstacles to information sharing for patient care coordination. See Also: How to implement a physical security strategy with privacy in mind The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' Office for Civil Rights released the 363-page final rule - HIPAA Privacy Rule: Changes to Support Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement and Reduce Regulatory Burdens - late Monday. It is slated for publication Thursday in the Federal Register. "Americans should never have to fight for access to their own health records," HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in a statement. "This rule modernizes HIPAA to serve patients and help providers spend more time delivering care and less time navigating bureaucracy." The rule becomes effective 60 days after publication, or on Jan. 19, 2027. HIPAA-regulated organizations must comply with applicable provisions 180 days after the effective date, or July 19, 2027, with additional time allowed for certain modifications to written business associate agreements.* HHS OCR issued the proposed HIPAA Privacy Rule modifications in January 2021, during the final days of President Donald Trump's first term. But the proposal remained on the back burner during the Biden administration (see: HHS Reveals Proposed Changes to HIPAA Privacy Rule ). The final rule retains several key patient-access and care-coordination provisions proposed in 2021 but abandons or scales back others that raised privacy concerns or would have increased administrative burdens on healthcare organizations. For example, HHS OCR dropped a proposal that would have relaxed HIPAA's minimum necessary standard for certain disclosures of sensitive health information. Among the most significant changes, the final rule cuts time in half for healthcare organizations to respond to patients' requests for access to their protected health information - from 30 calendar days to 15 days - with a one-time extension of up to 30 additional days under specific circumstances. The regulation also clarifies patients' rights to obtain their electronic health information through personal health applications, including consumer apps that are not subject to HIPAA. Healthcare organizations generally can't refuse to transmit records to patients' chosen personal health apps solely because they believe the applications lack adequate privacy or security protections, such as encryption at rest. The rule also prohibits covered organizations from imposing unreasonable identity verification measures that create barriers to patient access. Another condition involves verifying that demographic information associated with the token matches the patient's information in the covered entity's designated record set. HHS said these procedures can satisfy HIPAA's identity verification obligations. Healthcare organizations also may warn patients about privacy and security risks associated with particular apps. Before the rule's release, several healthcare industry groups signed a letter to HHS last week expressing concerns that potentially loosening identity verification requirements involving third-party apps could expose healthcare providers to security threats and regulatory scrutiny (see: Health Groups Warn HHS on Potential HIPAA Privacy Changes ). The signatories of the letter , including the College of Healthcare Information Management Executives - an association of healthcare CISOs and CIOs - did not immediately respond to ISMG's request for comment on the final rule. But HHS retained the minimum necessary standard for applicable healthcare operations disclosures, rather than adopting a proposed exception for certain care-coordination activities. The final rule also eliminates the requirement for covered healthcare providers to make a good-faith effort to obtain patients' written acknowledgment of receiving a Notice of Privacy Practices, a process HHS deemed unnecessarily burdensome. "I appreciate the deletion of the requirement for healthcare providers to obtain acknowledgments of receipt of the notice of privacy practices. The regulatory requirement was founded on good intentions but led to administrative burden and confusion with minimal corresponding benefit," said privacy attorney Adam Greene of the law firm Davis Wright Tremaine. Privacy attorney Kirk Nahra of the law firm WilmerHale said the final rule involves complicated issues stemming partly from tensions between competing public policy goals. "Given the passage of time I would have liked to see an additional stage to obtain new comments on these issues that have changed significantly since the proposal was first issued" five years ago, he said. Regarding the access to PHI provisions, "it is clear that they are interested in promoting patient access to records - although there is some risk that these principles, especially some of the identity confirmation issues, can create security concerns," he said. As for information sharing for coordinated care, "HHS chose this 'coordination' over individual privacy. That's not necessarily a bad decision but it is a complicated one - the rule essentially allows this disclosure over the objection or lack of permission from the consumer," he said. The provisions easing information sharing among healthcare organizations, health plans, social services agencies and other care-coordination partners could raise privacy concerns, particularly when patient information is disclosed to organizations outside HIPAA's regulatory umbrella. Such disclosures could also increase risks involving unauthorized access, secondary uses of data and cyberattacks. "Companies should remain cautious about these disclosures even if they are permitted," Nahra said. "The proposal would have led to a substantial unfunded mandate that would tax covered entities' already limited resources," he said. Overall, Greene said the final rule includes some helpful changes to the Privacy Rule, "but nothing earth-shattering." "I don't expect that compliance with the final rule will be difficult, but the changes to the notices of privacy practices and to policies and procedures around the right of access will take significant time and resources to implement," he said. Privacy attorney Iliana Peters of the law firm Polsinelli said her biggest concerns involve the administrative burdens HIPAA-covered organizations will face in implementing several of the changes. Those include updating policies and procedures governing uses and disclosures and also complying with patient access requirements, particularly to accommodate the new 15-day access deadline, "which is a very short amount of time," she said. Also, although organizations will no longer need to obtain patients' written acknowledgment of receiving a Notice of Privacy Practices, they still must update, redistribute and post their notices to comply with the rule changes. Regulated entities also must update their websites with required information about fees for accessing health records and revise applicable business associate agreements. As for information sharing for coordinated care, "HHS chose this 'coordination' over individual privacy. That's not necessarily a bad decision but it is a complicated one - the rule essentially allows this disclosure over the objection or lack of permission from the consumer," he said.

The provisions easing information sharing among healthcare organizations, health plans, social services agencies and other care-coordination partners could raise privacy concerns, particularly when patient information is disclosed to organizations outside HIPAA's regulatory umbrella. Such disclosures could also increase risks involving unauthorized access, secondary uses of data and cyberattacks.
"Companies should remain cautious about these disclosures even if they are permitted," Nahra said.
"The proposal would have led to a substantial unfunded mandate that would tax covered entities' already limited resources," he said.
Overall, Greene said the final rule includes some helpful changes to the Privacy Rule, "but nothing earth-shattering."

"I don't expect that compliance with the final rule will be difficult, but the changes to the notices of privacy practices and to policies and procedures around the right of access will take significant time and resources to implement," he said.
Privacy attorney Iliana Peters of the law firm Polsinelli said her biggest concerns involve the administrative burdens HIPAA-covered organizations will face in implementing several of the changes.

Those include updating policies and procedures governing uses and disclosures and also complying with patient access requirements, particularly to accommodate the new 15-day access deadline, "which is a very short amount of time," she said.

Also, although organizations will no longer need to obtain patients' written acknowledgment of receiving a Notice of Privacy Practices, they still must update, redistribute and post their notices to comply with the rule changes.
Regulated entities also must update their websites with required information about fees for accessing health records and revise applicable business associate agreements.
