Universities bring a distinct lens to AI, one grounded in long-term, open, and responsible inquiry. Empire AI is giving our faculty research teams access to unmatched computing power to take on questions in service of the greater good, from improving human health to building a more sustainable future, at a scale no single institution could access alone. We are grateful to Governor Hochul for her vision, leadership and investment in make New York a national model to demonstrate how public investment in academic AI research can accelerate discovery and benefit all New Yorkers.”

Executive Vice President for Research at Columbia University and Empire AI Board Member Jeannette M. Wing said, “Columbia researchers are using Empire AI to measure NYC traffic volume to improve public safety, to enhance long-term climate resilience to floods and extreme heat in New York, and to better predict mental health behavioral outcomes like anxiety and depression. And unlike today’s AI models which stop learning once they are released, one Columbia research lab is using Empire AI to build agents that, like the human brain, keep learning from experience throughout their lifetimes. None of this work could be done without the computational capability of Empire AI.”
New York's Growing Leadership in AI Science and Research and Safety

The groundbreaking complements Governor Hochul's broader efforts to establish New York as a national center for scientific discovery and responsible artificial intelligence. Last week, Governor Hochul launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University. Supported by a historic $30 million philanthropic gift from a group of donors led by Empire AI Board Chair Tom Secunda, alongside an initial $25 million SUNY research investment, the center will bring together more than 80 scientists and researchers from institutions across New York.

With Alpha and Beta already supporting researchers, the new Binghamton center advancing independent AI research, and construction of Gamma moving forward, Governor Hochul's original vision for Empire AI is becoming a permanent scientific resource designed to serve New Yorkers for generations.

This announcement builds on Governor Hochul’s nation-leading AI safety agenda, which also includes implementation of New York’s RAISE Act. Under that new law, large frontier AI developers will be required to register with the state and comply with strict safety, transparency and reporting requirements — including New York’s strongest-in-the-nation requirement to report any critical safety incident within 72 hours. The Governor also established the first-in-the-nation Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust (DIGIT) to implement the RAISE Act and oversee large frontier AI Developers.

New York’s shared AI research infrastructure is getting a permanent home . Gov. Kathy Hochul broke ground November 19, 2026, at the University at Buffalo on a supercomputing center that will house Empire AI Gamma, the consortium’s third phase. The project is intended to give researchers across New York’s universities access to more computing power. The Empire AI Research Computing Center will occupy 46,000 square feet on Service Center Road on UB’s North Campus. Hochul’s office says the permanent facility is expected to be completed by early 2028. UB gives a later target for becoming operational: late summer 2028 . The governor’s office describes Empire AI as a public-private initiative worth more than $500 million . That figure covers the initiative, not just this building. Its organizing principle is shared access: bringing public and private research institutions together around computing resources that, the state says, no single university could afford independently. Empire AI’s earlier systems have been operating at UB’s Downtown Campus. Empire AI Board Chair Tom Secunda said the initiative now has more than 1,500 registered users and hundreds of research projects underway. Alpha launched in 2024 with a philanthropic contribution from the Simons Foundation. Beta, a $40 million supercomputer at UB, became fully operational in August 2026. According to UB, the NVIDIA-powered Beta system delivers 11 times Alpha’s AI training capacity, 40 times its inference performance and eight times its data storage. extraction.body: Milestone Complements on New York’s Nation-Leading RAISE Act on Frontier AI Accountability and Launch of Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University to Advance Independent Research Into AI Safety and Security Governor Kathy Hochul today officially broke ground on the permanent home of Empire AI at the University at Buffalo, marking a major milestone in New York’s historic effort to lead artificial intelligence research for the public good. The groundbreaking launches the next phase of development for Empire AI Gamma, the full-scale supercomputing facility that will dramatically expand the computing power available to researchers at New York's leading public and private universities and establishing Empire AI as the most powerful academic AI research computer in the country. First announced by Governor Hochul in her 2024 State of the State address, Empire AI has grown into a more than $500 million public-private initiative that is already supporting groundbreaking research in medicine, climate science, advanced manufacturing and other fields, while establishing New York as a national model for responsible AI innovation. Today's groundbreaking comes just days after Governor Hochul launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University, a first-of-its-kind research initiative bringing together more than 80 scientists to independently study the safety, security and performance of advanced AI systems using Empire AI's computing infrastructure. Together, these investments are advancing the Governor's vision of a statewide AI research ecosystem that gives academic researchers the tools, infrastructure and expertise needed to accelerate scientific discovery and ensure artificial intelligence serves the public good. “Two years ago, we made a commitment to put New York at the forefront of the AI revolution — while ensuring safe and responsible AI development is a top priority — and today we are delivering on that promise,” Governor Hochul said. “Empire AI is already giving our brightest researchers the most powerful academic AI computing resources in the country, and now we're building the permanent home that will take this initiative to an entirely new level. From advancing medical breakthroughs to tackling climate change, we're proving that New York can lead the nation in artificial intelligence while building responsibly, creating opportunities and making sure this technology benefits all New Yorkers.” Building the Future of AI Research in New York Two years ago, we made a commitment to put New York at the forefront of the AI revolution — while ensuring safe and responsible AI development is a top priority — and today we are delivering on that promise.” Empire AI Board Chair Tom Secunda said, “Just two years ago, Empire AI was an ambitious idea, and today it is a national model for putting world-class computing power in the hands of academic researchers, with more than 1,500 registered users and hundreds of research projects already underway. Thanks to Governor Hochul's vision and leadership, New York has brought together government, universities and philanthropy to build a scientific resource that no single institution could create on its own. This groundbreaking takes that commitment to the next level, strengthening New York's leadership and helping shape the future of scientific discovery across the nation.” Rochester Institute of Technology President Bill Sanders said, “RIT has always believed that technology is most powerful when it is applied with purpose. This groundbreaking moves that vision forward on a statewide scale. Through Empire AI, RIT researchers and students will work alongside some of New York’s other leading institutions, combining extraordinary computing power with human creativity and ingenuity to advance responsible AI, accelerate discovery and create meaningful impact for our communities, our economy and our world.” Co-founder and Chair of the Simons Foundation Marilyn Simons said, “Many of the greatest scientific breakthroughs begin with a question no one has been able to answer. Empire AI gives more scientists the tools to tackle those questions. We are grateful to Governor Hochul for bringing together New York's leading research institutions and philanthropic partners to make this extraordinary shared resource possible. Today's groundbreaking is an investment in the next generation of scientists and in discoveries that will benefit us all.” State University of New York Chancellor John B. King Jr. said, “Empire AI is driving New York State’s leadership in leveraging AI to achieve research excellence that advances the public good. From accelerating the search for cures and treatments for disease to enhancing speech language therapy for children, and from advancing biotechnology research to tackling climate change, SUNY researchers are addressing some of society’s most pressing challenges thanks to Empire AI. SUNY is proud to host Empire AI at the State University of New York at Buffalo, and we are grateful to Governor Hochul for her vision and steadfast leadership.” The SUNY Board of Trustees said, “Visionary leadership from Governor Hochul makes it possible for SUNY and our higher education partners to pioneer research for the public good through Empire AI. The permanent Empire AI facility will accelerate groundbreaking research and innovations that improve communities throughout New York State and beyond.” Empire State Development President, CEO & Commissioner Hope Knight said, “Under Governor Hochul’s leadership, New York is proving that when we invest in broad, responsible access to cutting-edge technology, our entire economy wins. Today’s groundbreaking at the University at Buffalo marks a major step forward for Empire AI — creating jobs now while empowering New York’s students, researchers, and businesses to drive innovation, attract new investment, and deliver lasting economic benefits to communities across the state.” U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand said, “New York State is setting the national standard for responsible AI. Empire AI at the University at Buffalo represents a $500 million investment in our future, fueling cutting-edge research and proving that artificial intelligence can be harnessed safely as a powerful force for the public good.” Congressmember Tim Kennedy said, “For decades, the world has looked to New York State to lead the way in technological advancement. With this historic groundbreaking at UB, we continue that tradition by advancing research that benefits New Yorkers in a secure and responsible manner. As the next generation of researchers and entrepreneurs looks for where to call home, we’re keeping Western New York at the forefront of innovation.” State Senator Jeremy J. Zellner said, “Western New York has the talent and institutions to lead in the industries of tomorrow, and Empire AI puts us in a position to do just that,” said Senator Jeremy J. Zellner. “With its permanent home at the University at Buffalo, we are investing in groundbreaking research, economic opportunity, and Buffalo’s place in the future of technology. I thank Governor Hochul for ensuring our region is not watching the next technological revolution from the sidelines but helping lead it.” Assemblymember Bill Conrad said, “As we witness the lightning-speed advancement of artificial intelligence, we must consider how best to harness AI's grand potential for the advancement of humankind. Its future applications must be shaped by knowledgeable, responsible hands, and our state's consortium of universities, public and private, represent a world-renowned hub for that talent. I thank Governor Hochul for her foresightedness here, and I join in celebrating the partnerships that are solidifying UB's place in the realm of global research. Empire AI will establish New York State as a leader in supercomputing and a uniquely influential force in the shaping of AI's all-important future.” University at Buffalo President Caroline Attardo Genco said, “Today we break ground not only on a pioneering new facility, but on a lasting commitment to the people of Western New York and New York State. I am deeply grateful to Governor Kathy Hochul, whose vision and steadfast advocacy made this extraordinary resource a reality, and to our Empire AI partners for their invaluable collaboration. At UB, our researchers are already putting Empire AI to work on challenges in education and neuroscience, climate science and advanced manufacturing. As both the home of Empire AI and a neighbor invested in the future of our region, we embrace the responsibility that comes with those roles. The discoveries that begin here will improve lives, draw talent to our region and help our communities thrive for years to come.” New York University President Linda G. Mills said, “Governor Hochul has ensured that New York State is and will continue to be a leader in AI for years to come, contributing breakthroughs that will benefit the nation in ways we can only imagine today. New York University looks forward to its ongoing work with our university peers to drive scientific discovery—and has already deployed Empire AI’s world-class computing power to better understand the brain, to build more sustainable energy sources and novel materials, and to even improve AI itself.” CUNY Graduate Center President and Empire AI Board Treasurer Joshua Brumberg said, “The City University of New York’s participation in Empire AI has supercharged our researchers’ capabilities to solve pressing societal problems. It also allows us to conduct research for the public good and attracts to CUNY the best faculty and students who are excited to work in New York and gain access to Empire AI’s compute power.” Binghamton University President Anne D’Alleva said, “Empire AI is positioning New York, and especially the State University of New York, as the leader in safe and responsible AI that serves the public good. Binghamton University shares its congratulations with the University at Buffalo on the next phase of Empire AI Gamma. Our faculty and staff in the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research are looking forward to working with our partners at Buffalo and we thank Governor Hochul and the entire Empire AI team for its support of research and scholarship throughout the SUNY system.” Vice President for Research for the University of Rochester and Empire AI Board Member Steve Dewhurst said, “Empire AI has become an increasingly important resource for advancing research and innovation at the University of Rochester. Researchers across our institution are leveraging its capabilities to support a remarkable range of projects, spanning uses such as understanding brain-wide fluid flow, predicting the quantum dynamics of light-matter quasiparticles (polaritons), improving our ability to model climate change and much more. This breadth of use speaks to the transformative potential of Empire AI to accelerate scientific discovery and societal solutions by helping our researchers tackle complex challenges that traditional resources alone cannot address. Governor Kathy Hochul today officially broke ground on the permanent home of Empire AI at the University at Buffalo, marking a major milestone in New York’s historic effort to lead artificial intelligence research for the public good. The groundbreaking launches the next phase of development for Empire AI Gamma, the full-scale supercomputing facility that will dramatically expand the computing power available to researchers at New York's leading public and private universities and establishing Empire AI as the most powerful academic AI research computer in the country. First announced by Governor Hochul in her 2024 State of the State address, Empire AI has grown into a more than $500 million public-private initiative that is already supporting groundbreaking research in medicine, climate science, advanced manufacturing and other fields, while establishing New York as a national model for responsible AI innovation.

Today's groundbreaking comes just days after Governor Hochul launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University, a first-of-its-kind research initiative bringing together more than 80 scientists to independently study the safety, security and performance of advanced AI systems using Empire AI's computing infrastructure. “Two years ago, we made a commitment to put New York at the forefront of the AI revolution — while ensuring safe and responsible AI development is a top priority — and today we are delivering on that promise,” Governor Hochul said. “Empire AI is already giving our brightest researchers the most powerful academic AI computing resources in the country, and now we're building the permanent home that will take this initiative to an entirely new level. From advancing medical breakthroughs to tackling climate change, we're proving that New York can lead the nation in artificial intelligence while building responsibly, creating opportunities and making sure this technology benefits all New Yorkers.”

This groundbreaking takes that commitment to the next level, strengthening New York's leadership and helping shape the future of scientific discovery across the nation.”

extraction.body: Denmark's parliament has unanimously approved a security agreement with the United States, allowing for an expanded U.S. military presence in Greenland. The Folketing, Denmark's parliament, passed the agreement with a 109-0 vote on Thursday (November 19), as reported by Arctic Today . This decision marks the end of months of diplomatic tension between Denmark and the U.S. over President Donald Trump's interest in acquiring Greenland. The agreement, signed in New York on September 22, involves Denmark, Greenland, and the U.S. It supplements a 1951 defense accord and allows the U.S. to establish new military bases at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig in Greenland. The deal also permits the expansion of the Pituffik Space Base and the establishment of the Golden Dome missile defense shield, according to Al Jazeera . The agreement ensures that Greenland remains under Danish sovereignty while recognizing the island's right to self-determination. It also blocks non-NATO and non-EU states from gaining significant influence in sensitive sectors, preventing countries like China and Russia from strategic investments. Despite the smooth passage in Denmark, the agreement faced contention in Greenland's parliament, where it passed with 16 votes and seven abstentions earlier this month. The opposition party Naleraq criticized the deal, calling for a referendum and alleging that Greenland gains nothing from it. As reported by NBC5 , Greenland's Minister for Foreign Affairs, Múte B. Egede , accused Naleraq of leaking secret information, leading to a police report against the party. U.S. Ambassador to Denmark Ken Howery welcomed the agreement, stating it modernizes the partnership and strengthens security for the U.S., Denmark, Greenland, and NATO. He expressed optimism about deepening cooperation as the agreement is implemented. The agreement will remain in force even if Greenland gains independence, provided it joins NATO. It will officially take effect once the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs informs the U.S. that all procedures are complete.

Denmark’s Folketing unanimously ratified a security agreement with the United States covering Greenland on Thursday, with 109 members present voting in favour of the text without opposition or abstention. The agreement, signed in September and signed in New York on September 22, is aimed at bolstering security in the Arctic and North Atlantic and easing tensions over Donald Trump’s desire to annex the Arctic island. The deal supplements a 1951 accord on the US military presence in Greenland and allows the United States to build two military bases in Greenland.

The agreement also blocks countries outside the European Union and NATO from strategic sectors, in order to stop China or Russia from gaining influence over the territory, particularly through investments. The agreement is set to enter into force once the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs informs the US in a diplomatic note that procedures are complete.

The agreement remains in force even if Greenland gains full independence, and it reaffirms Danish sovereignty and the Greenlanders’ right to self-determination. The text is not subject to a vote by the US Senate because it is described as an executive agreement.

The ratification follows months of pressure tied to Donald Trump’s repeated calls for Greenland to become part of the United States and his refusal to rule out the use of military or economic force to seize control of the island. The dispute triggered a diplomatic crisis within NATO in January, forcing Denmark and Greenland into intensive negotiations that lasted for months before the agreement was approved by Greenland’s parliament earlier this month. Kenneth Howery, the U.S. ambassador to Denmark, welcomed the “strong support” in the Danish parliament for ratification of the deal “paving the way for it to enter into force.”

Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen, said the ratification could mark the beginning of a new phase because Washington could claim greater influence in security decisions and the extraction of some strategic resources. The Danish government can now formally notify the United States that both parliaments have consented to complete the ratification process, after which the Danish foreign ministry will inform the US in a diplomatic note that procedures are complete.

extraction.body: Denmark's parliament has unanimously approved a security agreement with the United States, allowing for an expanded U.S. military presence in Greenland. The Folketing, Denmark's parliament, passed the agreement with a 109-0 vote on Thursday (November 19), as reported by Arctic Today . This decision marks the end of months of diplomatic tension between Denmark and the U.S. over President Donald Trump's interest in acquiring Greenland. The agreement, signed in New York on September 22, involves Denmark, Greenland, and the U.S. It supplements a 1951 defense accord and allows the U.S. to establish new military bases at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig in Greenland. The deal also permits the expansion of the Pituffik Space Base and the establishment of the Golden Dome missile defense shield, according to Al Jazeera . The agreement ensures that Greenland remains under Danish sovereignty while recognizing the island's right to self-determination. It also blocks non-NATO and non-EU states from gaining significant influence in sensitive sectors, preventing countries like China and Russia from strategic investments. Despite the smooth passage in Denmark, the agreement faced contention in Greenland's parliament, where it passed with 16 votes and seven abstentions earlier this month. The opposition party Naleraq criticized the deal, calling for a referendum and alleging that Greenland gains nothing from it. As reported by NBC5 , Greenland's Minister for Foreign Affairs, Múte B. Egede , accused Naleraq of leaking secret information, leading to a police report against the party. U.S. Ambassador to Denmark Ken Howery welcomed the agreement, stating it modernizes the partnership and strengthens security for the U.S., Denmark, Greenland, and NATO. He expressed optimism about deepening cooperation as the agreement is implemented. The agreement will remain in force even if Greenland gains independence, provided it joins NATO. It will officially take effect once the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs informs the U.S. that all procedures are complete.

Customers have included Uber, Shopify, and Notion. Co-founder Chenyu Zhao and I spoke onstage toward the end of the day. Zhao and many others believe companies are gravitating toward platforms like his because frontier models are pricey and, in most cases, he says, unnecessary unless you need the very latest and greatest generalized intelligence. There are also growing concerns that frontier labs absorb too much of their customers’ know-how, even if only through the prompts used to get answers, a worry Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella raised in July . Fireworks has also gotten its first black eye, having disclosed two security incidents this fall. In one, hackers reached API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts; in the other, attackers breached its cloud provider, made their way into a development system, and nabbed customer data, including billing records and some datasets. Notion says AI chat transcripts from fewer than 1% of its workspaces were exposed, but it has disconnected from Fireworks. Uber says hackers stole the names, addresses, birth dates and driver’s license numbers of about 150,000 drivers through a vendor that TechCrunch identified as Fireworks . Fireworks will have to win back the confidence of customers like them. Fireworks, assigned a $17.5 billion valuation by its investors in summer, is reportedly in “ early talks ” for yet another round, though Zhao declined to comment. There’s money chasing everyone in the category, seems like. Rival companies Together AI and Baseten have announced massive rounds in recent months. On Wednesday, Palo Alto Networks said it will buy Applied Compute , which, like Fireworks, helps companies train and run custom AI models on their own data. The deal for the startup, founded just a year ago by former OpenAI researchers, is $4.5 billion, all of it in stock. Here’s some of what Zhao had to say. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. When you meet great co-founders, it’s obvious within five minutes that they’re really smart. I was sold after talking to Lin [Qiao] and Dima [Dzhulgakov]. It’s also important to find people who are genuinely nice, people you’ll enjoy working with. How do you describe Fireworks to a CEO who has never heard of it? I describe Fireworks as a specialized intelligence platform. OpenAI and Anthropic are building general intelligence. We use open models, which are often smaller, cheaper, and faster, and let companies add their own data to specialize them. That way you own your AI rather than being beholden to giant AI conglomerates. If you’re just using Opus or Sonnet, that’s not a differentiator. A few years ago I’d have said a year, a year and a half. Then came DeepSeek and a waterfall of fantastic open models. These days it’s at most six months behind, probably closer to three. If the models are so close behind, why are businesses slow to switch? Frontier models are a household brand, and before you find product-market fit, using the best model is low risk. But once you pass 10,000 or 100,000 users and you’re spending $10,000 to $100,000 a month on tokens, it’s time to think about open source. In July, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that companies using proprietary AI models pay twice , once in money and again in know-how. Do you think that warning had a material effect? We think we’ll live in a two-model world, with frontier and open models in parallel. You want the best intelligence for high-level planning, but you don’t need a frontier model for basic arithmetic. That’s why there’s so much interest in routing, and why people now think about cost per task, not just cost per token. Anthropic went public today. What do you think of its valuation? There’s one scenario in which it just continues to cement its place in this sort of oligopoly; there’s another where it starts to lose traction. On the record: I’ll probably call my broker tonight and buy a few shares. This is a long-term bet. In 10 years AI usage will be at a completely different scale, and that takes an incredible amount of capital, which is why these companies are going public. Fireworks has had a couple of security breaches recently. What do you tell customers? Every company is probably seeing an unprecedented frequency of attacks. For our incident, a lot of the motivation was LLM jacking: hunting through providers for API keys and secrets to sell tokens on illicit marketplaces. Our promise is zero data retention for inference traffic, and there’s no indication that has been compromised. Notion has disconnected from Fireworks. Did you lose other customers? “Muse gathers that based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share, which is how it remembers the person who just sent you an invoice is in fact the plumber who you previously hired to complete some work in your bathroom or which flowers your spouse said they liked best.”

8 as a personal AI agent that can handle tasks like sending emails, booking travel, shopping, and tracking goals.

Meta also recently patched a zero-day vulnerability in the Mac version of Muse that could allow malware already running on a user’s computer to hijack the agent and take advantage of permissions the user had previously granted it.

extraction.body: In typical Meta fashion, the company’s popular new AI agent Muse reportedly keeps detailed, regularly updated files on the people in users’ lives. Nearly a month after its launch, researchers are digging into how Muse works. It turns out the AI agent will openly share internal files and instructions when users ask, offering a peek at how it operates. One of the somewhat unsettling details is an hourly process that instructs Muse to create and update “a page for every person in the user’s life,” Wired reports . Independent AI safety and security researcher Karan Joshi extracted a trove of Muse instructions and system prompts through the app’s regular chat interface and shared the findings with Wired. Separately, The Future Society published system instructions from an exported copy of a Muse virtual machine. “What it seemed like to me—from all these prompts, system skills data, and things that they’re feeding into Muse—is that they want to understand your relationships that you have with real people,” Joshi told Wired. “They’re trying to know you like a friend, which is honestly pretty creepy.” The new details come just weeks after Meta launched Muse on Sept. 8 as a personal AI agent that can handle tasks like sending emails, booking travel, shopping, and tracking goals. To do all that, users give Muse access to a wide range of their apps and accounts. Muse has since climbed to the number-one spot on Apple’s U.S. App Store chart for free iPhone apps. But privacy and security concerns have emerged almost immediately. For instance, Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site in September, saying Meta had not notified the company in advance that the agent would access its online shop. The company also raised concerns about how Muse handles customer credentials and account data. Meta also recently patched a zero-day vulnerability in the Mac version of Muse that could allow malware already running on a user’s computer to hijack the agent and take advantage of permissions the user had previously granted it. Now, we have a better idea of just how much Muse keeps track of about users and the people in their lives, even if those people don’t use Muse themselves. According to system instructions published by The Future Society, these relationship pages can include a person’s name, how they are connected to the Muse user, recurring topics such as an upcoming apartment move or savings goal, and important dates like birthdays and anniversaries. Muse can also keep a history of the relationship, including events or milestones, as well as information about how close the user is to the person, what their relationship is built on, how they interact, and what the relationship appears to need at the moment. “For any agent to be useful and actually help you achieve your goals, it needs to have context about you and those you interact with,” a Meta spokesperson told Gizmodo in an emailed statement. “Muse gathers that based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share, which is how it remembers the person who just sent you an invoice is in fact the plumber who you previously hired to complete some work in your bathroom or which flowers your spouse said they liked best.” The spokesperson added that the information is stored in each user’s dedicated secure virtual machine, which Meta says cannot be accessed by other users’ agents. The new details come just weeks after Meta launched Muse on Sept. 8 as a personal AI agent that can handle tasks like sending emails, booking travel, shopping, and tracking goals. To do all that, users give Muse access to a wide range of their apps and accounts. Muse has since climbed to the number-one spot on Apple’s U.S. App Store chart for free iPhone apps.
But privacy and security concerns have emerged almost immediately.

For instance, Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site in September, saying Meta had not notified the company in advance that the agent would access its online shop. The company also raised concerns about how Muse handles customer credentials and account data.

Meta also recently patched a zero-day vulnerability in the Mac version of Muse that could allow malware already running on a user’s computer to hijack the agent and take advantage of permissions the user had previously granted it.
Now, we have a better idea of just how much Muse keeps track of about users and the people in their lives, even if those people don’t use Muse themselves.

According to system instructions published by The Future Society, these relationship pages can include a person’s name, how they are connected to the Muse user, recurring topics such as an upcoming apartment move or savings goal, and important dates like birthdays and anniversaries.

Muse can also keep a history of the relationship, including events or milestones, as well as information about how close the user is to the person, what their relationship is built on, how they interact, and what the relationship appears to need at the moment.

“For any agent to be useful and actually help you achieve your goals, it needs to have context about you and those you interact with,” a Meta spokesperson told Gizmodo in an emailed statement. “Muse gathers that based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share, which is how it remembers the person who just sent you an invoice is in fact the plumber who you previously hired to complete some work in your bathroom or which flowers your spouse said they liked best.”
The spokesperson added that the information is stored in each user’s dedicated secure virtual machine, which Meta says cannot be accessed by other users’ agents.

sources.title: Meta’s new Muse Charm device may cost $300
passages: Meta plans to charge $300 for Muse Charm, its upcoming Tamagotchi-like AI device that was teased at the company’s Connect event earlier this year, The Information has reported .
Indeed, $300 is arguably a pretty steep price for a product the size of a keychain, although it’s also a price point that’s in line with what other companies have been charging.
The wearable launched by Friend — the AI startup whose device lets you text and talk to an AI persona — is currently retailing for $250.

When reached for comment by TechCrunch, a Meta spokesperson didn’t deny the claims, merely providing the following statement: “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.”
It remains to be seen whether customers will bite or not.
AI wearables have had a rough go of it so far (here’s looking at you, Humane Ai pin ), but companies continue to iterate on the concept in an attempt to break through to a broader audience.

So far, Meta has made a relatively successful push into consumer AI, launching Muse — its agentic helper — along with a variety of cute avatars that users can use to give the system more of a personality.

sources.title: Meta’s new Muse Charm device may cost $300
passages: Meta plans to charge $300 for Muse Charm, its upcoming Tamagotchi-like AI device that was teased at the company’s Connect event earlier this year, The Information has reported .
Indeed, $300 is arguably a pretty steep price for a product the size of a keychain, although it’s also a price point that’s in line with what other companies have been charging.
The wearable launched by Friend — the AI startup whose device lets you text and talk to an AI persona — is currently retailing for $250.

When reached for comment by TechCrunch, a Meta spokesperson didn’t deny the claims, merely providing the following statement: “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.”
It remains to be seen whether customers will bite or not.
AI wearables have had a rough go of it so far (here’s looking at you, Humane Ai pin ), but companies continue to iterate on the concept in an attempt to break through to a broader audience.

So far, Meta has made a relatively successful push into consumer AI, launching Muse — its agentic helper — along with a variety of cute avatars that users can use to give the system more of a personality.

sources.title: Meta’s AI agent Muse is mixing up conversations and could be exposing private data, report says
passages: Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.

“Employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products,” a Meta spokesperson said in an email to TechCrunch. “Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Launched in September, Muse is one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads.

One employee told colleagues that Muse had randomly sent an extra message in a chat about weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
Update 11/19/2026 12:05 PM PT: The article was updated to include Meta’s comment.

In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn’t belong to them.

sources.title: Meta Employees Raise Privacy Concerns Over Muse AI Mixing Up Accounts: 5 outlets compared - NewsCord
passages: Meta launched its Muse AI agent in September 2026 with a promise that it was built from the ground up for privacy and security, but Reuters reviewed internal communications showing employees raising “significant concerns” about Muse’s handling of private data.

Reuters reported that internal posts described incidents where Muse appeared to be mixing up conversations between different user accounts, and employees flagged safety issues “as recently as launch week” while Meta proceeded with the September 2026 US launch as scheduled.
Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests employees said they never made and bank account balances that did not belong to them.

Muse had already been downloaded by more than 10 million people and Meta expected it to generate billions of dollars in revenue from AI, while La Nación described internal postings reviewed by Reuters as showing unsolicited actions including infiltrating encrypted personal messages and sending conversations that appeared destined for other people.

The Defense Watch said Reuters could not establish whether unfamiliar financial information represented actual exposure of another person’s data or information fabricated by the AI model, and the outlet described Meta’s position that many messages identified as possible account mix-ups were hallucinations and that some problems had already been addressed.
This article is an automated aggregation of coverage from news outlets.
Our editorials offer in-depth analysis curated by the NewsCord team.
5 outlets in this story. Read their headlines below .

Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told TechCrunch that “employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public,” and Roberts described Reuters’ examples as “isolated incidents.” Ars Technica quoted a Meta staffer writing “Hmmm,” after Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden, and Ars Technica also quoted the staffer’s out-of-context output about a coffee table pickup that “doesn’t seem to be yours.”
Meta Muse reportedly mixes conversations from different accounts, exposing private data.
Internal testing flagged Muse accessing encrypted private messages users did not expect.
Muse privacy invasions are freaking out Meta staffers, internal chats show

Claroc discovered that Muse’s chat-sharing feature exposed shared conversations through publicly searchable DNS records, and Claroc found that users who shared a conversation did not realize the resulting links were discoverable by anyone with the right DNS query.
Muse accessed private Signal messages on the device where it was installed, made possible by the broad Android notification permissions the app requests.

story.title: Meta’s AI agent Muse is mixing up conversations and could be exposing private data, report says

facts.text: Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.

extraction.body: Not many of them made it in, but Chinese clouds no longer care The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) allowed Nvidia and AMD to sell hundreds of thousands of advanced GPUs to entities that the Department of War classifies as “Chinese military companies” that help Beijing to build its military. That news comes courtesy of Brian Mast, chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who asked BIS to provide information about NVIDIA’s and AMD’s applications for the export licenses required to sell advanced AI chips to China. The congressman on Thursday revealed requests to sell 3.4 million AI chips to China, and that BIS approved the sale of 879,000 items. BIS refused to authorize some giant deals for Nvidia, which applied to sell 610,000 chips to Alibaba and 508,000 to TikTok owner Bytedance. But the agency allowed many other sales, including to Alibaba and Tencent. Mast points out that both of those companies are on the Department of War’s List of Chinese Military Companies , the designation it uses for entities deemed to be a “military-civil fusion contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base.” That’s a polite way of saying that Washington thinks China relies on these companies to operate and improve its military, and therefore to challenge America’s national security. Advanced chips are essential when designing nuclear weapons, stealthy submarines, or advanced aircraft. Those applications are the core reason the US bans exports of advanced GPUs to China, so that the People’s Liberation Army can’t develop advanced weapons. The congressman also claims that some of Nvidia’s applications were attempts to sell its wares to “chip-smuggling fronts to facilitate their sales of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies.” The New York Times reports that some of those front entities are linked to Megaspeed, the outfit fronted by suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang, whose intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a key factor in his resignation. Megaspeed is accused of what the US calls “diversion” – claiming to buy chips for one reason while intending to either ship them to China or rent them exclusively to Chinese companies in ways that breach the spirit of export restrictions if not the letter of the law. One of the documents Mast shared says “Every Nvidia and AMD application stated that the proposed transfer posed a ‘low’ risk of diversion.” Mast’s point therefore appears to be that the BIS has authorized sales that go against the clear intent of established policy, and the national interest, and that Nvidia and AMD may have been a little too optimistic in their assessment of diversion risk. Earlier this week, Washington adopted a new policy that outlaws allowing remote access to advanced AI chips, in the hope it would stop diversion and dent China’s AI ambitions. Two Chinese tech giants, Tencent and Alibaba, have signaled the policy had immediate impact. Chinese web giant Tencent on Wednesday said that new ban will reduce the quantity of advanced compute capacity available to the company and mean its efforts to train models will slow. Alibaba offered similar sentiments on Thursday. Speaking on the company’s earnings call, CEO Eddie Wu said the new policy “will definitely have some impact on the long-term construction of Alibaba Cloud's data centers both domestically and globally.” “Based on our initial assessment, the long-term target of 20 gigawatts may be lowered, which will also lead to a reduction in our overall capital expenditure plan,” he said. But both Tencent and Alibaba don’t see the new policy as creating long-term problems, because both companies believe Chinese chipmakers will be making advanced AI hardware at scale in 2027 or 2028. Alibaba’s Wu predicted his company “will go through a phase of the largest investment in AI infrastructure” once Chinese chipmakers get up to speed. Once that happens, Nvidia and AMD may not even be able to sell chips to China through backdoors. And for what it’s worth, even after the two sultans of silicon went through the front door by asking BIS for permission, many of the approved orders never resulted in shipments. The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) allowed Nvidia and AMD to sell hundreds of thousands of advanced GPUs to entities that the Department of War classifies as “Chinese military companies” that help Beijing to build its military.

That news comes courtesy of Brian Mast, chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who asked BIS to provide information about NVIDIA’s and AMD’s applications for the export licenses required to sell advanced AI chips to China.
The congressman on Thursday revealed requests to sell 3.4 million AI chips to China, and that BIS approved the sale of 879,000 items.
BIS refused to authorize some giant deals for Nvidia, which applied to sell 610,000 chips to Alibaba and 508,000 to TikTok owner Bytedance.
But the agency allowed many other sales, including to Alibaba and Tencent.

Mast points out that both of those companies are on the Department of War’s List of Chinese Military Companies , the designation it uses for entities deemed to be a “military-civil fusion contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base.” That’s a polite way of saying that Washington thinks China relies on these companies to operate and improve its military, and therefore to challenge America’s national security.
Advanced chips are essential when designing nuclear weapons, stealthy submarines, or advanced aircraft.
Those applications are the core reason the US bans exports of advanced GPUs to China, so that the People’s Liberation Army can’t develop advanced weapons.

The congressman also claims that some of Nvidia’s applications were attempts to sell its wares to “chip-smuggling fronts to facilitate their sales of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies.” The New York Times reports that some of those front entities are linked to Megaspeed, the outfit fronted by suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang, whose intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a key factor in his resignation.

Megaspeed is accused of what the US calls “diversion” – claiming to buy chips for one reason while intending to either ship them to China or rent them exclusively to Chinese companies in ways that breach the spirit of export restrictions if not the letter of the law.
One of the documents Mast shared says “Every Nvidia and AMD application stated that the proposed transfer posed a ‘low’ risk of diversion.”

Mast’s point therefore appears to be that the BIS has authorized sales that go against the clear intent of established policy, and the national interest, and that Nvidia and AMD may have been a little too optimistic in their assessment of diversion risk.
Earlier this week, Washington adopted a new policy that outlaws allowing remote access to advanced AI chips, in the hope it would stop diversion and dent China’s AI ambitions.
Two Chinese tech giants, Tencent and Alibaba, have signaled the policy had immediate impact.
Chinese web giant Tencent on Wednesday said that new ban will reduce the quantity of advanced compute capacity available to the company and mean its efforts to train models will slow.

Alibaba offered similar sentiments on Thursday. Speaking on the company’s earnings call, CEO Eddie Wu said the new policy “will definitely have some impact on the long-term construction of Alibaba Cloud's data centers both domestically and globally.”
“Based on our initial assessment, the long-term target of 20 gigawatts may be lowered, which will also lead to a reduction in our overall capital expenditure plan,” he said.
But both Tencent and Alibaba don’t see the new policy as creating long-term problems, because both companies believe Chinese chipmakers will be making advanced AI hardware at scale in 2027 or 2028.
Alibaba’s Wu predicted his company “will go through a phase of the largest investment in AI infrastructure” once Chinese chipmakers get up to speed.
Once that happens, Nvidia and AMD may not even be able to sell chips to China through backdoors.
And for what it’s worth, even after the two sultans of silicon went through the front door by asking BIS for permission, many of the approved orders never resulted in shipments.
That’s likely because Beijing needs to approve imports and chose not to do so while its own chipmakers develop improved products. ®

extraction.body: The Commerce Department approved applications to sell more than 3.4 million chips to the firms, lawmakers say [WASHINGTON] Lawmakers released confidential information on Thursday (Nov 19) showing that the Commerce Department had approved the sale of more than 800,000 advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies for the year, as of May 11, including several firms on a list of Chinese military companies maintained by the Pentagon. The department had received applications to sell more than 3.4 million of the chips to Chinese companies as at that date, lawmakers said. It approved 75,000 AI chips for Alibaba, a Chinese AI giant that The New York Times reported this week has ties with a military-linked laboratory . The release also showed that Nvidia had submitted an application in April to sell more than 40,000 of its advanced H200 chips to a company tied to Megaspeed and Alice Huang, the executive who US intelligence has concluded was a Chinese asset who had an affair with the former Nvidia CEO. The company – New Century Lettall Data Service – is part of a network of Chinese companies with ties to Megaspeed and Huang. Its historical ownership traces back in part to an investment firm controlled by Huang’s sister, where Kang Wei, whom Huang often introduced as her husband, was also executive director. The Commerce Department also approved 150,000 chips for Chinese tech conglomerate Tencent and its subsidiaries; 43,000 for Baidu, another Chinese AI firm; and 4,000 for BYD, a carmaker, the lawmakers said. They were Nvidia’s H200 chips and the equivalent from the chipmaker AMD, the MI325X. The lawmakers from the House Foreign Affairs Committee took special note of the Commerce Department’s approval of sales to the companies Maginfra, Beijing New Matrix Information Technologies and Aivres Systems. The committee cited reporting by The New York Times that had raised questions about those firms because of their ties to sanctioned entities and noted that many of the licence requests from Nvidia had listed the companies as entities that might install the systems in data centres. Two reports from The New York Times first raised concerns about the firms in September and October, saying that Aivres was the subsidiary of a sanctioned Chinese firm that had exported billions of dollars of advanced Nvidia chips to Megaspeed, the company at the centre of the Nvidia scandal. The New York Times reporters also visited the China offices of Maginfra and New Matrix and found them to be empty. No one present had heard of the firms, and scant information existed about them online, raising questions about whether they really existed. The revelations that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was having an affair with Alice Huang, along with a second woman at Nvidia, forced him to step down last week . The Justice and Commerce Departments said this week that Megaspeed was under criminal investigation for potentially smuggling chips into China. The incident has sparked criticism from lawmakers that the Trump administration, and the Commerce Department in particular, did too little to police the flow of sensitive technology to China. Officials both in the administration and on Capitol Hill have criticised the department for maintaining close ties to Nvidia, which it is charged with regulating. The Commerce Department has defended its processes, saying that it closely follows national security regulations. Every Nvidia and AMD application also stated that the proposed transfer posed a low risk of diversion, the committee’s release said. John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, said that all the company’s shipments were legal and authorised by the government, and that, despite receiving some licences, Nvidia had already stopped shipping H200s to China. Nvidia “did not and will not” ship an H200 to the company linked to Megaspeed, or any other company, he said. A spokesperson for AMD said the company complied with applicable U.S. laws and regulations and had a rigorous process to ensure compliance. A spokesperson for the Commerce Department said the disclosure was evidence of the department’s transparency with Congress about licensing activity. Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. government agencies, he said. President Donald Trump approved the sale of the H200 to China in December under unusual conditions. He required the chips, which are assembled in Taiwan, to be routed through the United States on their way to China, so that the government could collect a 25 per cent tariff on their value and perform a security check. Wary of the arrangement and eager to promote its own technology, the Chinese government ended up approving few purchases from its firms. Nvidia said in its earnings this week that it would halt sales of its H200 chips to China, though it did not give a reason for the move. In its statement, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said that withholding the information was “contrary to the national interest”. The committee plans to hold hearings next month with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and his deputy Jeff Kessler, who has had a special role in approving license applications. Rep Brian Mast who chairs the committee, called Maginfra and New Matrix “fake companies”, and said that if the Commerce Department granted approvals to the firms, “obviously that is of tremendous concern to us”, he said. Rep Gregory W Meeks said that the public deserved to know how decisions to sell technology to China were made, and that Congress needed to “conduct rigorous oversight”. “Over the past month, the administration’s handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk,” he said. extraction.body: See more of our coverage in your search results. An alleged Chinese spy developed a “close relationship” with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, setting off alarms among US intelligence officials who were secretly monitoring her communications, according to a report. The woman, Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen who has served as a top executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer and cloud partner that provides AI computing power to Chinese companies including Alibaba, the New York Times reported Thursday. US intelligence agencies concluded that Alice Huang — seen in photos enjoying whiskey and dining with the tech titan — was secretly funneling information to Beijing, according to the paper, which cited people briefed on classified intelligence findings. US electronic surveillance identified Jensen Huang as one of Alice Huang’s contacts, but the report offered no evidence that he knew of her alleged intelligence activities. The Times could not determine what information she passed along or how valuable it was to Chinese authorities. The report did not address whether the relationship was romantic in nature. Photos posted online in June 2024 showed the duo at a Taipei, Taiwan, bar after a local tech show, where they reportedly quaffed whiskey with other AI bigshots. They were also seen together in May 2025 , exiting a Taipei restaurant following a business dinner with AI suppliers. In a video of the scene, Alice Huang is seen standing a few feet behind the Nvidia boss with a big grin on her face while he banters with local journos. US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions that it helped Chinese firms circumvent US export restrictions and smuggle advanced Nvidia chips into China, the Times reported. Megaspeed operates as a middleman, purchasing Nvidia chips through the US arm of Inspur, a Chinese server manufacturer, and renting computing power from its Southeast Asian data centers to Chinese companies, according to the Gray Lady. Inspur’s parent company has been blacklisted by Washington for funneling technology to China’s military, although its American subsidiary remains free of sanctions, according to the Times. Nvidia is the world’s most valuable publicly traded company, boasting a market capitalization of roughly $5.2 trillion. Its advanced chips have become the backbone of the artificial intelligence boom, giving Huang enormous clout in Silicon Valley and Washington as the US races to maintain its technological edge over China. The feds have banned Nvidia from selling its best chips to Chinese companies for years. Jensen Huang is married to Lori Mills Huang, whom he met while studying electrical engineering at Oregon State University. The couple has two children, Spencer and Madison, both of whom work at Nvidia. President Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings roughly a year ago but chose not to take action, according to the Times, which added that he was wary of disrupting Nvidia’s lucrative chip sales and further complicating trade relations with China. Jensen Huang has cultivated close ties with Trump , attending a high-dollar donors’ dinner at Mar-a-Lago, Fla., with his wife, personally lobbying the president to allow Nvidia to continue selling chips to Beijing, the Times reported. Nvidia subsequently donated at least $20 million to Trump’s White House ballroom fund, according to a person familiar with the matter cited by the Times. The chipmaker also pledged to invest $500 billion in US manufacturing — a top Trump priority — while Huang successfully pressed the administration to loosen restrictions on AI companies and chip exports to China. Although US officials initially believed Jensen Huang did not know of Alice Huang’s alleged espionage activities, some senior Trump administration officials now doubt that the Nvidia boss “could have remained unaware” of her intelligence-gathering role for Beijing, according to the Times. It remains unclear whether US intelligence agencies have formally changed their assessment. Nvidia pushed back against suggestions that Jensen Huang’s dealings with the alleged Chinese intelligence operative were suspicious, describing Megaspeed as a typical regional cloud customer. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected,” an Nvidia spokesperson told The Post. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” The company insisted that its regional cloud customers receive “ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets” and “zero information relevant to national security.” Nvidia also said it regularly receives government updates about potentially problematic individuals and companies, adding that it “always” takes appropriate action. “We’re confident that if the US government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know,” the spokesperson said. The chipmaker also rejected allegations that its technology was being diverted through Megaspeed, saying the claims were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.” It maintained that Beijing has blocked American AI chips rather than sought them through regional cloud providers. “China opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called ‘Chinese spy’ narrative,” Chinese embassy spokesperson Liu Chang told The Post. “We urge the US to stop its malicious efforts to block and suppress China and its groundless smears and slanders, and do more things that are conducive to sci-tech exchanges and cooperation between the two countries.” The Post has sought comment from the White House and Megaspeed.

extraction.body: Not many of them made it in, but Chinese clouds no longer care The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) allowed Nvidia and AMD to sell hundreds of thousands of advanced GPUs to entities that the Department of War classifies as “Chinese military companies” that help Beijing to build its military. That news comes courtesy of Brian Mast, chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who asked BIS to provide information about NVIDIA’s and AMD’s applications for the export licenses required to sell advanced AI chips to China. The congressman on Thursday revealed requests to sell 3.4 million AI chips to China, and that BIS approved the sale of 879,000 items. BIS refused to authorize some giant deals for Nvidia, which applied to sell 610,000 chips to Alibaba and 508,000 to TikTok owner Bytedance. But the agency allowed many other sales, including to Alibaba and Tencent. Mast points out that both of those companies are on the Department of War’s List of Chinese Military Companies , the designation it uses for entities deemed to be a “military-civil fusion contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base.” That’s a polite way of saying that Washington thinks China relies on these companies to operate and improve its military, and therefore to challenge America’s national security. Advanced chips are essential when designing nuclear weapons, stealthy submarines, or advanced aircraft. Those applications are the core reason the US bans exports of advanced GPUs to China, so that the People’s Liberation Army can’t develop advanced weapons. The congressman also claims that some of Nvidia’s applications were attempts to sell its wares to “chip-smuggling fronts to facilitate their sales of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies.” The New York Times reports that some of those front entities are linked to Megaspeed, the outfit fronted by suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang, whose intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a key factor in his resignation. Megaspeed is accused of what the US calls “diversion” – claiming to buy chips for one reason while intending to either ship them to China or rent them exclusively to Chinese companies in ways that breach the spirit of export restrictions if not the letter of the law. One of the documents Mast shared says “Every Nvidia and AMD application stated that the proposed transfer posed a ‘low’ risk of diversion.” Mast’s point therefore appears to be that the BIS has authorized sales that go against the clear intent of established policy, and the national interest, and that Nvidia and AMD may have been a little too optimistic in their assessment of diversion risk. Earlier this week, Washington adopted a new policy that outlaws allowing remote access to advanced AI chips, in the hope it would stop diversion and dent China’s AI ambitions. Two Chinese tech giants, Tencent and Alibaba, have signaled the policy had immediate impact. Chinese web giant Tencent on Wednesday said that new ban will reduce the quantity of advanced compute capacity available to the company and mean its efforts to train models will slow. And for what it’s worth, even after the two sultans of silicon went through the front door by asking BIS for permission, many of the approved orders never resulted in shipments. The department had received applications to sell more than 3.4 million of the chips to Chinese companies as at that date, lawmakers said. It approved 75,000 AI chips for Alibaba, a Chinese AI giant that The New York Times reported this week has ties with a military-linked laboratory . The release also showed that Nvidia had submitted an application in April to sell more than 40,000 of its advanced H200 chips to a company tied to Megaspeed and Alice Huang, the executive who US intelligence has concluded was a Chinese asset who had an affair with the former Nvidia CEO. The company – New Century Lettall Data Service – is part of a network of Chinese companies with ties to Megaspeed and Huang. Its historical ownership traces back in part to an investment firm controlled by Huang’s sister, where Kang Wei, whom Huang often introduced as her husband, was also executive director. The Commerce Department also approved 150,000 chips for Chinese tech conglomerate Tencent and its subsidiaries; 43,000 for Baidu, another Chinese AI firm; and 4,000 for BYD, a carmaker, the lawmakers said. They were Nvidia’s H200 chips and the equivalent from the chipmaker AMD, the MI325X. The lawmakers from the House Foreign Affairs Committee took special note of the Commerce Department’s approval of sales to the companies Maginfra, Beijing New Matrix Information Technologies and Aivres Systems. The committee cited reporting by The New York Times that had raised questions about those firms because of their ties to sanctioned entities and noted that many of the licence requests from Nvidia had listed the companies as entities that might install the systems in data centres. Two reports from The New York Times first raised concerns about the firms in September and October, saying that Aivres was the subsidiary of a sanctioned Chinese firm that had exported billions of dollars of advanced Nvidia chips to Megaspeed, the company at the centre of the Nvidia scandal. The New York Times reporters also visited the China offices of Maginfra and New Matrix and found them to be empty. No one present had heard of the firms, and scant information existed about them online, raising questions about whether they really existed. The revelations that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was having an affair with Alice Huang, along with a second woman at Nvidia, forced him to step down last week . The Justice and Commerce Departments said this week that Megaspeed was under criminal investigation for potentially smuggling chips into China. The incident has sparked criticism from lawmakers that the Trump administration, and the Commerce Department in particular, did too little to police the flow of sensitive technology to China. Officials both in the administration and on Capitol Hill have criticised the department for maintaining close ties to Nvidia, which it is charged with regulating. The Commerce Department has defended its processes, saying that it closely follows national security regulations. Every Nvidia and AMD application also stated that the proposed transfer posed a low risk of diversion, the committee’s release said. John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, said that all the company’s shipments were legal and authorised by the government, and that, despite receiving some licences, Nvidia had already stopped shipping H200s to China. Nvidia “did not and will not” ship an H200 to the company linked to Megaspeed, or any other company, he said. A spokesperson for AMD said the company complied with applicable U.S. laws and regulations and had a rigorous process to ensure compliance. A spokesperson for the Commerce Department said the disclosure was evidence of the department’s transparency with Congress about licensing activity. Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. government agencies, he said. President Donald Trump approved the sale of the H200 to China in December under unusual conditions. He required the chips, which are assembled in Taiwan, to be routed through the United States on their way to China, so that the government could collect a 25 per cent tariff on their value and perform a security check. Wary of the arrangement and eager to promote its own technology, the Chinese government ended up approving few purchases from its firms. Nvidia said in its earnings this week that it would halt sales of its H200 chips to China, though it did not give a reason for the move. In its statement, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said that withholding the information was “contrary to the national interest”. The committee plans to hold hearings next month with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and his deputy Jeff Kessler, who has had a special role in approving license applications. Rep Brian Mast who chairs the committee, called Maginfra and New Matrix “fake companies”, and said that if the Commerce Department granted approvals to the firms, “obviously that is of tremendous concern to us”, he said. Rep Gregory W Meeks said that the public deserved to know how decisions to sell technology to China were made, and that Congress needed to “conduct rigorous oversight”. “Over the past month, the administration’s handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk,” he said. extraction.body: See more of our coverage in your search results. An alleged Chinese spy developed a “close relationship” with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, setting off alarms among US intelligence officials who were secretly monitoring her communications, according to a report. The woman, Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen who has served as a top executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer and cloud partner that provides AI computing power to Chinese companies including Alibaba, the New York Times reported Thursday. US intelligence agencies concluded that Alice Huang — seen in photos enjoying whiskey and dining with the tech titan — was secretly funneling information to Beijing, according to the paper, which cited people briefed on classified intelligence findings. US electronic surveillance identified Jensen Huang as one of Alice Huang’s contacts, but the report offered no evidence that he knew of her alleged intelligence activities. The Times could not determine what information she passed along or how valuable it was to Chinese authorities. The report did not address whether the relationship was romantic in nature. Photos posted online in June 2024 showed the duo at a Taipei, Taiwan, bar after a local tech show, where they reportedly quaffed whiskey with other AI bigshots. They were also seen together in May 2025 , exiting a Taipei restaurant following a business dinner with AI suppliers. In a video of the scene, Alice Huang is seen standing a few feet behind the Nvidia boss with a big grin on her face while he banters with local journos. US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions that it helped Chinese firms circumvent US export restrictions and smuggle advanced Nvidia chips into China, the Times reported. Megaspeed operates as a middleman, purchasing Nvidia chips through the US arm of Inspur, a Chinese server manufacturer, and renting computing power from its Southeast Asian data centers to Chinese companies, according to the Gray Lady. Inspur’s parent company has been blacklisted by Washington for funneling technology to China’s military, although its American subsidiary remains free of sanctions, according to the Times. Nvidia is the world’s most valuable publicly traded company, boasting a market capitalization of roughly $5.2 trillion. Its advanced chips have become the backbone of the artificial intelligence boom, giving Huang enormous clout in Silicon Valley and Washington as the US races to maintain its technological edge over China. The feds have banned Nvidia from selling its best chips to Chinese companies for years. Jensen Huang is married to Lori Mills Huang, whom he met while studying electrical engineering at Oregon State University. The couple has two children, Spencer and Madison, both of whom work at Nvidia. President Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings roughly a year ago but chose not to take action, according to the Times, which added that he was wary of disrupting Nvidia’s lucrative chip sales and further complicating trade relations with China. Jensen Huang has cultivated close ties with Trump , attending a high-dollar donors’ dinner at Mar-a-Lago, Fla., with his wife, personally lobbying the president to allow Nvidia to continue selling chips to Beijing, the Times reported. Nvidia subsequently donated at least $20 million to Trump’s White House ballroom fund, according to a person familiar with the matter cited by the Times. The chipmaker also pledged to invest $500 billion in US manufacturing — a top Trump priority — while Huang successfully pressed the administration to loosen restrictions on AI companies and chip exports to China. Although US officials initially believed Jensen Huang did not know of Alice Huang’s alleged espionage activities, some senior Trump administration officials now doubt that the Nvidia boss “could have remained unaware” of her intelligence-gathering role for Beijing, according to the Times. It remains unclear whether US intelligence agencies have formally changed their assessment. Nvidia pushed back against suggestions that Jensen Huang’s dealings with the alleged Chinese intelligence operative were suspicious, describing Megaspeed as a typical regional cloud customer. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected,” an Nvidia spokesperson told The Post. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” The company insisted that its regional cloud customers receive “ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets” and “zero information relevant to national security.” Nvidia also said it regularly receives government updates about potentially problematic individuals and companies, adding that it “always” takes appropriate action. “We’re confident that if the US government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know,” the spokesperson said. The chipmaker also rejected allegations that its technology was being diverted through Megaspeed, saying the claims were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.” It maintained that Beijing has blocked American AI chips rather than sought them through regional cloud providers. “China opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called ‘Chinese spy’ narrative,” Chinese embassy spokesperson Liu Chang told The Post. “We urge the US to stop its malicious efforts to block and suppress China and its groundless smears and slanders, and do more things that are conducive to sci-tech exchanges and cooperation between the two countries.” The Post has sought comment from the White House and Megaspeed.

sources.title: Nothing's Screen-Free AI Device Spotted in Leaked Photo Ahead of December Launch - BigGo Finance
passages: Nothing's upcoming AI device, which the company has said will ship without a screen, has surfaced in a photo posted online, offering the fullest view yet of a product expected to be unveiled next month.
The design language echoes Nothing's existing hardware, which pairs transparent casings with visible light strips.
Leaker Yogesh Brar also identified the device as Nothing's coming AI product, according to the reports.
Once added, BigGo Finance appears first in Google Search Top Stories, so you get the broadest, most up-to-the-minute, and most comprehensive global financial news first.
What is known is that the gadget lacks a display and carries a large button labeled "Talk" alongside the record key, pointing to voice-driven features such as live translation and note-taking.
Nothing has not announced pricing or a release date beyond the December window.
The image came from Sebastian Ingrosso, a DJ and member of Swedish House Mafia, who shared it on X with a tag pointing to Nothing's account.
It shows a small rectangular unit roughly the size of a pack of gum, split down the middle.
The right side carries red and green indicator lights and a record button, matching a teaser that Nothing co-founder Carl Pei posted earlier this month.
Two units appear to be stacked in the shot, and the bottom section shows a pogo-pin connector, though it is unclear what accessories would attach to it.

Said device has no screen and apparently has multiple physical buttons.
The ‘@nothing’ tag confirms it’s the same device.
