extraction.body: John Deere announced on November 19, 2026 that it acquired Orchard Robotics, which operates as Orchard AI, bringing plant-level crop intelligence for specialty-crop growers into its precision-agriculture operations. Financial terms were not disclosed. Orchard AI is a San Francisco-based agricultural technology company founded in 2022. The acquisition combines its crop-level information with Deere’s equipment and farm-technology expertise. Tim Marquis, Deere’s director of Farm Systems Innovation, explained the operational connection: “This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field.” Orchard AI’s system uses vehicle-mounted, AI-powered cameras to collect data on individual trees, vines and plants throughout the growing season. Deere said the system analyzes hundreds of images per tree on each pass, producing yield estimates, fruit counts, fruit-size and color data, canopy measurements and other crop-condition information. Its FruitScope software lets growers visualize those measurements and apply them to farm-management decisions. Deere said the platform is intended to improve the efficiency of labor, time and inputs by giving growers a detailed view of conditions across their operations. Those details matter because months of work and investment can depend on decisions made within narrow windows. A missed spray application or mistimed harvest can affect fruit quality, yield and an entire season’s profitability. Weather, labor constraints and changing crop conditions add further pressure when growers must determine what each block needs and complete the work. Deere said the combined capabilities could inform pruning and thinning, place crop treatments where they are needed and identify blocks ready for harvest. In one example, the integrated software identifies areas with higher bloom counts and generates a prescription showing where to spray. Recommendations could be delivered to a mobile device for in-field application or to an in-cab G5 display. Deere described these delivery routes as possibilities for the integrated technology. Tyler Klick of Redwood Empire Vineyard Management was an early user of Orchard AI’s technology. He said its crop scans gave him greater visibility into vineyard conditions and provided useful precision-farming insights. Orchard AI CEO Charlie Wu said joining Deere would accelerate the company’s mission, with the aim of extending AI-powered crop intelligence to growers globally. Justin Rose, president of Deere’s Worldwide Agriculture & Turf Division for Small Ag & Turf, said Deere wants to preserve Orchard AI’s speed of innovation and close, direct customer relationships while using Deere’s scale and capabilities to reach more growers. The operational value of the acquisition depends on converting plant-level measurements into timely work in the field. Deere’s challenge is to extend that capability to more specialty-crop operations while retaining the development speed and customer relationships it identified as Orchard AI’s strengths. Financial terms were not disclosed. Orchard AI is a San Francisco-based agricultural technology company founded in 2022. The acquisition combines its crop-level information with Deere’s equipment and farm-technology expertise. Tim Marquis, Deere’s director of Farm Systems Innovation, explained the operational connection: “This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field.” Orchard AI’s system uses vehicle-mounted, AI-powered cameras to collect data on individual trees, vines and plants throughout the growing season. Those details matter because months of work and investment can depend on decisions made within narrow windows. A missed spray application or mistimed harvest can affect fruit quality, yield and an entire season’s profitability. Weather, labor constraints and changing crop conditions add further pressure when growers must determine what each block needs and complete the work. Deere said the combined capabilities could inform pruning and thinning, place crop treatments where they are needed and identify blocks ready for harvest. In one example, the integrated software identifies areas with higher bloom counts and generates a prescription showing where to spray. Recommendations could be delivered to a mobile device for in-field application or to an in-cab G5 display. Deere described these delivery routes as possibilities for the integrated technology. Tyler Klick of Redwood Empire Vineyard Management was an early user of Orchard AI’s technology. He said its crop scans gave him greater visibility into vineyard conditions and provided useful precision-farming insights. Orchard AI CEO Charlie Wu said joining Deere would accelerate the company’s mission, with the aim of extending AI-powered crop intelligence to growers globally. Justin Rose, president of Deere’s Worldwide Agriculture & Turf Division for Small Ag & Turf, said Deere wants to preserve Orchard AI’s speed of innovation and close, direct customer relationships while using Deere’s scale and capabilities to reach more growers. The operational value of the acquisition depends on converting plant-level measurements into timely work in the field. Deere’s challenge is to extend that capability to more specialty-crop operations while retaining the development speed and customer relationships it identified as Orchard AI’s strengths.
